title: Double-Leaf Fire Door Set
subtitle: Commercial + Institutional
text: double-leaf fire door set commercial + institutional the coordinated hardware a pair of fire doors needs to latch: a closer on each leaf and a coordinator that makes them close in the right order. a pair of fire doors with two closers and no coordinator will close in whichever order the springs decide. when the active leaf arrives first it lands on the edge of an open inactive leaf, the latch never reaches the strike, and the assembly stops being a rated fire door — every fire test certificate assumes the door was latched. this set is the three-part answer: a closer sized to each leaf, and the dc02 coordinator across the frame head to hold the active leaf back until the inactive one is home. the coordinator is mechanical — no power, no signal, nothing to drift out of adjustment. sizing is where a set like this is specified wrong. leaf weight, closer capacity and coordinator range all have to agree. the dc02 covers leaves of 55–100kg; the closers below cover 40–85kg, so the usable overlap for a coordinated pair runs from 55kg to 85kg. above 85kg we do not currently make a closer, and the honest answer is that the closer, not the coordinator, is the limit. confirm before ordering: leaf weight and width for both leaves, door thickness, whether the pair is rebated or carries an applied astragal, what hardware sits on the inactive leaf, and the fire rating the assembly has to hold. dc02 ju-093 ju-088 ju-072 ju-073

text: panic bar with outside trim set commercial + institutional a fire door that has to open freely from inside and stay controlled from outside needs two pieces, not one: the push bar and the keyed lever that works through it. this is the pair, and what has to agree between them. a panic bar alone answers only half the specification. it releases the latch from inside under pressure, which is what the escape route requires — but it leaves the outside face blank, and a blank outside face means the door cannot be opened by staff, maintenance or a fire officer without propping it, which is how a rated door ends up wedged. the outside trim is the other half. model 015 is a keyed lever that operates the 310 bar's latch from outside, supplied with three brass keys and suited to doors up to 80mm thick. inside, the 310 is a 900mm painted iron bar with a 1.5-hour fire rating, available in red or black. the reason these are specified together rather than separately is that the trim has to match the bar it works through — the lock case, the spindle and the fixing centers are set by the bar, not by the handle. a trim bought to suit a different bar will mount and will not operate, and the failure is discovered at installation rather than at goods-in. confirm before ordering: the door thickness, the leaf width, the handing, whether the outside lever should be keyed alike with other doors on the building, and the fire rating the assembly has to hold. color is a decision too — the bar is stocked red and black, and red on a corridor that is otherwise black reads as an afterthought. 310 015

title: ANSI Grade 1 or EN 1125: Which Standard Your Exit Device Has to Meet
subtitle: Insight
text: ansi grade 1 or en 1125: which standard your exit device has to meet they are not two grades of the same thing. ansi/bhma a156.3 rates an exit device by cycles and force; en 1125 tests whether a panicking crowd can get out. which one you need is decided by the country your building is in, not by which sounds stronger. a buyer comparing exit devices across two catalogs will see "ansi grade 1" on one and "en 1125 certified" on the other and reasonably assume these are two ways of saying the same thing, one of which is better. they are not comparable at all. they are two regulatory worlds that test different properties for different reasons, and the question is never which is higher, it is which one the authority having jurisdiction over your building will accept. ansi/bhma a156.3 is the american standard for exit devices, and it grades them 1, 2 or 3 by durability. grade 1 is the heavy-duty tier: it survives the most operating cycles and the highest static and dynamic loads. the grade is fundamentally a statement about how long the device will keep working under abuse, which is why an american specifier writes grade 1 for a school corridor and accepts grade 2 for a back-of-house door that four people use a day. in the united states the fire-safety requirement itself comes from a separate document (nfpa 101 or the ibc) and the device also has to be listed for fire doors, usually by ul, if the opening is rated. en 1125 asks a different question entirely. it is the european standard for panic exit devices, and its subject is a crowd that does not know the building, in the dark, pushing. the test that defines it applies force to the bar and asks whether the door releases; the device must open with a single motion, from any point along the bar, without prior knowledge of how it works. that is why en 1125 devices are horizontal bars rather than knobs or levers, the standard is written around the behavior of a body moving at speed, not around a hand. ## the en 1125 classification code, and the digits that decide a purchase an en 1125 certificate does not say "certified" and stop. it carries a ten-digit classification code, and each digit records a separate property that was tested. a buyer who reads three of those digits will catch most of the mismatches that reach site. durability: en 1125 sets this as a graded cycle count: grade 6 is 100,000 cycles and grade 7 is 200,000. on a school or a stadium concourse this is the digit to read first, because it is the one that separates a device that survives the building from a device that survives the handover. door mass: also graded, and it is the digit most often ignored on a glazed or steel leaf: grade 5 covers doors up to 100kg, grade 6 up to 200kg, grade 7 above 200kg. a device rated for a 100kg leaf on a 180kg steel fire door is uncertified in that position no matter what the front of the certificate says. suitability for fire and smoke doors: a separate digit again, and not implied by any of the others. a device can be fully en 1125 compliant and carry no fire-door approval at all, the two are tested under different regimes and a fire opening needs both. type of operation: this digit distinguishes the push bar from the push pad, and it is a specification decision rather than a style one. we have a whole article on which to choose and why the choice changes with door width; the relevant point here is that the code records which one was tested, and a report for one does not cover the other. two more digits describe the projection of the bar into the doorway and the corrosion regime it was tested to, worth checking on a narrow corridor and on a coastal building respectively. we are naming the digits that decide a purchase rather than reproducing the standard. the report is the authority, and reading it against the specific project is a five-minute job that belongs to whoever signs the schedule. the distinction that catches buyers out is the one between en 1125 and en 179. both are european, both cover escape hardware, and they are not interchangeable. en 1125 is for panic situations: public buildings where the occupants are strangers to the layout, cinemas, shopping centers, schools, stadiums. en 179 is for emergency situations: buildings where the occupants know the exits, such as offices and staff-only areas, and where a lever handle or a push pad is acceptable because nobody will be pressing against the door in a crowd. specifying en 179 hardware on a public assembly door is a compliance failure even though the hardware is certified, because it is certified for the wrong situation. so the selection rule is short. if the project is in the united states, canada or a market that follows the american model, you need ansi/bhma a156.3 at the grade the specification calls for, plus a ul fire listing if the door is rated. if the project is in europe, the united kingdom, or one of the many markets (much of latin america, the gulf, parts of africa and asia) that have adopted the european standards, you need en 1125 for public buildings and en 179 where the occupants are familiar with the exits. nothing about the mechanism changes the answer; the country does. ## "en 1125 certified" is not a specification it is a claim, and it is the line that produces most of the arguments at inspection. a specification is the claim plus the four things that make it checkable against what arrives in the crate. the standard and the operation type: en 1125 or en 179, and push bar or push pad. this decides the hardware category before anything else does, and it follows from who uses the building rather than from what looks better on the drawing. the two graded digits that the building imposes: durability for the traffic, door mass for the leaf. both are project facts the specifier already knows and the supplier cannot guess, a 200kg steel leaf is not something anybody infers from a model number. the fire route, stated separately: if the opening is rated, say so and say what evidence is required: the device's own suitability for fire and smoke doors, and the rating of the assembly it sits in. these are two documents, not one, and asking for them together at tender is cheaper than discovering at handover that only one exists. the exact model, in the exact configuration: model number, outside trim, latch, and any strike or coordinator it works with. per the point above about tested assemblies, this is the line that makes the certificate mean something: a report against a model you did not order proves nothing about the one you did. written out, that is one line in a schedule rather than a page. something close to: *en 1125 panic exit device, push bar, durability grade 7, door mass grade 6, suitable for fire and smoke doors, model and trim as scheduled, certificate to be supplied against the model number on the order.* a supplier who can answer that line has a product. a supplier who answers it with a photograph of a certificate for a different model has answered a different question. two practical consequences follow, and both cost money when they are missed. the first is that certification covers a tested assembly, not a shape. a device certified with a particular latch, a particular outside trim and particular fixings is certified in that combination; swapping the trim for a cheaper one, or fitting the bar with a strike it was not tested against, voids the claim even though every part looks the same. when you ask a supplier for a certificate, ask which model and which configuration it covers, and check the model number on the report against the model number on your order. the second is that the door matters as much as the device. a fire-rated opening is a rated assembly (leaf, frame, hinges, closer, seals and exit device together) and a certificate for the device alone says nothing about the assembly. on a double door, the sequence in which the two leaves close is part of that assembly, which is why a door coordinator is a safety component rather than an accessory. ordering two single-point devices for a pair of doors produces a pair that does not seal, and an inspector will fail it. ## who actually decides, and what a supplier cannot tell you neither standard decides anything by itself. what decides is the authority having jurisdiction over the building: the body that signs off the fire strategy and issues the occupancy certificate. a standard is the language that authority accepts; it is not the authority. that has a consequence worth stating plainly, because it cuts against the interests of anybody selling hardware. we cannot tell you what your inspector will accept. a factory knows what its devices were tested to and can hand you the report. it does not know your local code, your insurer's schedule, or what the fire officer on that district has asked for on the last three projects. a supplier who answers "yes, that complies" about a building they have never seen is telling you something they are not in a position to know. so the order of the questions is: the authority first, the standard second, the model third. in practice that means the fire strategy or the tender document names the standard, the specifier turns it into the classification digits above, and only then does a model number enter the conversation. buyers who run it in the other direction (pick the device, then look for a standard that fits it) are the ones who discover at inspection that the certificate is for the right product in the wrong category. one more thing that catches projects in markets that have adopted european standards without being in europe. a standard and a marking regime are two different things. a device can be tested to en 1125 by a laboratory anywhere; whether a particular market additionally requires a specific conformity marking, a named notified body or a local approval is a question for the authority in that market, and the answer varies. ask the tender what evidence it wants, not just what standard it names. none of this makes the choice hard. it makes the sequence fixed, and a fixed sequence is what stops a compliant device arriving on a door it is not certified for. where canton hyland stands, plainly. we manufacture push-bar exit devices across fire-door, alarmed, multi-point, exterior-trim and special-application types. en 1125 test reports exist for specific models, and much of what we make is tested in our customers' names, at their cost, so for the model you name we will tell you which report covers it and whose name it is in. we do not hold ansi/bhma certification today. ce and ansi testing in our own name is being prepared, and until it is issued we say so rather than implying otherwise; a supplier who claims both for the same product without two sets of reports is claiming something no laboratory issued. if your project is american-specified, tell us at inquiry stage and we will tell you honestly whether we can serve it now. if it is european-specified, ask for the report against the exact model you intend to buy, and read the model number twice. 001 023 et 027 301-s 309-d 310 316-d 320

title: A Brass Piano Hinge Is Usually Not Brass
subtitle: Insight
text: a brass piano hinge is usually not brass in this trade "brass piano hinge" almost always names the finish, not the metal. ours is iron under a matt black or polished brass finish, in 1", 1-1/4", 2" and 3" widths, and our own catalog claimed stainless steel until 16 september, which is a good illustration of how the confusion survives. search for a brass piano hinge and almost everything you find will be an iron hinge with a brass finish on it. that is not a scam and it is not sloppy writing by the suppliers; it is how this product has been named in the trade for a century. but it is the reason a buyer can order what they believe is a solid brass continuous hinge and receive a steel one that looks identical, and the difference only appears in year three, on the outside of a building, as rust bleeding out from under the plating. a piano hinge (a continuous hinge, in a specification) is one long hinge instead of three short ones. it runs the whole height of the leaf, so the load is carried along the entire edge rather than concentrated at three knuckles. that is why it turns up on piano lids, on lockers, on toolbox lids, on access panels and on any door that is thin, long or handled roughly enough that a conventional butt hinge would eventually tear out of it. because it carries load everywhere rather than at three points, the material matters less for strength than people assume and more for corrosion than people expect. an iron continuous hinge is stiffer than a brass one of the same section (brass is the softer metal) so "upgrading" from iron to solid brass is not a structural improvement. what solid brass buys is that the metal under the surface is the same metal as the surface, which is the whole question on an exterior or a coastal opening. this is the same trap our article on finish codes describes in the north american system, and it is worth naming as one idea rather than two. in ansi/bhma a156.18, 626 is satin chrome on a brass base and 652 is satin chrome on a steel base: identical in a photograph, different in every other respect. "brass piano hinge" is that distinction collapsed into a product name, and the name keeps the half that photographs well. our own catalog had it wrong, and it is worth saying exactly how wrong because it shows what the error looks like from the inside. the record read model "brass piano hinge", material "stainless steel 304", and a width field that had been mangled in an import into `1"1-1/4 "2 "、3"`. three claims, and no two of them could both be true. it stayed that way until somebody searched for what buyers were actually typing, found the query, and looked at the record behind it. what it says now is what the factory told us on 16 september 2026: the leaf is iron. the widths are 1 inch, 1-1/4 inch, 2 inch and 3 inch. the photograph on that page shows two of them, one in matt black and one in a polished brass finish, and the brass one is the reason the model is called what it is. the stainless steel claim is gone, because it was never true. what we still do not publish on that record is the part a specifier needs next: the length it is supplied in, the leaf thickness, the pin material, the knuckle pitch and any load figure. those are five dashes, not five estimates. we know the hinge is iron and we know the four widths; we have not been given the rest, and a leaf thickness invented from a photograph is exactly the kind of number that gets a submittal rejected. ask and we will go back to the factory with your question rather than answering it ourselves. for the wider range, counted on 22 september 2026: this site publishes 29 hinge records. nineteen are stainless steel in various grades, four are iron (the brass piano hinge, bl027, ih01 and f100 ss), two are solid brass (b024 and b025), and four carry no material row yet. if your specification says brass and means the metal, say so in those words, because a finish code will not carry that meaning and a model name plainly does not either. if it says brass and means the color, an iron or stainless leaf with a polished brass finish is cheaper, stiffer and entirely legitimate, as long as everybody knows which one was ordered. ## one more name that does not match its metal recounting the range for the paragraph above turned up one more case of exactly the problem this article is about, and it would be odd to write about names that mislead and then leave it unmentioned. it is the f100 ss. the ss in the model name reads as stainless steel; the material row on the record says iron. one of those two is wrong, and we do not yet know which. until the factory confirms it, treat the f100 ss as unconfirmed on material and ask before ordering it anywhere corrosion matters. the four hinge records with no material row at all (aah024, bl029, ssh021 and the record titled stainless steel door hinge) are the other half of the same lesson. a hinge called stainless steel with an empty material row is a name, not a specification. until the row is filled, treat the material as unconfirmed, whatever the title says, and ask for it in writing. the same applies to any supplier, not only to us. ## how to tell what a hinge is made of none of this should depend on trusting a label, ours included, so here are the checks a buyer can make with a sample in hand. a magnet: iron and ordinary steel are strongly magnetic; brass and copper are not magnetic at all. that one test separates a brass-finished iron hinge from a solid brass one in a second. stainless steel is the complication: grade 304 is essentially non-magnetic as annealed but can become slightly magnetic where it has been bent or worked, and grade 201 is often weakly magnetic. so a weak pull means "probably stainless, check the grade", a strong pull means iron or steel, and no pull at all on a yellow hinge means brass or copper. a cut edge or a hole: plating covers the faces; it does not always cover the inside of a screw hole or a cut end. look there, or file a small hidden corner. brass is yellow all the way through. a plated iron hinge shows gray under the color. weight, with care: brass is denser than steel, so a solid brass hinge is noticeably heavier than a steel one of the same size, but only in a side-by-side comparison of identical dimensions, which is rarely what you have. the document, not the page: for a project, ask for the material in writing against the model number and finish on your order. a test report or a mill certificate for the material is better still. a product page (including this one) is a description; the purchase order is the specification. ## continuous hinge or butt hinges a piano hinge is the right answer on a long, thin or roughly handled leaf, but it is not automatically the better hinge. butt hinges are easier to adjust, easier to replace one at a time, and the normal choice on a standard door. ball-bearing butt hinges carry a heavy or frequently used leaf smoothly at three or four points, and our range lists them by size with a bearing count in the model code, the 4bb suffix on many of the records above. a continuous hinge earns its place where the leaf itself is the weak point: a lid or panel that would twist between three hinges, a locker door that is slammed a thousand times a term, an access panel where tamper resistance matters because there is no exposed knuckle to attack. on a conventional timber door, three good butt hinges usually outperform a continuous hinge of doubtful material. ## what a continuous-hinge specification has to say because this is a product that is so often misnamed, the specification has to carry more than usual. the material, in words ("solid brass", "stainless steel 316", "iron with polished brass finish") rather than a color or a name. the finish, separately. the length, and whether it is supplied in stock lengths to be cut or cut to size. the open width, which is what our 1, 1-1/4, 2 and 3 inch figures describe. the leaf thickness, the pin material and whether the pin is fixed or removable. and the hole pattern, if the hinge has to meet existing holes. we can answer the first two and the width for the brass piano hinge today, and not the rest. write the rest into your inquiry anyway: each unanswered line is a question we will take to the factory rather than a number we will estimate for you. ## where the metal question actually costs money indoors, a plated iron hinge and a solid brass one can serve side by side for decades and nobody will ever know which is which. the difference is paid for outdoors: on an exterior door, a garden gate, a boat, anything within reach of salt air or a swimming pool. there the plating is eventually breached (at a knuckle that wears, a screw head that is driven, an edge that is knocked) and what happens next depends entirely on the metal underneath. iron rusts and stains the finish around it; solid brass darkens but does not bleed. for those openings the choice is really between solid brass and a suitable stainless grade, and our article on stainless steel grades 304, 201 and 316 covers which grade belongs where. brass piano hinge bl027 ih01

title: NBR 11742 and NBR 11785: What a Brazilian Inspection Checks on Fire Door Hardware
subtitle: Insight
text:
nbr 11742 and nbr 11785: what a brazilian inspection checks on fire door hardware a fire door in brazil is approved twice, once in the laboratory and once at the avcb inspection, and the hardware is part of both. what the two abnt standards ask of a push bar and a pair of doors, what inspectors fail, and what to ask a supplier before the first container. in brazil, a fire door is approved twice. the first time in a laboratory, when it is tested to abnt nbr 11742. the second time in the building, when the fire department inspects it for the avcb, the certificate that lets the building open. the certificate's name changes from state to state; the inspection does not. hardware is part of both, and it is the second one where it usually fails. this is written for anyone who sells, installs or maintains fire doors in brazil and buys hardware from abroad. it explains what the two standards ask of the hardware, what the inspection checks in practice, and what to ask a chinese supplier, us included, before the first container. it does not replace the abnt text: whoever signs an inspection report has to read the standard. ## nbr 11742: the door, and everything fixed to it nbr 11742, revised in 2018, covers the fire-rated emergency exit door on vertical-axis hinges: classification, manufacture, identification, installation, maintenance and testing. the door is classified by its fire resistance in minutes, in classes such as p-60, p-90 and p-120, with no intermediate classes. for a hardware buyer, three points matter. first, the door is tested with its hardware fitted, so replacing a hinge, a lock or a push bar with another model changes the assembly that was tested. second, on a pair of doors, the 2018 revision, as brazilian door makers summarize it, requires a closing sequence selector, so the active leaf closes after the inactive one. third, the door leaves the factory identified, with its maker, the standard's number, the year, the batch and the model, and with the photoluminescent sign obrigatório manter fechada (keep closed). ## nbr 11785: the push bar nbr 11785 is the push bar standard, and it classifies a bar three ways. by actuation: push or touch. by locking: horizontal, vertical, or horizontal and vertical. and by use: class c for an emergency exit door with no fire rating, class f for a fire door, and class h for doors in very frequent use. two practical consequences follow. the bar on an nbr 11742 door is class f; a class c bar on a fire door is a mistake the schedule does not show and the inspection does. and since the 2018 revision, the bar has to span at least 50% of the leaf width. on a 900mm (35-7/16") leaf, a 450mm (17-11/16") bar is the minimum, however well a shorter one is made. ## what the inspection checks at an avcb inspection, the hardware failures repeat: a push bar that is jammed, chained, padlocked, or needs too much force; a closer that does not bring the door home to the stop; a worn hinge or the wrong type; damaged intumescent seals; and a product with no traceable origin or no report. four of the five are maintenance. the fifth is purchasing, and it is the only one that starts before the door is hung. that is where the supplier comes in. a bar that works perfectly but whose report does not name the exact model fails for lack of paper. the right question to a supplier is not whether the product is good. it is what is written, about which model, and in whose name. ## what to ask before you order | question | why it matters | our answer today |
| --- | --- | --- |
| is the bar class f to nbr 11785? | a fire door requires class f | we hold no nbr 11785 test in our own name. the test can be done in the name of the brand that sells the bar |
| does the report name the model, and whose name is it in? | a report on another model does not cover yours | we show what exists, with issuer, reference and model covered |
| how long is the bar? | at least 50% of the leaf width | 650 to 1110mm depending on the model; the 320 and 330 are made to the length ordered |
| does the pair latch top and bottom? | neither leaf should depend on the other to stay shut | 316-d, 320, and the 309-d set for both leaves |
| is there a closing sequence selector? | required on pairs by the 2018 revision | dc02, for leaves of 55–100kg | ## the honest route for a private label for a brand selling under its own name in brazil, the route that works is this: choose the model, receive samples identical to production, test them at an accredited laboratory in your brand's name, and only then order the container, with the same model, the same material and the same finish as the tested sample. we supply the samples, the drawings and the data sheet. if a detail of the product has to change to pass the test, we change the tooling. what we do not do is say a product meets a brazilian standard before somebody has tested it. a fire door is only as good as the weakest part fixed to it, and the inspector knows that. better to find out on the sample than on the day of the avcb. 320 316-d 309-d dc02 314

title: Entrance, Privacy, Passage: Choosing Between Twelve Cylindrical Locks
subtitle: Insight
text: entrance, privacy, passage: choosing between twelve cylindrical locks 587, 607, 5807, 5870, 592, 598, 575, 578, 9210, 595, 609 and 5831 look like twelve choices and are mostly one choice made twelve times. nearly all of them take a 60/70mm adjustable backset and a 35–45mm (1-3/8" to 1-3/4") door, so the decision is function first, chassis second, and one of the twelve goes to a 90mm (3-9/16") backset when the others stop at 70. a cylindrical lock (a knob or lever set that fits two bored holes rather than a mortised pocket) is the commonest lock in the world, and choosing one from a catalog is harder than it should be because the model numbers do not tell you what differs. this piece takes the twelve numbers in our own selected range and says plainly which decisions actually separate them. the first thing to know is how much they have in common. across 607, 592, 598, 575, 595 and 609 the backset is stated as 60mm (2-3/8") or 70mm (2-3/4") adjustable and the door thickness as 35mm (1-3/8") to 45mm (1-3/4") adjustable. that is not laziness in the data; it is the point of a bored lock. one part covers the two backsets the world installs, and the same part covers most residential and light commercial door thicknesses, so a specification error on either of those two rows is recoverable on site rather than in a container. one correction to earlier versions of this page: the 587 was listed here with the same backset and door range, but none of its eleven records publishes either row, so it has been taken out of that sentence until the factory confirms them. so the real first decision is function, and there are three that cover most doors. entrance is keyed on the outside and always free on the inside. privacy is the bathroom and bedroom function: a turn button inside, no key, and a small emergency release outside. passage is not a lock at all, it latches the door and has no locking function in either direction, which is what you want on a corridor door that has to stay closed against smoke but must never trap anybody. then there is a fourth group that most catalogs bury, and it is the one an institutional project needs. the 5807 is published with functions named communication lock, classroom lock and exit latch. a classroom function keys from the corridor side only, so a teacher can lock the door from inside the room without a key being required to leave it. if your specification names a school, a clinic or a hall of residence, look at the 5807 first, because the other eleven in this range are specified around the entrance-privacy-passage set. the chassis is the second decision and it is mostly a decision about the building's traffic. most of these are stainless steel; the 5870 is published in one variant as iron plus stainless steel and in another as stainless steel 304/201; the 592 and 595 are published as brass or stainless steel, which means the base metal is a choice the buyer has not made yet. that last point matters more than it reads, a finish specification written in bhma numbers cannot be answered until the base metal is settled, for the reason set out in our article on finish codes. the 5831 is the outlier and it is the reason a range this size exists at all. its backset is published as 60, 70, 80 or 90mm (3-9/16") adjustable and its door thickness as 35 to 50mm (1-3/8" to 1-15/16"), where the rest of the range stops at 70mm (2-3/4") and 45mm. that is a lock for a thicker leaf and a deeper stile, a security door, a heavier timber door, a door where the ironmonger has already discovered that a 70mm backset puts the knob too close to the edge. if a survey comes back with a backset over 70, this is the number to quote. the 5870 sits between the two: 60mm (2-3/8")/70mm on some variants, 70mm only on others, and a door thickness published as 35–50mm (1-3/8" to 1-15/16") rather than 35–45mm (1-3/8" to 1-3/4") on one variant. if you are standardizing a project on one part number, that difference between variants is worth confirming against the specific finish code you are ordering, because it is not constant across the model. one honest gap. the 9210 is in this selected range and carries four published variants, and it has no specification rows at all, no backset, no door thickness, no function. we are not going to fill those in by analogy with its neighbors, because a backset copied from a similar-looking lock is exactly the kind of plausible number this site refuses to publish. if the 9210 is the one you want, ask us and we will measure it against the drawing. ## reading the model code: finish first, function last the twelve numbers stop looking like twelve choices once you read the letters after them. on most of this range the suffix is two pairs: the first pair is the finish and the last pair is the function. 587 mbet, 587 mbbk and 587 pbps are one lock body in two finishes and three functions, et is entrance, bk is the privacy (bathroom) function with a turn button inside, and ps is passage. the finish pairs follow the same logic: on the 575 and 598 pages ac is published as antique copper (us11), ss as satin stainless steel (us32d) and sn as satin nickel. the commercial models carry longer function codes because they carry more functions. the 5807 is published as sscl (communication), sscr (classroom), ssel (exit latch) and ssr (storeroom); the 5870 adds sscc, published as entrance and communication. these are our codes, not an industry standard, so the rule on a purchase order is simple: quote the full code, and check it against the function row on the product page rather than decoding it from memory. a two-letter slip between et and ps is the difference between a door that locks and one that cannot. ## light duty or heavy duty: what the label actually changes the range divides into two lines, and it is worth being exact about what separates them, because the obvious assumption is wrong. the 587 and 578 are published as light duty, for standard residential use. the 5807, 5870 and 5831 are published as heavy duty, for commercial offices, schools and heavy-duty residential doors. what does not separate them in our data is the cycle figure. wherever a cycle row is published, on either line, it reads 200,000 cycles, and both with a solid steel chassis and latch case, zinc plated. so the cycle number is not a reason to choose one over the other on this site, and we would rather say so than let a buyer infer a difference we have not published. what the data does show is a different trim construction (wrought stainless steel or brass on the light-duty line, zinc die-cast electroplated or solid brass on the heavy-duty line) and a different intended application. neither label is a test grade. light and heavy duty are our own application guidance; they are not an ansi/bhma grade, and nothing on this page should be read as a claim to one. if your specification calls for a graded cylindrical lock, the specification is asking for a certificate, and the answer to that is a document, not a model number. ## the functions that get misread on site entrance, privacy and passage are rarely confused. the three that cause trouble are the institutional ones, because each looks like a lock you already know. storeroom, in the usual meaning of the term, is locked on the outside at all times and opened only by key, while the inside stays free, right for a plant room or a stock room, wrong for an office, where a person who steps out without a key is locked out every time. classroom locks from the corridor side by key. communication is the connecting-door function, and it is the one most often ordered by name without anyone checking which side does what. for those three, do not rely on the name. ask for the function description of the specific code on the specific door, and put it on the door schedule next to the door number. it costs a line on a spreadsheet and removes the single most common reason a cylindrical lock is swapped after installation. ## keying a building's worth of them the 578 and the heavy-duty models are published with a 5-pin tumbler cylinder, a brass plug and two nickel-plated brass keys; the 587 is published with a solid brass or zinc-and-brass cylinder and no pin count, so ask if the pin count matters to your keying. on every one of them the latch is deadlocking on keyed functions. the light-duty 587 and 578 are published as able to be keyed alike to our deadbolt series or master keyed; the heavy-duty entries are published as able to be keyed alike to deadbolts. if a heavy-duty door needs to sit inside a master key system, say so at inquiry rather than assuming it, because that is exactly the kind of capability we will not claim on a page until it is written against the model. the practical point is timing. keying is done when the cylinders are pinned, which is before the locks are packed, so a keying schedule that arrives after the order is an order that has to be reopened. decide which doors share a key, which doors need a master, and which doors must never open to anyone else's key, and send that with the door schedule. our article on master key systems sets out how many levels a building actually needs. ## the strike and the frame one row almost nobody reads until the latch fails to catch: the strike. on the 575, 592, 595, 598 and 607 it is published as a 57mm (2-1/4") curved lip as standard, with a 70mm (2-3/4") lip available on request. the lip guides the latch bolt over the frame as the door closes. where the frame has a wide stop or a deep casing, a short lip lets the latch strike the frame edge instead of riding onto the plate, and the door has to be pushed shut. if your frames are anything other than a plain timber lining, measure the stop and the casing and ask for the longer lip at the same time as the lock, not after the first complaint. handing is the one decision you do not have to make. every variant in this range that publishes a handing row is fully reversible, left or right hand, so a door schedule does not need a handing column for those. the few variants with no handing row (the 5807 commercial codes among them) are worth one question before the order. for a quotation, three rows settle it: the function on each door, the backset your survey found, and the leaf thickness. finish comes after those three and never before, because the finish never changes what fits and the first three always do. send a door schedule if you have one; we will answer it line by line rather than sending a catalog back. 607 acbk 587 mbet 5807 sscl 5870 acet 592 sset

title: Cross-Referencing a Lock You Already Buy
subtitle: Insight
text: cross-referencing a lock you already buy a lot of the searches that reach us are somebody else's model number, another factory's rim lock, another brand's hinge, a part code off an old invoice. they are all the same question: what do i order to get this again. six dimensions decide the answer, and the model number is not one of them. look at the search terms that bring people to a hardware factory's site and a pattern appears immediately: a great many of them are another company's model numbers. a rim lock from one brand, a concealed hinge from another, a latch code off a twenty-year-old carton, a part reference from a catalog that is out of print. nobody types those hoping to read about us. they type them because they have a part that works, the supplier is gone or slow or expensive, and they need to know what to order to get the same thing again. it is a good question and it has a precise answer, which is that a lock is defined by its geometry and not by its name. two locks with the same six numbers are interchangeable regardless of what either is called. two locks with the same name and one different number are not. for a mortise lock, those six are: backset, from the face of the door to the center of the spindle; center distance, between the spindle and the cylinder or keyhole; faceplate length and width; case height and depth; spindle size, almost always 8mm (5/16") square but worth confirming; and door thickness range. get those six and the substitution works. miss the center distance and the handle and the cylinder will not both line up with the holes already cut in the door, and the door is the thing you cannot change. for a rim lock or night latch the list is shorter but the same in character: backset, case size, whether the cylinder is single or double, latch extension, and the strike type, because a rim strike and a rim deadbolt keeper are different castings and the frame is already prepared for one of them. for a hinge: leaf height and width, knuckle count, pin type, and whether it is a fixed pin or loose. a hinge that is 3mm (1/8") taller than the mortise already routed into the frame is a hinge that does not fit, and nothing about the finish or the grade changes that. what does not carry across, and should be ignored when cross-referencing: the model number itself, the finish name, and the grade designation. finish naming is not standardized between factories (one supplier's satin nickel is another's brushed nickel is another's sn) so match a finish by looking at a sample rather than by matching a word. grade designations are standard-specific: an ansi grade and an en classification measure different things under different tests and neither translates into the other by arithmetic. the practical route, and it is short. measure the part you have, or photograph it beside a ruler with the faceplate visible. send those numbers, the door thickness, and whether it is a left or right hand door. our engineering desk will come back with the model that matches, or (and this is the part worth saying) with a straight answer that we do not make one. a near-miss recommended as an equivalent is how a container of unusable metal happens, and we would rather lose the line than send it. one more thing, for anyone replacing a part in an existing building rather than specifying a new one: check the strike and the keep before you order the lock. in a retrofit the frame is the constraint, not the door, and the item that most often makes a substitution fail is not the lock body at all, it is the strike plate cutout, which was made for the old part and will not be remade. ## what a complete set of numbers looks like it helps to see the six mortise numbers written out for a real part, because it shows how little is needed and how exact it has to be. our lc07 85×45mm publishes them like this: center distance 85mm (3-3/8"), backset 45mm (1-3/4"), faceplate 240 × 23mm (9-7/16" × 7/8"), case height 173mm (6-13/16"), case depth 72mm (2-13/16"), with a latch throw of 26mm (1") and a bolt projection of 18.5mm (3/4"). measure your existing lock to that level of detail and a match (or a clear "we do not make one") is a single reply away. notice that the model name carries two of those numbers (85 and 45) and that this is common across the trade. it is a convenience, not a guarantee: a case named 85 × 45 by one factory can still differ from another's in faceplate length or case depth, which is exactly why the other four numbers matter. ## measuring a mortise lock you have removed if the lock is out of the door, the measurements are quick and a steel rule is enough. backset: from the outer face of the faceplate to the center of the spindle hole. measure to the face of the faceplate, not to the case behind it: the difference is the faceplate thickness, and it is enough to put a lever off-center on the door. center distance: from the center of the spindle hole to the center of the cylinder hole or keyhole. faceplate: overall length and width, and whether its ends are square or radiused, because a radiused faceplate goes into a routed recess that a square one will not fill. case: height and depth, measured on the case body. spindle: across the flats of the square hole. door thickness: from the door, at the lock position. then note the two things that are not dimensions but still decide the match: the latch direction (which way the bevel faces) and whether the lock has a deadbolt as well as a latch, and how far it throws. ## measuring a lock that is still in the door often the lock cannot come out until the replacement has arrived. in that case the faceplate length and width, the backset (from the door edge to the spindle center) and the center distance (spindle to cylinder, measured on the door face) can all be taken with the lock in place, and they are the four that matter most. case height and depth can usually be inferred from the faceplate and the door, but say that they are inferred rather than measured, so the engineer answering knows which numbers are certain. ## photographs that actually help a photograph is a good substitute for a measurement only if it is taken to be measured from. photograph each face square-on, not at an angle, with a ruler lying in the same plane as the part (against the faceplate, not in front of it). include one photograph of the faceplate end-on, one of the case side with any markings, and one of the strike on the frame. markings stamped into a case or a faceplate are often the fastest route to an identification, so make sure they are legible. if there is no ruler to hand, a coin or a bank card of known size in the same plane is far better than nothing. ## when a near-miss can still work not every mismatch is fatal, and it is worth knowing which ones sometimes can be managed and which never can. a faceplate slightly shorter than the old recess can sometimes be covered with a packing or cover plate. a case slightly shallower than the old pocket can usually go into it. a different center distance or backset cannot be managed: the holes through the door are already drilled, and a lever or cylinder in the wrong place is visible on both faces for the life of the door. so if a reply says "this one fits except for the faceplate", it is worth a conversation. if it says "this one fits except for the center distance", it does not fit. ## cross-referencing the parts around the lock the same principle (geometry first, names ignored) works for the other parts people most often need to replace, but each has its own short list. a euro cylinder is matched by profile, overall length and split: a 70mm cylinder can be 35/35 or 30/40, and those are different parts. then the cam, and whether it is a double cylinder, a key-and-thumbturn or a half cylinder. our articles on euro cylinder length and split, and on our 45-to-90 range, go through the details. a pull handle is matched by center distance first (the distance between its fixing points) because only that decides whether the new handle uses the existing holes. overall length, grip diameter and projection come next, and on a glass door the hole size in the glass, which cannot be changed. a hinge, as above, by leaf height and width, knuckle count and pin, and on a replacement by the exact size of the recess already routed into the frame. a door closer is the part where a like-for-like is least likely by name alone: match the fixing centers on the door and frame, the arm type, and the closing power for the leaf, and expect that a closer from a different maker will usually need a new fixing plate rather than dropping onto the old holes. in every case, the photographs and measurements described above are what turns a part number we do not recognize into a part we can match, or into a straight answer that we do not make it. the short version, for any part: measure it, photograph it square-on beside a ruler, note the door it came from, and send all three together. a name alone gets a guess. numbers and pictures get a match, or an honest no, which is worth almost as much, because it sends you to the right supplier the same day instead of after a container has landed. lc07 85×45mm 5681 ssh017

title: A 25mm Throw and a Collar That Spins: Deadbolts D101 and D102
subtitle: Insight
text: a 25mm throw and a collar that spins: deadbolts d101 and d102 a deadbolt does one job the latch above it cannot: it throws a solid bolt that no card and no shim will move. ours throw 25mm (1"), in zinc die-cast with a hardened steel roller pin against sawing, on a five-pin solid brass cylinder, and the free-turning collar is the detail that matters most and photographs least. a deadbolt is the second lock on a door, and it exists because the first one cannot do this job. a latch is sprung, so it can be pushed back; a deadbolt is thrown by a key or a turn and has no spring behind it, which means the only way past it is through the bolt, the door or the frame. everything worth specifying about one follows from that sentence. the throw is the first number and ours is 25mm (1") on both the d101 and the d102. twenty-five millimeters is the figure most specifications mean when they ask for a full-throw or one-inch deadbolt, and the reason it is a specification at all is the frame: a bolt that engages less than about 20mm (13/16") can be forced by spreading the jamb, which is a two-minute attack with a car jack that does not look like forced entry afterwards. the bolt itself is published as zinc die-cast with a hardened steel roller pin. the roller pin is the anti-saw feature and it works mechanically rather than by hardness alone: a hacksaw blade drawn across it makes the pin rotate, so the teeth skate instead of cutting. it is a detail that costs almost nothing to include and is left out of cheap deadbolts, and it is invisible in a product photograph, which is why it belongs in a comparison rather than in a showroom. the cylinder on the d101 is published as a five-pin tumbler with a solid brass plug and two nickel-plated keys. five pins is the residential standard; the plug being solid brass rather than a zinc casting is what lets it be re-pinned cleanly, which matters on any building where keys will be changed between tenants. if your project needs more than five pins or a restricted keyway, that is a different conversation and worth having before the order. the feature that decides more attacks than any of the above is the free-turning cylinder trim. the collar around the cylinder spins freely, so a wrench or a pipe put on the outside of the lock turns the collar and not the mechanism. without it, the commonest forced entry on a deadbolt is simply twisting the whole cylinder out of the door, which takes about as long as it takes to describe. both the d101 and the d102 publish it. both are fully reversible, left or right hand, and both publish an internal chassis of zinc-plated steel with exposed trim available in stainless steel, brass or steel. finishes differ between the two: the d101 is published in antique brass (us5) and antique copper (us11) among others, the d102 in antique copper and polished brass (us3). those us numbers are the older convention; antique finishes are relieved rather than uniform, so they are not translatable to a single bhma number, for the reason set out in our finish-code article. the row that turns these from a component into a specification is keying: both are published as keyable to pair with an entrance bored lock. that is what a building actually wants, one key for the lever set and the deadbolt on the same door, rather than a tenant carrying two. it also means the deadbolt has to be ordered in the same keying group as the lock above it, which is a decision taken at order stage and not afterwards. if the door you are working on cannot take a bored deadbolt at all (because it is glazed, because the stile is too narrow, or because it is an existing door nobody wants to drill twice) the rim night latch is the alternative, and we have written that range up separately. a 564 or a 1073 mounts on the face and needs one hole, and the rim deadbolt versions of those throw the same 25mm. it is a different fixing, not a lesser lock. ## the door preparation, and why it matches the lock above two rows decide whether a deadbolt fits the door at all, and on the d101 and d102 they are the same two rows as on our cylindrical locks: a backset adjustable between 60mm (2-3/8") and 70mm (2-3/4"), and a door thickness of 35mm (1-3/8") to 45mm (1-3/4"). that match is deliberate rather than convenient. a door bored for one of our entrance locks at 60mm takes the deadbolt at 60mm too, the two sit in a vertical line, and one key can work both, which is the arrangement the keying row exists to support. outside that door range, say so before the order. a leaf thicker than 45mm needs a longer cylinder and tail piece, and a leaf thinner than 35mm leaves the trim unable to clamp properly. both are solvable; neither is solvable on site with the parts in the box. ## single or double cylinder: a decision about the building the d101 dspb is published as single cylinder, for entrance doors: a key outside, a thumbturn inside. a double-cylinder deadbolt needs a key on both faces, and the argument for it is always the same: glass within reach of the lock, where someone could break a pane, reach through and turn the thumbturn. the argument against it is also always the same, and it is stronger: in a fire, the key has to be found before anyone gets out. many jurisdictions restrict or prohibit double-cylinder deadbolts on doors used for escape, for exactly that reason, and the rule that applies to your door is the local one, not ours. if the glass is the problem, the better fixes are usually to change the glass or move the lock, not to put a key between the occupants and the street. we will supply what the building allows; the decision belongs to whoever answers for the building. ## a 25mm throw only works if the frame holds a full-throw deadbolt is a strong bolt going into a weak place. the bolt passes into the strike on the frame, and the strike is screwed to the frame lining; on many doors that lining is a thin strip of softwood nailed to the structure behind it. kick the door and the bolt does not break, the lining splits and the strike comes away with it. so the most effective security upgrade on a deadbolt costs almost nothing: screws long enough to pass through the lining into the structural frame behind it, at the strike and at the hinges on the opposite edge. that is general practice rather than a feature of our product, and it is worth putting in the installation note on any schedule, because the installer who fits the lock is rarely the person who will be asked why it failed. ## rekeying between tenants both models are published with the cylinder removable for rekeying, and with a solid brass cylinder. that pairing is what makes a deadbolt economical on a rented building: when a tenant leaves, the cylinder comes out and is re-pinned to a new key instead of the whole lock being replaced. it is also why keying belongs in the order rather than after it: a deadbolt ordered to match the lever set on the same door should arrive in the same keying group, and a building that expects to rekey often should say so, so the keying plan leaves room for it. ## what the rest of the family publishes, and what it does not the d101 is published in several finishes, including antique brass (us5), antique copper (us11) and polished brass; the d102 in antique copper (us11), polished brass (us3) and satin stainless steel (us32d). for an exterior door in a coastal climate, satin stainless is the finish to ask about first, and it is worth asking which trim material comes with it, since the trim is published as stainless steel, brass or steel. there is also a keyed deadbolt lock set, published with the same core specification: 25mm throw with the hardened steel roller insert, 5-pin tumbler with a solid brass plug, free-turning trim and keying to pair with an entrance lock. two records in the family publish nothing at all: the d01 ab and the d103 ac carry photographs and no specification rows. we are not going to fill them in from their neighbors. they may well share the d101's throw and backset, but a throw copied from a similar-looking deadbolt is a number nobody tested. if either is the one you want, ask and we will measure it. ## comparing two deadbolt quotations two deadbolts at different prices usually differ in rows that do not show in a photograph, so compare them row by row rather than by picture. the rows that matter, in the order they matter: the throw (25mm or less); an anti-saw insert in the bolt, and what it is made of; free-turning trim around the cylinder; the cylinder, pin count, and whether the plug is solid brass or a casting; whether the cylinder is removable for rekeying; the backset and door-thickness range; the number of keys; and whether it can be keyed to the lock above it. our d101 dspb publishes every one of those rows; the d102 records publish all of them except the pin count, which we will confirm on request. a quotation that leaves several of them blank is not necessarily a worse lock, but it is a lock you are being asked to buy without knowing. for a quotation: the door thickness, whether the deadbolt is single or double cylinder, and whether it is keyed with the lock above it. that third one is the question most inquiries leave out and the one that determines how the keys arrive. d101 dspb d102 ac 564 1073d

title: Why a Double Fire Door Needs a Coordinator, and How to Size One
subtitle: Insight
text:
why a double fire door needs a coordinator, and how to size one a pair of fire doors with two closers will close in whichever order the springs decide. if the active leaf arrives first, the astragal holds it open and the door does not latch, so the assembly is no longer a fire door. a coordinator forces the order. this is what it has to match to work. a single door closes one way. a pair does not. put a closer on both leaves of a double door and each one obeys its own spring, its own hydraulic setting and whatever the wind is doing in the corridor at that moment, so the two leaves arrive in whichever order they happen to arrive. on an ordinary pair of doors that is untidy. on a fire door it is the difference between a rated assembly and a hole in a wall. the reason is the overlap. a double fire door has an astragal or a rebate where the leaves meet, and that overlap belongs to the inactive leaf: the active leaf must close on top of it. if the active leaf gets there first, it lands against the edge of an open inactive leaf and stops. the latch never engages the strike. what you are left with is a door that looks shut, is not latched, and will be pushed open by the pressure difference a fire creates long before the leaf itself fails. every fire test certificate in the world assumes the door was latched. a door coordinator is the mechanical answer. it sits across the top of the frame, holds the active leaf back while the inactive leaf completes its swing, and then releases it. there is no power, no signal and no adjustment to drift: an arm is held, then it is let go, in the right order, every time. the canton hyland dc02 works this way, zinc-plated steel, 397 × 120mm (4-3/4") across the frame head, supplied with two support brackets and its fixings. the part that gets specified wrong is the pairing. a coordinator is not an alternative to closers; it is a component that only does anything when both leaves already have one. three items have to agree with each other: the leaf weight, the closer power on each leaf, and the coordinator's rated range. the dc02 is rated for leaves of 55–100kg. pick a closer whose capacity band contains the actual leaf weight, then check that the weight sits inside the coordinator's range as well. from our own closer range, the bands are: ju-051 at 15–30kg on doors to 800mm (31-1/2") wide; ju-061 at 25–45kg to 850mm (33-7/16"); ju-073 at 40–65kg to 850mm (33-7/16"); ju-088 at 40–65kg to 950mm (37-3/8"); ju-072 at 40–65kg to 1050mm (41-5/16"); and ju-093 at 45–85kg to 1050mm (41-5/16"). all are aluminum bodies with a 180° maximum opening angle. the overlap that matters for a coordinated pair starts at 55kg, which is where the dc02's range begins, so ju-072, ju-073, ju-088 and ju-093 are the four that can carry a leaf the dc02 is also rated for. there is a gap in that list and it is better said than discovered on site: above 85kg we do not currently offer a closer. the dc02 is rated to 100kg, and a 90kg leaf is a real specification on a hardwood or steel-faced fire door, but our heaviest closer stops at 85. if your leaves are heavier than that, the coordinator is not your constraint, the closer is, and we would be specifying past our own range to tell you otherwise. ask us and we will say so rather than sell you a pair that cannot hold the door. two more things decide whether the assembly works, and neither is on the coordinator's datasheet. the first is what else is on the inactive leaf: flush bolts or a two-point lock have to be fully home before the active leaf lands, which is the same sequencing problem one component further down. the second is the closing force after coordination, a coordinator adds a restraint to the active leaf's swing, so a closer set at the bottom of its band to feel light in the hand may no longer have the authority to latch against a seal. set the closer for the door, then confirm it still latches with the coordinator fitted. ## two kinds of coordinator, and which one your pair takes catalogs list coordinators as one line. they are two mechanisms with different failure modes, and the choice is made by the head of the frame rather than by preference. bar coordinator: a horizontal bar across the soffit of the frame, held down by the active leaf and released when the inactive one passes. it suits pairs with an astragal on the inactive leaf and needs a frame head deep enough to take the bar without fouling the closers. it is the type most often specified, and the one most often ordered too short, the bar has to span the full clear opening, not the leaf. gravity coordinator: a pivoting arm that drops as the inactive leaf closes. it needs less head depth and is the answer where the soffit is shallow or already crowded, but it is more sensitive to being installed out of level. a gravity unit on a frame that has settled will release early. | | bar | gravity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| needs frame head depth | more | less |
| sensitive to frame level | less | more |
| spans | full clear opening | the inactive leaf only |
| fails as | bar bends, stops holding | releases early, leaves land wrong |
| diagnosing | visible from the floor | needs a ladder | both are held down by the active leaf, so both have a weight range of their own, a coordinator sized for a 40kg leaf will be held open by a 90kg one and never release. ## the astragal decides more than it looks like it does `installation coordinator bars overlapping astragals double doors` is a query that reaches this page, and the phrasing is exact: the astragal is what creates the problem the coordinator solves. the astragal is the vertical strip that closes the gap at the meeting stile. it is fixed to one leaf and overlaps the other, so the leaves can only close in one order. three things follow from that and all three get missed. which leaf carries it decides which leaf is active: the astragal goes on the inactive leaf and the active leaf closes over it. get that backwards on the schedule and the coordinator is fitted to hold back the wrong leaf. its thickness is the gap you see when the order is wrong: a pair that will not quite close, standing open by three or four millimeters, is almost always an astragal problem rather than a closer problem. adjusting the closers will not fix it; they are doing exactly what they were set to do. on a fire pair it is usually intumescent: the strip expands under heat to seal the meeting stile, which means it is part of the rated assembly and cannot be substituted for a plain aluminum one because the plain one fitted. our page on what a test report actually covers sets out why a substitution inside a tested assembly is a change to the test. ## what actually goes wrong, in the order it goes wrong the coordinator is left off the schedule: the most common failure by a wide margin, and it happens because schedules are written leaf by leaf while a coordinator belongs to the pair. neither leaf's row has a place for it. the flush bolts are manual when they should be automatic: the inactive leaf needs holding, and a manual bolt means somebody bends down twice a day. on a fire pair that somebody eventually stops bending, and the inactive leaf is then unsecured. the closers are set to fight the coordinator: if the active closer is faster than the inactive one, the coordinator is holding back a door that wants to arrive first, it will work, and it will wear. set the inactive leaf to close first with margin, then set the active one. nobody checks it after handover: a coordinator is a moving part above head height that nobody looks at. the check takes five seconds: let both leaves go from fully open and watch the order. if the active one lands first, something is out. ## what to send us, and why each field is there both leaf weights and widths, because the coordinator and both closers are sized from them. door thickness, because it sets the astragal and the bolt lengths. whether the pair is fire rated, because that decides whether anything on the opening can be substituted. and a photograph of the frame head, because that one image answers the bar-or-gravity question faster than any description. one sentence closes the whole topic. a coordinator belongs to the opening, not to either leaf, so it needs its own line on the schedule, its own weight check against both leaves, and its own five-second test at handover. every failure above is a version of that line being missing. what to send us when you ask for a quotation: the leaf weight and width for both leaves, the door thickness, whether the pair is rebated or has an applied astragal, what hardware sits on the inactive leaf, and the fire rating the assembly has to hold. with those we can tell you which closer pairs with the dc02 for your doors, or tell you that your leaves are outside what we make, which is an answer we would rather give before the container ships than after. if you supply fire door hardware to installers, ask for the coordinator, the closers and the panic bars for the same pair in one quotation: all three are sized from the same leaf data. that is also the cheapest fix available on a double door: one row added to a schedule, before anything is ordered, rather than a return visit with a ladder after handover. dc02 ju-093 ju-088 ju-072 ju-073 ju-061 ju-051

title: The Door Schedule: How Hardware Is Actually Specified
subtitle: Insight
text: the door schedule: how hardware is actually specified projects do not buy locks. they buy door types, and each door type is a set of hardware that has to agree with itself. the document that decides this is the door schedule, and it is worth understanding before you quote against one. a manufacturer's catalog is organized by product: lock cases here, lever handles there, closers somewhere else. a building is not organized that way. a building is a list of doors, and every door needs a set of hardware whose parts have to agree with each other, the same backset, the same handing, the same fire rating, the same finish. the document that records this is the door hardware schedule, and on a commercial project it is what the order is actually written from. if you sell into projects and have never seen one, this is roughly what a row looks like. a door type, say a fire-rated cross-corridor door leaf. its dimensions and handing. then a hardware set: a lock case with a stated backset and center distance, a lever set on the plate that matches that center distance, a euro cylinder keyed into the building's master system, a pair of hinges rated for the leaf weight, a closer with the right power size, and (because it is on an escape route) an exit device rather than a lock on the egress side. one row. seven line items. every one of them has to be compatible with the other six. two consequences follow, and they are the reason this document is worth understanding. the first is that a project buyer is never comparing your lock against a competitor's lock. they are comparing whether your lock fits the set. a case with an 85 mm (3-3/8") center distance and a 55 mm (2-3/16") backset is either right for the plate and the door preparation already specified, or it is not, and no amount of quality argument moves that. this is why the dimensional questions arrive before the price questions, and why a supplier who answers them slowly loses the inquiry before quoting. the second is that hardware sets are where the quantities live. a schedule does not say two hundred locks. it says thirty of set hw-01, ninety of hw-02, and so on, and each set expands into its line items. a distributor pricing from a schedule needs the sets to expand cleanly into products they can order, which means a manufacturer who can supply the whole set is worth more than a cheaper one who supplies part of it, not because of loyalty, but because a split set means two lead times, two shipments and a coordination risk that lands on the distributor. the practical implication for anyone reading a schedule for the first time: read down the set, not across the catalog. take one hardware set and satisfy every line in it before moving to the next. if a line cannot be matched, say so at that point rather than at quotation, because a set with a gap is more useful to the buyer as an early question than as a late surprise. there are three questions worth asking before you quote against a schedule at all. which sets are on escape routes, because those are governed by regulation rather than preference and the hardware is not interchangeable with the rest. whether there is a master key system, because if there is, the cylinders are a single coordinated order and not a per-door line item. and what the finish is across the project, because finish is usually specified once for the whole building and then repeated silently in every row. ## the columns, and what each one controls schedules vary in layout from one consultant to the next, but the columns that matter are nearly always the same, and each one controls a different decision. door number and location tie the row to the drawings; they are how a site team finds the door and how a query gets answered without confusion. door type and leaf size (width, height and thickness) decide what physically fits: lock case, hinge size, bar length. material of leaf and frame decides the fixings and sometimes the product. fire rating decides whether the whole set is governed by a tested assembly rather than by preference. handing decides which way handed parts are made or assembled. and the hardware set reference points to the list of parts, with a quantity, a finish and usually a remarks column where the keying is recorded. the two columns most often left blank are handing and leaf thickness, and they are the two that most often turn a correct product into the wrong one on site. ## handing on a schedule handing is described in two conventions, and a schedule should say which it is using. north american schedules usually write lh, rh, lhr and rhr (left hand, right hand, and the reverse-bevel versions for doors that open outward). many european schedules instead describe the direction the door closes, clockwise or anticlockwise, seen from a stated side. the two can describe the same door, but a letter from one convention read in the other is a reliable way to receive a full set of handed parts the wrong way round. our article on handing (left, right and universal) goes through both, and why a universal part does not remove the need for the column. the good news for buyers is that many parts are published as reversible. our cylindrical locks, deadbolts, rim locks and most of our tubular lever sets are published as fully reversible, left or right hand, so handing on those is an assembly step rather than a separate part. lock cases, some exit devices, closers and anything with a bevelled latch facing one way are where the handing column still has to be right. ## one hardware set, written out here is the kind of set the row above expands into, written for a hypothetical internal timber door on a single leaf, with an office on one side and a corridor on the other. *hw-02, 1 lock case, 85mm center distance, 60mm backset, euro profile, for timber doors (our lc04 publishes exactly those rows); 1 pair of levers on plate, drilled for an 85mm center distance; 1 euro cylinder, length to suit a 44mm leaf, keyed to the building's master system; 3 hinges, sized to the leaf; 1 door stop, chosen against the lever projection; finish satin stainless throughout.* every line in that set has to agree with at least one other. the levers have to match the lock case's center distance, or the cylinder hole lands in the wrong place. the cylinder length follows the leaf thickness and the lever plates together. the stop follows the lever. the finish has to be the same on all of them, and if hw-02 appears on ninety doors, every one of those agreements is multiplied by ninety. ## mistakes that come from the layout, not the products a schedule is a table, and tables produce their own errors. pairs counted as one door: a pair of doors is usually one row with two leaves, and some parts are per leaf while others are per opening. flush bolts, a coordinator and an astragal belong to the pair; hinges and stops belong to each leaf. a quantity copied straight from the row count will be wrong on every pair. finish specified once and assumed everywhere: the finish is often written in a general note at the top and then omitted from the rows. a supplier reading rows alone will quote the default finish; a supplier who reads the note will quote correctly. read the notes before the rows. keying in the remarks: keying groups are usually in a remarks column or a separate keying schedule, not in the hardware set. a cylinder line with no keying information is incomplete, however carefully the cylinder is specified. revisions: schedules are reissued during a project, and each revision can change sets silently. quote against a stated revision, write that revision on the quotation, and ask for the change list when a new one arrives rather than re-reading the whole document. ## how we reply to a schedule when a schedule arrives, the reply we aim to send is set by set rather than line by line: for each hardware set, whether we can complete it, complete it except for named items, or not complete it, and for every item we cannot supply, which item and why. that reply is usually more useful to a distributor than a priced list, because it shows at once where a second supplier is needed and how much of the project one order can cover. prices follow for the sets we can complete, against the revision we read. ## sending the schedule any format we can read is better than a summary of it, but some are better than others. a spreadsheet export is best, because the sets can be expanded and counted without retyping. a pdf is fine. a photograph of a printed page is enough to start. whatever the format, send the general notes and the keying schedule along with the rows (the notes are where the finish and the fire strategy usually live) and include the revision letter, so that our reply and your next revision refer to the same document. a schedule without its notes is a list of doors; with them, it is a specification we can answer. our catalog is organized by product because that is how a catalog has to be organized. but the inquiries that turn into orders almost never arrive product by product. they arrive as a schedule, or as a photograph of one, and the answer that wins is the one that reads the set rather than the line. if you have a schedule, send it, the useful reply is which sets we can complete, which we can complete except for one item, and which we cannot, and that reply is faster than a line-by-line quotation. 001 lc04 85*60 607 pbbk f100 ss

title: DS013 and DS011 Are Not the Same Kind of Thing
subtitle: Insight
text: ds013 and ds011 are not the same kind of thing somebody searched "door stopper ds013 vs ds011" and landed on us. it is a fair question and the answer is that only one of them is a door stopper, ds011 is a flush bolt, which does the opposite job. here is how to tell three commonly confused items apart before they are on the order. this article exists because of a search. somebody typed "door stopper ds013 vs ds011" into bing and arrived here, and they were right to expect a comparison, the two model numbers sit one apart in our own catalog and look like siblings. they are not. ds013 is a door stopper. ds011 is a flush bolt. they are not variants of one product, they are two different products that happen to be numbered next to each other, and if the numbering misled somebody enough to make them search for a comparison then the honest thing is to publish the answer rather than let them work it out from a photograph. a door stop takes an opening door and stops it before it hits something. that is the whole of the job. ds013 is a zinc alloy floor or wall stop measuring 110 × 66mm (2-5/8"), available in ten finishes. its whole design problem is arresting a moving door without transmitting the shock into the fixing, which is why the working part is rubber and the metal exists to hold the rubber in the right place and survive being kicked. a flush bolt is the opposite. it holds a leaf shut and still, and it is fitted into the edge of the door so nothing protrudes. ds011 is a brass flush bolt in nine finishes. on a pair of doors it is what keeps the inactive leaf from moving so the active leaf has something solid to latch against; without it a double door flexes and the lock never feels right no matter how good the lock is. nothing about it stops a door swinging, that is not what it is for. the third item in this family of confusions is a door holder, sometimes sold as a hold-open. it keeps a door open on purpose, which is not the same as stopping it. a stop is passive and takes an impact; a holder is active and resists a closing force, often a door closer's. specifying a stop where a holder was wanted produces a door that closes every time somebody lets go of it, and the complaint that comes back is "the stopper does not work" when the stopper is working exactly as designed. so the selection is a sequence of three questions, and none of them is about finish. what is the door doing wrong, swinging too far, drifting shut, or moving when it should be still? where can you fix something, floor, wall, or the door edge? and what is the floor made of, because a stop fixed into 6mm (1/4") of tile over screed is a stop that will come out with the tile. for stops specifically, projection is the number that decides whether it works, and it is the one most often left off an inquiry. our range runs from low floor domes to tall wall stops: ds05 is a ø44 × 24mm (15/16") floor dome, ds09 is 42mm (1-5/8") long, ds010 is a ø42mm (1-5/8") dome, and ds01
