is a stainless steel wall stop 96mm (3-3/4") high with a 70mm (2-3/4") projection on a 34mm (1-5/16") base. that 70mm (2-3/4") is not a styling choice, it is the distance between the wall and the point on the door that will hit it, and if the handle projects further than the stop does, the handle finds the wall first. one consequence of that worth stating plainly: a door stop is selected against the handle, not against the door. measure from the wall to the outermost point of the lever or knob when the door is open, and pick a stop at least that long. this is the single most common reason a stop is ordered, installed, and then replaced. and on our own numbering: ds is not a product-type prefix here. it runs across stops (ds01, ds02, ds05, ds09, ds010, ds013, ds022) and it also carries ds011, which is a flush bolt. we would rather say so than let the sequence imply a family that does not exist. when you send an inquiry, name the job ("floor stop, 70mm projection, satin nickel") and the model number becomes a check rather than the whole specification. ## flush bolts: length is most of the specification ds011 is one flush bolt; most of ours are numbered fb, and the question buyers search for (fb005, fb001) is almost always a question about length. a flush bolt on a pair of doors does two jobs, one at the top of the inactive leaf and one at the bottom, and the two are usually different lengths for a reason that has nothing to do with appearance: the top bolt has to be operated by someone standing on the floor. so on a tall leaf the top bolt is long, to bring its lever down within reach, and the bottom bolt is short. that is why the range is published by length rather than as one part. the fb005 is brass in 6, 8, 10, 12 and 24 inch lengths (152, 203, 254, 305 and 610mm). the fb001 family is stainless steel or brass in 8, 10, 12 and 24 inch lengths, and the fb001 ss in 8 inches is published for doors 30–45mm (1-3/16" to 1-3/4") thick. the fb012 is stainless steel from 3 to 10 inches, 30mm (1-3/16") wide. the fb016 is stainless, 7 inches, 24mm (15/16") wide. and our stainless steel flush bolt family, for surface or mortise installation on the inactive leaf of paired doors, is published with a width of 22 and lengths of 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12, without units on that page. they are almost certainly millimeters and inches like their neighbors, but that is a guess, so confirm them with us before ordering. the lengths are in inches because that is how the market orders them, even where the doors are measured in millimeters. write both on the order if there is any chance of confusion; a 10 inch bolt ordered as "10" by someone thinking in centimeters is a very short bolt. width is the second row, and it is about the door edge, not the bolt. a flush bolt is let into the edge of the leaf, so its faceplate has to fit the edge with timber to spare on either side. a 30mm-wide faceplate on a 35mm (1-3/8") leaf leaves very little either side of the plate; the fb016's 24mm (15/16") plate leaves more. on a thin leaf, pick the bolt by its width first and its length second. ## the keep and the socket are part of the bolt a flush bolt engages something: a keep in the head of the frame at the top, and a socket in the floor at the bottom. neither is optional and both are forgotten more often than the bolt. the floor socket in particular has to be set into the floor, and, like the floor keep of a top-and-bottom exit device, it belongs with the floor finish rather than after it. on a pair of doors that people walk through all day, a socket that fills with dirt stops the bolt seating and the inactive leaf starts to move again, which is the very problem the bolt was bought to solve. ask what socket comes with the bolt, and plan for where it will sit before the floor is laid. ## our stops, by type the ds range is small enough to read in full, and grouping it by what each stop actually does makes the choice quick. floor domes and low floor stops sit on the floor where the door face meets them. the ds05 is a stainless steel dome at ø44 × 24mm (1-3/4" × 15/16"), the ds010 a zinc-alloy dome at ø42mm (1-5/8"), and the ds09 a zinc-alloy stop 42mm long and 35mm high (1-5/8" × 1-3/8"). low stops are the least likely to be tripped over and the most likely to be missed by a door with a deep handle, so check the handle before choosing one. the wall stop is the ds01: stainless steel, 96mm (3-3/4") high, with a 70mm (2-3/4") projection on a 34mm (1-5/16") base. it is the one to use where the floor cannot take a fixing, a heated screed or a finished stone floor, or where the door must stop well short of the wall because the handle projects. the ds013 works either way, on the floor or on the wall: zinc alloy at 110 × 66mm (4-5/16" × 2-5/8"), in ten finishes, which makes it the easiest of the range to match to the rest of the hardware on a door. two more are published with their material and finishes but no dimensions yet: the ds02 in stainless steel and the ds022 in zinc alloy. we will not size them from a photograph. ask, and we will measure them against the drawing. what the range does not include is a holder. none of our published stops is described as holding a door open against a closer, so if the door is meant to stay open, that is a question for us rather than a model on this page. when you ask, say how much closing force the holder has to resist, because a light catch loses to a closer every time, and the complaint that follows is always about the wrong product. ## one opening, one list the three products in this article are often bought for the same pair of doors, so it is worth writing them down together. for a typical pair: a long flush bolt at the top of the inactive leaf and a short one at the bottom, with their keep and floor socket; a stop for each leaf chosen against the handle projection; and a holder only if the doors are meant to stay open, with the closing force it has to resist. that is one short list per opening, and it replaces three separate inquiries, each of which, on its own, invites the wrong product. ds013 ds011 ds01 ds05

title: One Opening, One Order: The Hardware Set for a Double Fire Exit Door
subtitle: Insight
text:
one opening, one order: the hardware set for a double fire exit door a double fire exit door takes six lines of hardware, and every one is sized from the same four facts about the leaves. here is the set in the order it has to be decided, the places where two correct lines contradict each other, and what we need to quote it as one opening. most orders for a double fire exit door arrive as a list: push bars, a trim, two closers, a coordinator. every line on that list can be right on its own and the door can still fail on the day it is hung, because the lines were chosen one at a time and the door is judged as a whole. the device on the inactive leaf has to agree with the one on the active leaf. the trim has to fit the device and the door. the closers have to agree with the coordinator, and all of them have to agree with the weight of the leaves. so we treat a double door as one opening and quote it that way. below is the set in the order it has to be decided, the models we make for each line, and the places where two correct lines most often contradict each other. ## start with the leaves, not the catalog four facts about the leaves decide everything that follows: the width and weight of each leaf, the door thickness, and which leaf is active. the active leaf is the one people use every day. the inactive leaf carries the astragal and closes first. width and weight size the closers and the coordinator. thickness sizes the trim and the spindle. the active and inactive split decides which device goes where. a quotation built before these four are known is a guess with prices on it. ## lines 1 and 2: a device on each leaf if both leaves count toward the escape width, both leaves need a device a person can push. an inactive leaf held shut by manual flush bolts cannot be opened by somebody in smoke who does not know the bolts are there, and an inspector will read that leaf as a wall with hinges. on a pair, the usual answer is a device that latches at the head and the threshold on each leaf, so neither leaf depends on the other to stay shut. three of our devices are made for that. the 309-d is supplied as a set for both leaves, active and inactive, with a 1110mm (43-11/16") bar, aluminum alloy and iron, powder-coated. the 316-d latches top and bottom, has an aluminum alloy body in a flame-retardant abs housing, and reverses for left or right hand; its outside lever is optional and priced separately. the 320 is a two-point device engaging head and threshold, non-handed, in red or black, with an 8×8 or 9×9mm spindle. the 306-d is also listed for double doors, but its dimensions are not published yet, so ask before you put it on a schedule. if only the active leaf is an escape route and the inactive leaf opens only to move furniture through, flush bolts on the inactive leaf can be acceptable. that is a decision for the fire engineer on the project, not for the supplier, and it belongs on the schedule in writing rather than in anybody's assumption. ## line 3: the outside trim, on the active leaf the push bar opens the door from inside. anything that has to happen from outside is a separate line: a trim, a lever and plate fitted to the outside face that drives the same latch through a spindle. it goes on the active leaf. the inactive leaf normally has nothing outside, because nobody should be opening it from the corridor. two choices decide the trim. the first is function: keyed, like the 023 et, where a key decides whether the outside lever works, or passage, like the 023 ps, where anybody can walk in. the second is door thickness, because a trim's spindle and fixing screws are made for a range, and the range is printed. the 028 and 037 fit doors of 35–55mm (1-3/8"–2-3/16"), the 039 fits 45–50mm (1-3/4"–1-15/16"), the 015 fits doors up to 80mm (3-1/8") and the x2 up to 90mm (3-9/16"). a 60mm (2-3/8") fire door with a trim made for 55mm is a trim that will not pull up tight to the face. ## lines 4 and 5: a closer on each leaf each leaf needs its own closer, chosen for the leaf it hangs on. our ju range runs from the ju-051 at 15–30kg to the ju-093 at 45–85kg, on leaves up to 1050mm (41-5/16") wide. the two leaves of a pair are often different widths. if they are, the two closers may be different models, and that is correct rather than a mistake. ## line 6: the coordinator the coordinator makes the inactive leaf close first, so the active leaf lands on the astragal and latches. our dc02 is rated for leaves of 55–100kg, which pairs it with four of our closers: ju-072, ju-073, ju-088 and ju-093. the dsl02 is a 304 stainless coordinator with an adjustable closing force; its weight range is not published yet, so ask. our article on door coordinators covers the sizing in detail. the short version is that the leaf weight has to sit inside the closer's band and inside the coordinator's range at the same time, and above 85kg we do not currently make a closer. ## what comes from the door maker the astragal, the intumescent seals and the leaves themselves come from the door maker, and they are part of the tested assembly. so is every device on it. that is the one rule above all six lines: a fire door is tested as an assembly, so the hardware on it has to match what was tested, down to the model. ask for the test report, check that it names the model you are buying, and check whose name it is issued in. much of what we make is tested in our customers' names, at their cost; testing in our own name is being prepared. we would rather you asked than assumed. ## where two correct lines contradict each other | line | against | what goes wrong | what to check |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| trim | door | a trim made for 35–55mm on a 60mm door | door thickness against the trim's printed range |
| trim | device | an 8mm spindle in a 9mm follower | the spindle square on both, in writing |
| closer | coordinator | a 45kg leaf under a dc02 rated from 55kg | leaf weight inside both ranges |
| inactive leaf | active leaf | a panic bar on one leaf, hand-thrown bolts on the other | the escape width on the drawing |
| finish | finish | red push bars, satin trim, a silver coordinator | one finish for the opening, stated once | every row in that table is two lines that were each checked against the catalog and never against each other. none of them is expensive to fix on a schedule. all of them are expensive to fix on a building. ## if you sell openings, not items many of our customers are brands and distributors who sell this set to installers under their own name. for them the set is the product: one quotation, one sheet of leaf data, one finish, and cartons labeled to their specification, by opening if that is how their installers work. ask for the set that way and we will quote it that way. if a line is outside our range, as a closer for a leaf over 85kg is, the quotation will say so, before the container ships rather than after. ## what to send us six things quote the whole opening: the width and weight of each leaf; the door thickness; which leaf is active; whether both leaves count toward the escape width; whether the outside needs a key, free passage or nothing; and one finish. with those, we check every line against every other line before anything is made. 309-d 316-d 320 023 et 023 ps dc02 dsl02 ju-093 ju-072

title: Which Exit Device Standard Your Project Is Actually Under
subtitle: Insight
text: which exit device standard your project is actually under en 1125 and ansi/bhma a156.3 are not two grades of the same thing. they come from different building codes, measure different failures, and a device built to one is not automatically acceptable under the other. the standard is decided by where the door is, not by what you prefer. buyers ask us for "a ce panic bar" or "an ansi grade 1 exit device" as though the two were points on one scale, with ce somewhere below ansi or the other way round. they are not. they are two separate regulatory systems, written by different bodies for different building codes, and the question of which one applies is settled before anyone chooses a supplier, by where the door is and what the authority having jurisdiction there enforces. en 1125 is the european standard for panic exit devices operated by a horizontal bar, on escape routes used by the public. its companion, en 179, covers emergency exit devices operated by a lever or push pad, for buildings where the occupants know the building and are unlikely to panic, a staff corridor rather than a cinema. the distinction is about the people behind the door, not the hardware: en 1125 assumes a crowd pressing forward, which is why the operating element has to run most of the door width and release under a load applied anywhere along it. ansi/bhma a156.3 is the north american standard for exit devices, and it grades products 1, 2 or 3 on a cycle-test basis. a grade 1 device is tested to a higher cycle count than grade 3; both are grade-rated exit devices. that is a durability classification, and it is doing a different job from en 1125's, which is a conformity assessment against a set of pass/fail requirements including fire performance and release force. "grade 1" and "en 1125" are not comparable claims. a device can hold one, both, or neither. fire rating is a third axis again, and the one most often collapsed into the other two. a fire-rated exit device has been tested as part of a fire door assembly, and the certificate covers that assembly (the leaf, the frame, the hinges, the closer and the device together) not the device on its own. this is why a supplier who answers "is it fire rated?" with a simple yes is either simplifying or has not read their own report. ask what assembly was tested, and by whom. so the practical sequence is: where is the door, what does the local authority enforce, is it on an escape route, will the public use it, and is the opening fire rated. those five answers select the standard. only then does the hardware conversation start, and by that point most of the catalog has already been excluded. where we sit in that: our en 1125 test evidence is a report from intertek testing services shenzhen ltd., guangzhou branch, reference 130722068gzu-001, issued 7 november 2013, and it covers one model, kd070/30-290. there is also a ce certificate of conformity to en 1125:2008 from celab in italy, 2010, covering the panic exit device series. we publish both with their exact scope on our certifications page, and we do not present either as blanket approval for every device we make, because it is not. if your specification needs current evidence against the current edition of a standard for a specific model, the honest answer is often that a re-test is required, and it is better to know that before the order than after the inspector asks. one thing worth checking early, whichever standard applies, is whether the device suits the door leaf you actually have. a rim device fixes to the face of the door and needs a strike on the frame. a mortise device needs a lock case pocket cut into the leaf edge. a vertical-rod device throws bolts into the head and threshold and is what a pair of doors with no center mullion requires. getting that wrong is not a compliance problem, it is a physical one, and it is discovered on site. ## single leaf, pair of doors: the device follows the opening our article comparing ansi grade 1 and en 1125 goes through the certificate itself, the classification digits and the one-line specification. this one is about the step before and after the certificate: whether the device physically suits the opening, because a compliant device on the wrong leaf is still the wrong device. on a single leaf the usual answer is a rim device: the bar mounts on the face of the door and its latch engages a strike on the frame. the 316-s is that arrangement, surface mounted, push to open, published for fire doors and emergency exit doors, and reversible left or right. a pair of doors is where specifications go wrong, because the inactive leaf has nothing on the frame to latch into unless there is a center mullion. without one, the latching has to go up and down instead of sideways. the 316-d is published with top and bottom latching for exactly that case. the 320 engages the head and the threshold as a two-point locking device for tall doors or higher security, and its length is made to the customer's request rather than cut from a standard bar. the 309-d is a paired set that coordinates the active and inactive leaf, published with a 1110mm (43-11/16") bar for fire-rated double escape doors. one honest gap here: the 306-d is listed as a double-door device, distinguished from the 306-s by leaf count, and its dimensions are not yet published. we will not size it by analogy with its neighbors, ask, and we will measure it. top-and-bottom latching brings one site consequence that belongs in the specification, not the snag list. a bottom bolt needs a keep in the floor, and that keep has to be set with the floor finish, not drilled into it afterwards. on a stone or resin floor, forgetting it until the doors are hung means cutting a finished floor. ## the outside of the door is a separate decision the device is on the escape side. what happens on the other side is a second choice, and it changes both the price and the part list, so it deserves its own line on the schedule. the options run from nothing at all (an exit-only door with a plain outside face) to a lever that is always free, to a lever that is locked and opened by key. our trims cover that spread. the 023 ps is a passage trim. the 016 is an outside lever with a key, key operated and reversible. the 028 is an external lever with key-operated locking and unlocking. the x2 is a brass trim supplied with three brass keys. the 023 etan is an anti-pick keyed trim for doors where the outside face is exposed to tampering. the row that gets missed is door thickness, because it belongs to the trim as much as to the device. the 028 is published for doors of 35–55mm (1-3/8" to 2-3/16"), the 039 for 45–50mm (1-3/4" to 1-15/16"), the 015 for doors up to 80mm (3-1/8") and the x2 for doors up to 90mm (3-9/16"). a trim that fits the device and not the leaf is a trim that arrives and cannot be fixed. check the leaf thickness against the trim, not just against the bar. and check the quotation, because on some of our devices the outside lever is not part of the price. the 316-s and 316-d are both published with the outside lever as optional and not included in the listed price. comparing that price against a competitor's device-plus-trim figure is comparing half an assembly with a whole one. ## pairs of doors: which leaf closes first a pair of doors with an overlapping astragal (the strip on one leaf that covers the meeting gap) has to close in order. if the leaf carrying the astragal arrives first, the other leaf closes against it and stops short, and on a fire door a leaf that has not latched is a door that has failed. the fix is a door coordinator, which holds the active leaf open until the inactive leaf has closed, and it belongs on the schedule from the start, not after the first failed test. our article on the door coordinator for double fire doors covers the fitting in detail. on the escape side, each leaf still has to open from inside with one movement. that is why a coordinated set such as the 309-d treats the active and inactive leaf as two devices designed to work together, rather than two single devices bolted onto one opening. ## alarms, dogging, and what an authority may refuse two optional functions change what the authority will say about a door. an alarmed device, such as our 314, keeps a door available for escape while discouraging casual use: it is published with key access from outside, push-bar exit from inside and a built-in alarm, in 650, 800 and 1000mm lengths (25-5/8", 31-1/2", 39-3/8") or to order. dogging holds the latch retracted so a door can be pushed freely during opening hours; the 314 lists it as an option. dogging is where specifications meet regulation. a door that must latch to perform (a fire door being the usual case) is commonly not allowed to be held unlatched by the hardware, and some authorities have their own rules on alarmed exits. we supply the function; whether it may be used on a particular door is the authority's decision, and the right time to ask is before the device is chosen. ## the five lines, filled in here is what the door schedule described below looks like when it is actually written for one opening, a hypothetical pair of doors from a school hall onto an escape corridor: *timber leaves, 54mm thick; pair of doors, no center mullion, overlapping astragal; fire rated to the local requirement; the authority enforces en 1125; outside access by keyed lever for staff only.* those five lines alone decide most of the part list: a top-and-bottom latching or coordinated pair device rather than a rim device, a door coordinator because of the astragal, a keyed trim published for a 54mm leaf, and a question to the authority about dogging before anyone offers it. none of that needed a model number to begin with, which is the point. send us the door schedule rather than a product code. what we need is the leaf material and thickness, whether the opening is single or double, whether it is fire rated and to what, which standard the authority enforces, and whether outside access is required, and if so, by lever, by key, or not at all. that is five lines, and it is enough for our engineering desk to name the devices that can actually be specified rather than the ones we would like to sell. 307 305 310 311

title: 70 Is the Total, Not the Split
subtitle: Insight
text:
70 is the total, not the split the number in 70sn is the overall length of the cylinder in millimeters. it says nothing about how that 70mm (2-3/4") is divided either side of the cam, and the division is the part that decides whether the key turns once the door is hung. a euro-profile cylinder is described by one number in almost every catalog in the industry, ours included: 45, 50, 55, 60, 65, 70, 80. that number is the overall length in millimeters, measured end to end. it is genuinely useful and it is genuinely incomplete, because two cylinders of exactly 70mm (2-3/4") can be completely different parts. the cam sits somewhere along that length, the little bar that turns and throws the bolt, driven by the fixing screw that passes through it. the length is divided either side of that cam, and the two halves are quoted as a split: 35/35, 30/40, 40/30. all three are 70mm cylinders. only one of them fits your door. which one depends on what is in front of and behind the lock case. measure from the fixing-screw hole in the edge of the door (that is the cam center) outward to the finished face on each side, and include everything the cylinder has to pass through: the door leaf, any escutcheon or rose, a decorative plate, a security rosette. the outside measurement is the outside half; the inside measurement is the inside half. round each up to the next 5mm (3/16") that a cylinder is actually made in. getting it short is obvious on site: the key will not enter far enough, or it enters and will not turn because the cam cannot clear. getting it long is the more expensive mistake, because it looks fine. a cylinder standing proud of the escutcheon is the single easiest thing on a door to attack (it gives a tool something to grip and lever against) and on an external door that projection is what an insurer or a specification will pick up on. as a working rule, keep projection to about 3mm (1/8") or less on the outside face. this is also why a cylinder is the wrong item to standardize across a mixed order. doors on one project are rarely one thickness: a 40mm (1-9/16") internal leaf, a 45mm (1-3/4") entrance leaf and a glazed screen with a 10mm (3/8") patch fitting all take different splits, and a pallet of one size means somebody on site is going to force something. here is the part of this we should say plainly about our own catalog. our cylinder pages publish the overall length (45mm (1-3/4"), 47mm (1-7/8"), 54mm (2-1/8"), 56mm (2-3/16"), 60mm (2-3/8"), 65mm (2-9/16"), 70mm, 80mm (3-1/8"), 90mm (3-9/16")) the material, the finish options and the key count. they do not publish the split, because the split is an order variable rather than a property of the model. we would rather say that than print a default like 35/35 that would be right often enough to be believed and wrong often enough to cost somebody a container. so the practical route is short. tell us the door thickness and what is mounted on each face, and our engineering desk will come back with the split, or confirm the one you have specified. if you already work in splits, send them as splits, 30/40 outside/inside is unambiguous in a way that "70mm" is not. either way, say which side is outside; a 30/40 and a 40/30 are the same cylinder installed backwards, and backwards means the reinforced half is facing the wrong way. ## the length table `euro cylinder lengths` is one of the queries that brings people to this page, and a paragraph is the wrong shape for that answer. here is the table. the euro profile is measured from the center of the fixing screw hole, outward in both directions. the overall length is the two halves added together, and the smallest half the profile physically allows is 27.5mm, which is why 55mm is the shortest double cylinder that exists anywhere. | overall | standard splits available | suits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 55mm | 27.5/27.5 | the thinnest door the profile can serve |
| 60mm | 30/30 | a common flush timber door |
| 65mm | 30/35 | one face thicker than the other |
| 70mm | 30/40 · 35/35 | the most common length on site |
| 75mm | 35/40 | a deeper escutcheon on one side |
| 80mm | 30/50 · 35/45 · 40/40 | thick leaf, or a security rose outside |
| 85mm | 35/50 · 40/45 | rebated or panelled doors |
| 90mm | 40/50 · 45/45 | thick leaf with deep furniture both sides | two things to read out of that table rather than from the bare number. the same overall length is several different cylinders: a 70mm can be 30/40 or 35/35, and they are not interchangeable on a door whose two faces differ. ordering "70mm" without the split is ordering one of two or three parts and hoping. the steps are 5mm, and they are not negotiable: there is no 62.5mm cylinder, because each half moves in 5mm increments from 27.5. a door that lands between two sizes takes the next size up, and the cylinder stands proud by the difference, which is why the rounding rule only ever goes one way. ## our nine lengths, and the one row we cannot fill our catalog publishes cylinders in nine overall lengths: 45, 47, 54, 56, 60, 65, 70, 80 and 90mm. the 70mm is the largest group by a wide margin, nineteen of the forty-five records. the three short ones (45, 47 and 54mm) sit below the 55mm double-cylinder floor, which tells you something the catalog does not say outright: they are single-sided. a 45mm overall cannot be two halves of at least 27.5mm each. and here is the row we cannot fill. across all forty-five cylinder records, the number that state an inside and outside half is zero. not one publishes its split. we publish the overall length and stop. that is a gap rather than a policy, and it is the reason the ordering route below is what it is. until the splits are measured and published, the only honest way to get the right cylinder is to tell us the door and let us size it, which is slower than reading a table and is better than guessing at one. ## what the length number does not tell you four things decide whether a cylinder is right, and only one of them is in the number. the split, as above, which half goes outside. the keyway: every cylinder in one master key system must share a keyway, and a keyway is a physical profile, not a preference. two cylinders of identical length from two suppliers will not accept each other's keys. the pin count and the security features: six pins is not five pins, an anti-drill insert is not standard, and a reinforced cam is a different part. none of these appear in a length. the cam: the bar that actually throws the bolt comes in more than one shape and angle, and the wrong cam in a correct-length cylinder will turn without moving anything. so a length alone is the beginning of a specification rather than the whole of one. send the overall length you measured and the model of the lock it goes into, and the remaining three fall out of that pair. ## four forms, and why the length is written differently for each the same profile is sold in four forms, and the length convention changes between them. this is where a correct-sounding order still arrives wrong. double cylinder, keyed both sides. the length is the two halves added: 30/40 is a 70mm. both numbers matter and the order of the pair matters, because the first is conventionally the outside. half cylinder, keyed one side only, blank the other. the blank end is a fixed 10mm stub on most profiles, so a "45mm half" is 10 plus a 35mm keyed half. half cylinders go into rim locks, cabinet locks and anything where the inside face is not accessible or not wanted. thumbturn cylinder, keyed outside, turn inside. sized exactly like a double, but the turn projects beyond the escutcheon and that projection is not part of the length. do not add it and do not subtract it; size the half to the escutcheon face as normal and let the turn stand proud. one-sided with a fixed knob, less common, and the one most often confused with a thumbturn on an order. it does not rotate a cam from inside at all. the practical consequence is a single line on the purchase order. name the form, then the split. "70mm double, 30/40" cannot be misread. "70mm" can be, and on a door with a thumbturn it usually is. ## if you are replacing rather than specifying take the old cylinder out before you order, if the building lets you. one screw in the edge of the door releases it; the cylinder then slides out once the key is turned a few degrees to clear the cam. with it in your hand, measure from the center of that screw hole to each end separately. those two numbers are the split, and they are the thing a catalog length cannot give you. write them down in the order outside-first, and photograph the cam end beside a rule. what not to do is measure the old cylinder end to end and order that number. it gives the overall and discards the split, which is the half of the information that decides whether the new one fits the same way round. one last thing worth confirming at the same time, because it costs nothing to ask and it is the second most common cylinder omission: keying. our cylinders ship keyed to differ with three keys as standard, and five is available. keyed alike within a group, or a master key suite across a building, is a decision that has to be made before the cylinders are pinned, not after they arrive. 70sn 65sn 80sn 45bn

title: 45 to 90: Reading Our Euro Cylinder Range
subtitle: Insight
text: 45 to 90: reading our euro cylinder range in this range the model number is the overall length in millimeters, so 45, 54, 60, 70, 80 and 90 are six lengths rather than six products. all are solid brass. what the letters after the number mean is partly documented and partly not, and this article says which is which. the euro-profile cylinder is the one part of a european door that a buyer can order wrong in the most ways, because almost everything about it is encoded into a short string. in our catalog that string starts with a number, and the number is the total length of the cylinder in millimeters. the selected range runs 45, 54, 60, 70, 80 and 90, which is six lengths of one product rather than six different products. that total is not the split. a 70mm (2-3/4") cylinder is most often 35/35, but 30/40 and 40/30 are also 70, and they are different parts that fit different doors, the split is measured from the center of the cam outwards, and the cam is where the fixing screw passes through. we have written that out at length in a separate article, because it is the single most common ordering mistake on this component, and this piece will not repeat it. every cylinder in this range is published as solid brass. that is worth stating because brass is not the cheapest way to make a cylinder and the difference is not visible from outside: a brass body machines to a tighter tolerance than a zinc casting, which is what keeps a five-pin mechanism turning smoothly after a decade of a key being pushed at it slightly off-axis. it is also the reason these cylinders can carry a bhma finish number where a zinc-alloy part cannot, a156.18's base groups are steel, brass and stainless, and zinc is not one of them. the finishes are published as a list rather than per variant: polished brass (pb), chrome plated (cp), satin nickel and the rest of our standard set. those letters are documented on our finish and order-code pages, and a finish code on a cylinder behaves the same way as a finish code on any other product, it names an appearance, and the bhma number needs the base metal as well, which here is always brass. the letters after the finish are the part that is not fully documented, and we would rather say so than invent it. several variants in this range carry dk, kt or ik, and those are function codes in our own internal system whose meanings the factory has not yet confirmed to us in writing. they are on the list of six order codes we are waiting on, one finish letter and five function letters. until that comes back, ask for the function in words in your inquiry and we will match it to the code rather than the other way round. two lengths in the selected range carry no published specification rows at all: the 60 and the 90. five variants of the 60 and four of the 90 are in the catalog with photographs and no material, finish or size row. the length is in the model number and that is genuinely all we publish about them today. it is on the factory list with the rest, and until it comes back the honest answer to "what is the 60 made of" is that we will ask rather than that it is brass like its neighbors, even though it almost certainly is. the 70 is the one to look at first if you are choosing a standard for a project, simply on the weight of the range: nineteen published variants against six for the 80 and three for the 45. that is the length the catalog is built around, and a project standardized on 70mm (2-3/4") has the widest choice of finish and function without a special order. if your doors need something else, the length is a manufacturing variable rather than a stock decision, so ask. a cylinder is also the component most often keyed, and keying is a separate conversation from length. any of these can be supplied keyed alike within a group, or built into a master key system, our article on master key levels sets out how many tiers a building actually needs, and the answer is usually fewer than the inquiry asks for. what matters at the ordering stage is that keying is decided before the cylinders are cut, and that the keying chart is a document somebody has to own. ## profile before length everything above assumes the door takes a euro profile, and that is the first thing to check, not the length. the profile is the shape of the hole (the keyhole-shaped section a euro cylinder slides into) and a cylinder of the right length and the wrong profile does not go in at all. our catalog also carries a single oval cylinder, the profile used in several markets outside the euro-profile world: it is published as solid brass, 30mm (1-3/16") with extension sizes optional, with a 6-pin mechanism, three keys, and an external single-cylinder form. if the lock case you are replacing came from a market that does not use the euro profile, send a photograph of the hole before you send a length. ## what "anti-theft" in a model name does and does not tell you several 70mm variants in this range carry anti-theft in the model name, 70anti-theft, 70pb anti-theft, and three chrome-plated versions carrying dk or kt codes. it would be easy to read that as a security rating. it is not one, and we should say so plainly: the name is how those variants are listed, and none of them publishes a test standard or a test result behind it. where they publish rows at all, those rows are the same as their neighbors' (solid brass, 70mm, the standard finish list) and one of them publishes none. a security claim on a euro cylinder means something specific in europe, and a buyer who needs one should ask for it by name. en 1303 is the european standard for cylinders, and its classification includes a key-related security grade from 1 to 6 and an attack resistance grade from 0 to d. those two digits are what a specification is asking about when it says "high security". a product description that says anti-theft, anti-pick or anti-snap without those digits, or without a named test, has told you what the seller hopes rather than what was tested. the attack a euro cylinder is most often exposed to is mechanical rather than clever. the profile is weakest at the cam, where the body narrows around the fixing screw, so a cylinder that stands proud of the door can be gripped and broken there. nothing on our pages claims resistance to that attack, and we will not imply it. what any buyer can control is the length: a cylinder chosen so that it sits close to flush with the escutcheon gives an attacker far less to grip than one that sticks out by 10mm (3/8") because the next size up was easier to order. our door-thickness-to-cylinder-length table exists for exactly that choice. ## protecting the cylinder instead of upgrading it where a door genuinely needs more than a standard cylinder, one answer is to protect the cylinder rather than replace it. the xf-1 is a cylinder protector, not a cylinder: it is published as hardened steel at hrc58, for anti-drill and anti-pry protection, fixed by a concealed internal through-bolt, and intended for armoured doors, security doors and entrance doors. it is supplied in pvd, satin, polished and antique finishes. the hardness figure is the useful number here, because it is what a drill bit meets first, and the through-bolt fixing matters as much, a protector held on by face screws can be prised off before anyone touches the cylinder. a protector is only as good as the door it is fixed to, and it adds depth on the outside face. if you are adding one to an existing door, measure the new projection against the cylinder length, so the protector does not leave the cylinder recessed so far that the key cannot turn it fully. ## keys: how many, and who holds them the number of keys supplied is published on some variants and not on others. the 47bsik is published with three or five keys available; the single oval cylinder with three keys, and a normal key or, as an option, what the listing calls a computer key. if the key form matters to your market, ask for a photograph of the key itself rather than relying on the name. more keys is not more security. every key is a copy of the access to a door, and the useful question at ordering is not how many come in the box but how many the building needs and who will hold them. on a project, that answer belongs in the keying chart, next to which cylinders are keyed alike, which sit under a master, and which must open to no other key. the chart is the document that outlives the order: when a key is lost in five years' time, it is what tells whoever is responsible which cylinders have to change and which do not. ## reading the range as a whole put the published lengths side by side and the shape of the range is clear. the 70mm length has nineteen variants; the 80 has six; the 60 has five; the 90 four; the 45 three; and the 54, 56, 65 and 47 have one or two each. so a project standardized on 70mm has the widest choice of finish and function without a special order, and the further a door is from that length the more worthwhile it is to ask whether the cylinder is a stock item or a production run. either is possible. only one of them is fast. 70 sndk 80 snkt 45bn 65sn

title: 650 to 1110mm: Which Push Bar Length Your Door Takes
subtitle: Insight
text: 650 to 1110mm: which push bar length your door takes bar length is the dimension most often left off an exit-device inquiry, and the one that cannot be corrected on site. our published lengths run 650, 800, 900, 1000, 1040, 1050 and 1110mm (43-11/16"), some adjustable and some not, and which of those your door takes is decided by the leaf width rather than by the model you liked. almost every exit-device inquiry we receive names a model and a finish. a good proportion of them do not name a door. that is the wrong way round, because the bar has to suit the leaf it is fitted to, and unlike a finish or a trim it is not something that can be adjusted with a file once the container has landed. the published lengths across our range are 650, 800, 900, 1000, 1040, 1050 and 1110mm (43-11/16"). some models carry one figure and some carry several: the 307 is published at 1000mm (39-3/8"), the 311, 303 and 310 at 900mm (35-7/16"), the 305 at 1040mm (40-15/16"), the 308 at 1050mm (41-5/16"), the 309-d pair set at 1110mm, the 315 (which the catalog lists as a pry latch) at 800mm (31-1/2") or 1000mm, and the 314 at 650, 800 or 1000mm and marked customizable. three are published as adjustable: the 300 at 900mm, and the 302 and 302-s at 1040mm. two more, the 320 and 330, are recorded simply as made to the length the customer asks for. the spread is not a styling choice; it is a range built to cover the door widths this industry actually installs. the rule that matters is that the bar is sized to the leaf, not to the opening. on a double door, each leaf takes its own device, and the leaf is roughly half the clear opening less the meeting stile, so a 1800mm (70-7/8") pair is not two 1800mm (70-7/8") bars and is not two 900mm (35-7/16") bars either. working from the opening width rather than the leaf width is the single most common way a schedule arrives with the wrong length on it. nor should a bar be specified longer on the theory that longer is safer. a bar that overhangs the leaf fouls the frame, the stop or the adjacent leaf, and on a pair it prevents the doors closing. a bar that is short of the leaf leaves a strip at the hinge side or the lock side where a person arriving at speed makes contact with the door rather than with the bar, which is exactly the failure the device exists to prevent. both errors look minor on a drawing. adjustable is a real feature and it is not universal, so it is worth asking about by name. where a model is published as adjustable, the bar can be trimmed or set within a range to suit the leaf; where it is not, the length is the length. if your project has several door widths and you would prefer one part number across all of them, tell us at the inquiry, because the answer changes which models are candidates before anything else is discussed. three measurements make an exit-device inquiry answerable on the first reply. leaf width, leaf thickness, and whether the opening is a single or a pair. two more make it complete: whether the door is fire rated and to what, and whether the outside face needs to open at all, because outside trim is a separate order line with its own finish and its own handing, and a device ordered without it arrives as a door that opens one way only. there is one number in our published range that is not a bar at all, and it is worth flagging because it appears in the same field. one record's size row reads 175 × 53 × 73mm (2-7/8"), which is a case dimension rather than a bar length; that model is an exit-device lock case and belongs with the mortise bodies rather than with the bars. if you are reading our size column across the range, that is the row that does not mean what its neighbors mean. finally, a measurement we do not publish and will not estimate: we do not state a minimum or maximum leaf width against each bar length. the arithmetic looks obvious, and it is not, the usable width depends on the stile, the trim, the strike and on double doors the meeting stile as well. send the leaf width and we will answer against the actual model. a number we worked out from a drawing is worth something; a number we worked out from a formula is worth nothing, and this site has a rule about the difference. ## measuring the leaf so the length question has an answer "leaf width" sounds unambiguous and is measured three different ways on site, so it is worth saying which one we mean. measure the door leaf itself, edge to edge, at the height the bar will sit, not the frame, not the clear opening, and not the width of the wall opening on the drawing. on a panelled or glazed door, note the stile widths as well: the vertical members at the hinge and lock edges are where the device's end fittings sit, and on a narrow-stile aluminum door they are the constraint that matters more than the overall width. our article on narrow-stile aluminum doors covers why that door type needs its own conversation. on a pair, measure each leaf separately. leaves in a pair are often unequal (a wider active leaf and a narrower inactive one) and each takes a device sized to itself. and note the meeting stiles: whether there is a center mullion, whether the leaves overlap with an astragal, and how wide the gap is. those three facts decide whether the pair needs rim devices, vertical-rod devices or a coordinated set, which our article on exit device standards and double doors goes through. ## mounting height is the other number length is only half of fitting a bar. the other half is height, and it is set by the standard or the code rather than by taste. en 1125 expects the operating bar to be fitted between 900mm and 1100mm (35-7/16" to 43-5/16") above the finished floor. in north america, nfpa 101 puts panic hardware between 34 and 48 inches (864 to 1219mm). those ranges overlap, which is convenient, but they are not identical, and the edition your authority enforces is the one that counts. check the current text rather than a figure remembered from a previous project. height interacts with the door. a mid-rail on a panelled or glazed leaf may sit exactly where the bar needs to go, or exactly where it must not, and a kick plate or a vision panel can collide with the device's end fittings. mark the bar height on the door elevation before ordering, and look at what else is already drawn at that height. ## push bar or touch bar, and why length matters differently for each everything above is about the bar's length across the leaf, and it applies whichever operating element the device uses. but the choice between a traditional push bar (a cross bar pivoting on two end fittings) and a touch bar, where the whole flat bar is the operating surface, changes how forgiving the length is. our article comparing push bars and touch bars is the piece on this site that ai search engines cite most often, and it sets out that choice properly. the short version for length: on either type, the operating surface should cover as much of the leaf as the standard requires, and a bar that is short of the leaf leaves a strip where a person pushes the door rather than the device. ## cutting to length, and when not to only models published as adjustable should be cut or set to length: on our range, the 300, 302 and 302-s, plus the 314 marked customizable and the made-to-length 320 and 330. a fixed-length device cut down on site is no longer the device that was supplied, and on a fire or escape door that can matter to whoever signs the door off. if none of the adjustable models suits the project, ask for a made-to-length device at the order stage rather than planning to modify one at installation. where a project has many door widths, it is often cheaper overall to standardize on one adjustable model than to order a different fixed length for every opening. it is one part number, one finish and one set of spares, and the site team only has to learn one device. ## three doors, written the way we need them here is what a small schedule looks like when it arrives answerable: three hypothetical openings on one project, written in the form this article has been asking for. *d01: single leaf, timber, 1000mm wide, 54mm thick, fire rated, stiles 120mm, bar height to local code, keyed lever outside.* *d02: pair, unequal leaves 1100mm and 700mm, no center mullion, overlapping astragal, steel, 45mm thick, not rated, exit only.* *d03: single glazed aluminum leaf, 900mm wide, narrow stiles of 60mm, 50mm thick, push pad preferred.* nothing in those three lines names a model, and nothing needs to. d01 is a length and trim question on a rated door. d02 is two devices of different lengths plus a decision about vertical latching and a coordinator. d03 is mainly a stile question before it is a length question. each of those gets answered against a specific model and a specific leaf, which is the point of sending the leaf rather than a guess at the bar, and the reason we do not publish a width chart that would pretend to answer all three from a formula. if you only remember one thing from this article, make it the order of the questions: leaf first, stiles and meeting edges second, height third, and the bar last. a schedule written in that order almost never comes back with the wrong length on it. 307 311 305

title: US26D, 626, 630: A Finish Code Is Not a Color
subtitle: Insight
text:
us26d, 626, 630: a finish code is not a color a north american specification writes 626, not "satin chrome". the number encodes the base metal as well as the appearance, so 626 and 652 are the same color and different products. of 519 published canton hyland records, 77 can be given a number honestly; the other 442 cannot, and each has a reason. a buyer arrived in september carrying a competitor's part number, `rxfse25r510l32d3`. the manufacturer never resolved and it did not matter, because one fragment of it identified the buyer completely: 32d. that is not a color name, it is a code in the north american finish system, and a purchaser who writes it is specifying to ansi/bhma. our own catalog answers in a different language (sset, acbk, cpbk) house codes that mean nothing outside our price list. this article is the translation, and the important half of it is where the translation stops. start with the part everybody already knows. us26d and 626 are two ways of writing the same appearance, satin chromium plated; the us number is the older convention and the three-digit number is ansi/bhma a156.18. most cross-reference charts on the open web print exactly this, two columns wide, and stop. that chart is incomplete in the one way that costs a container. a bhma number encodes the base metal as well as the appearance. a156.18 designates the base in the code itself: steel, brass and bronze, and stainless steel are three different groups. so 626 is satin chromium plated on a brass or bronze base. 652 is satin chromium plated on a steel base. they are the same color, they photograph identically, and they are not the same product, different corrosion resistance, different price, different service life. a specifier who writes 626 and receives 652 has been given a substitution, and on a public building that is a rejected submittal. 630 is the one that breaks the pattern, and it is also the most specified finish in north america. it is not a plating at all: 630 is satin stainless steel, solid, with the finish worked into the metal rather than applied on top of it. this is why 630 cannot be offered as an alternative to 626 on price. there is nothing to wear through, because there is no coating; and there is nothing to plate, because the part is already the metal the finish names. the practical consequence is that a finish code alone cannot be mapped to a bhma number. our catalog records a finish field and a separate material field, and the number only exists where both are known. cp on brass and cp on steel are two different bhma numbers, and the finish field does not say which. so the mapping in our system takes both fields and returns nothing whenever either half is unknown or names more than one metal. run that across the catalog and 77 of 519 published records gain a number, about fifteen per cent. the commonest are 630 and 629, satin and bright stainless, which is what you would expect from a catalog whose largest material group is stainless steel; then 605 bright brass, 625 bright chrome, 626 satin chrome, 619 satin nickel. one record resolves to 652 rather than 626, and that single record is the whole argument of this article: same color, steel base, different number. the other 442 are worth listing, because a supplier who will not say why a field is empty is usually hiding a guess. on 277 records no finish is stated at all, which is a question for our factory and is on the list. on 20 the material field is empty. on 22 the material names more than one metal, "brass or stainless steel" is a choice the buyer has not made yet, so there is no base to designate. eighteen are antique brass, which is a family of relieved finishes rather than one a156.18 number, and twelve say "stainless steel" without saying satin or polished, where 630 and 629 both fit and guessing picks one. fifty-six are zinc alloy, and that group deserves its own sentence because it is a fact about the part rather than a gap in our data. a156.18's base materials are steel, brass and bronze, and stainless. zinc alloy is not among them, and neither is aluminum. a specification calling for 626 on a brass base cannot be met with a zinc-alloy casting however close the color comes, and a buyer is better told that before a sample than after a submittal. saying so costs us inquiries we would have lost anyway at the review stage. ## four questions people actually type, answered in order these are not invented examples. they are the four finish questions that most often bring people to this page, and each one has a short correct answer that the code tables do not give. ### "is 652 the same finish as us26d?" they look identical and they are different codes, because the number encodes the metal underneath. us26d maps to 626, satin chromium plated on brass or bronze. 652 is satin chromium plated on steel. same plating, same appearance, different base metal, and therefore a different bhma number. it matters in two places and nowhere else. it matters to corrosion, because a chrome layer is a barrier and what happens when that barrier is scratched depends entirely on what is beneath it. and it matters to matching, because a 626 lever beside a 652 closer will agree on day one and may not agree in year five, as the two bases weather differently under the same plating. so if a specification says 626 and a supplier quotes 652, that is not necessarily a substitution to reject, but it is a substitution, and it should be written down as one rather than allowed to pass as the same line. | appearance | on brass / bronze | on steel | on stainless |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| bright chromium | 625 | 651 | – |
| satin chromium | 626 (us26d) | 652 | – |
| bright stainless | – | – | 629 |
| satin stainless | – | – | 630 | ### "can a chrome finish be satin?" yes. "chrome" names the metal, not the gloss: chromium plating is deposited the same way either way; the difference is what was done to the surface underneath before plating and, on some parts, after. a bright chrome part was polished before it went in the bath. a satin chrome part was grained, blasted or brushed first, and the chrome faithfully reproduces whatever texture it was laid over. that is why a satin chrome finish cannot be "polished up" on site into a bright one, the texture is below the plating, not in it. the same logic explains a question that follows it constantly: two satin chrome parts from two suppliers can both be correct and still not match, because "satin" is not a measured quantity in the finish code. if the match matters, the tool for it is a gloss measurement and a signed reference sample, which our page on powder coating and ral sets out in full, the principle is identical whether the coating is chrome or powder. ### "what does sn mean, and what is echswc?" sn is satin nickel: it is one of the small set of two-letter marks that almost every hardware maker uses the same way: pb polished brass, ab antique brass, ac antique copper, sn satin nickel, ss stainless steel, cp chrome plated, mb matt black, orb oil-rubbed bronze. echswc is not a finish code at all: it is a manufacturer's internal part string, and no public table will resolve it, we could not resolve it either, and said so. what is useful is the method for taking apart a code you do not recognize, because it works on anybody's: read it from the right. finish marks sit at the end, because they are the last thing decided before packing. strip the trailing two or three characters and check them against the common set above. what remains in front is usually the model, and what sits between is frequently a function or a size. if nothing resolves, the code belongs to a numbering scheme that is private to that maker, and the only reliable move is to send a photograph of the part itself, not the string. ### "is there a 626 for steel?" no, the steel equivalent is 652: this is the same fact as the first question, read from the other direction, and it is worth stating separately because people search it separately. the trap here is a catalog that lists "626" against a steel product. that is not necessarily dishonest; it usually means the catalog is using 626 loosely to mean "satin chrome" rather than as a bhma designation. but if you are cross-referencing into a specification written in bhma numbers, that loose usage is exactly what will cause a rejected submittal, the reviewer is checking a number, not an appearance. one habit closes all four of these at once: write the appearance and the base metal as two separate fields on the order, never as one code. "satin chrome, on brass" cannot be misread by anybody in the chain, in any country, in any convention. a bare `626` can be, and on a steel part it will be. the same applies to stainless steel: write the grade beside the finish, because 630 does not tell 304 from 316. so, in practice: if your specification is written in bhma numbers, send us the number and the model you are cross-referencing, and we will answer with a number or with a dash and the reason. a dash costs you one question. a plausible number costs whoever installs it a rejected submittal, and it is the reason most finish charts on this industry's websites should be read as marketing rather than as specification. 5870 acet 607 sset 3431 sset

title: Fitting a Euro Cylinder: Five Steps, and the Two Everyone Skips
subtitle: Insight
text: fitting a euro cylinder: five steps, and the two everyone skips a euro cylinder goes in and out through the lock case, held by one screw, and the whole job takes two minutes once the cylinder is the right length. almost every failed fitting is one of two things: the cam was not turned before it was pushed through, or nobody tried the key with the door shut. the euro profile exists so that a lock case and the thing that unlocks it can be separate products, made by different factories, replaced independently. that is why the same shape turns up on a door in buenos aires and a door in kraków, and it is why fitting one is a two-minute job rather than a carpentry job. the whole cylinder passes through the lock case from one face of the door and is held by a single screw. nothing else fastens it. before any of that, the cylinder has to be the right length, and that is a measuring job rather than a fitting job, it is covered separately in our note on why 70 is the total and not the split. everything below assumes you are holding a cylinder that already suits the door. if you are not, no amount of care at the door will help: a cylinder 5mm (3/16") too short will not turn, and one 10mm (3/8") too long is a security problem rather than an inconvenience. step one, remove what is there. put the key in the old cylinder and turn it about fifteen to twenty degrees, far enough that the cam, the small bar underneath that actually throws the bolt, is drawn back inside the profile. the cam sticks out below the barrel; while it does, the cylinder cannot pass through the lock case. most seized removals are not seized at all, they are a cam still standing proud. step two, take out the fixing screw. it sits in the edge of the door, in the lock case faceplate, level with the middle of the cylinder, one screw, usually the only thing on that faceplate that is not holding the lock itself in. with the screw out and the key still turned, the cylinder draws out by the key. if it does not move, the cam is not clear; turn the key a little further rather than pulling harder. step three, offer the new one the same way. key in, cam turned clear, slide it through from the outside face. step four, fit the screw. it passes through the center of the cylinder (through the cam's own axis) so it will only enter when the cylinder is at the exact depth. that resistance is a feature: a screw that goes in easily at the wrong depth would leave the cylinder loose. tighten it firmly and stop there. it is a small screw in brass, and it is the part that shears if you treat it like a structural fixing. step five is the one that decides whether the door is secure, and it takes ten seconds: look at how far the cylinder stands out from the escutcheon or handle rose. flush to about three millimeters proud is right. more than that gives a tool something to grip, and a cylinder that can be gripped can be snapped, which is the single most common way a euro-profile door is opened without a key. too far recessed is a different failure: the key does not seat and the rose fouls the barrel. if the projection is wrong, the cylinder is the wrong length or the wrong split, and no amount of tightening fixes it. now the two steps everyone skips. the first: test the key from both faces, and test the thumbturn if there is one, before you put the handles back. the second, and this is the one that comes back as a complaint: test it again with the door closed. a door under its own weight sits differently in the frame than it does swinging open, and a latch or deadbolt that clears comfortably on an open door can bind against a strike that has moved two millimeters. every cylinder we have ever had returned as faulty and tested fine on the bench was this. what we supply and what you should confirm with us. our cylinders are solid brass, in euro profile, and the catalog carries nine overall lengths, 45, 47, 54, 56, 60, 65, 70, 80 and 90mm (3-9/16"), the length being the leading figure of the model number. what the catalog does not publish for every model is the split, the cam type and the keyway, so send the door thickness and what is mounted on each face and we will confirm all three against the model before you order. if the doors are going to be keyed alike or master keyed, settle that in the same conversation, the keyway has to be common across the whole system and it cannot be changed later. ## when it will not come out one of the queries that reaches this page is worth quoting in full, because it is somebody standing at a door right now: "euro profile cylinder removal, door unlocked, retaining screw, cam alignment". that is four separate things going wrong at once, and they have one cause between them. the cylinder only slides out when the cam (the flat bar on the underside, the part that actually throws the bolt) is turned to sit inside the profile outline. if the cam projects past the profile by even a millimeter, it catches on the lock case and the cylinder will not move, no matter how hard it is pulled. so the sequence, when it is stuck: the fixing screw must be fully out, not loosened: it is a long machine screw through the faceplate in the edge of the door, and on a thick door it can be 60mm or more. half a turn left in the thread is enough to hold the cylinder. take it right out and put it somewhere, it is the one part that never comes with the new cylinder. the key must be in, and turned, not at rest: about fifteen to twenty degrees, which is less than it feels. at rest the cam sits proud. turned too far, it comes proud on the other side. there is a window of a few degrees where it clears, and finding it is a matter of turning slowly while pulling gently rather than turning hard. "door unlocked" is the trap in that query. an unlocked door feels like the right state and often is not. what matters is the cam position, not the bolt position, and on some lock cases the cam sits proud precisely when the door is unlocked. if it will not move with the door unlocked, try it with the latch held back and the key turned the other way. pull straight, from the outside face: the cylinder comes out the way it went in. levering it sideways bends the cam and then it will never clear. if all four are right and it still will not move, stop. a cylinder that is seized in the case is usually a case problem rather than a cylinder problem, and forcing it turns a ten-minute job into a new lock case. ## cam alignment on the way back in the same geometry going the other way, and one extra thing that catches people. turn the key on the new cylinder until the cam is inside the profile, slide it through from the outside, and then (before the fixing screw) look through the screw hole in the faceplate. you should see the threaded hole in the cylinder body lined up behind it. if you see metal instead of a hole, the cylinder is a few millimeters out and forcing the screw will cut a new thread in brass. that misalignment has two usual causes. the cylinder is in from the wrong face, so the halves are reversed. or it is the wrong length and the screw hole simply cannot reach. once the screw starts by hand, it is aligned. never start that screw with a driver, brass takes a cross-thread without complaint and you will not feel it happen. ## the three tests before you put the tools away both faces, with the door open: key from outside, key or turn from inside, four times each way. a cylinder that binds on the fourth turn will bind on the fortieth. both faces, with the door closed: this is the one people skip, and it is where a wrong length shows up. a cylinder that works open and binds closed is being squeezed by the escutcheon or is fouling the keep. withdraw the key at rest, from both faces: a key that will not come out at zero is a cam that is not returning, and it means the cylinder is under load from the fixing screw, back the screw off a quarter turn and retest. ten seconds each, thirty seconds in total, at the one moment when fixing anything costs nothing. every one of those three failures becomes a return visit if it is found later. one last note for anyone ordering a replacement rather than a new build. a euro cylinder is a standard profile, not a standard product: the profile guarantees it will pass through the case, not that it will match the key you already have, the cam angle your lock expects, or the finish on the rest of the door. tell us the model you are replacing if you know it, and photograph the old cylinder beside a ruler if you do not. that photograph settles more questions than any form we could send you. keep the old cylinder until all three pass. it is the only reference you have for the split if the new one turns out wrong, and it costs nothing to leave it in a drawer for a week. and if the new one goes into a master key system, keep the old one until the key schedule has been updated as well: the removed cylinder is the physical record of which key opened that door before. 70sn 65sn 80sn 45bn

title: Handing: The One-Letter Answer That Holds Up Orders
subtitle: Insight
text:
handing: the one-letter answer that holds up orders left, right or universal is a single character on an order line and the most common reason a quotation goes back for clarification. it is decided by where the hinges are and which way the door opens, and the two conventions in use disagree with each other. handing describes which edge of the door the hinges are on and which way the leaf swings. it matters because a lever has to fall the right way, a latch bolt has a bevel that must face the frame, and a lock case machined for one hand will not close on the other. it is one letter, and it is the field most often left blank on an inquiry. there are two conventions and they do not agree. the european method stands the observer on the side the door opens towards (the pull side) and calls it left-handed if the hinges are on the left. the american method (ansi/bhma a156.115) stands the observer outside, on the side you would use a key from, and adds "reverse" for doors that swing away. the same physical door is din-left under one and right-hand-reverse under the other. this is why "left-handed" written on its own is not an answer. it is an answer plus an assumption about which convention the reader uses, and the reader is on the other side of the world. the unambiguous way to say it is to describe the door: hinges on the left as you look at it from the corridor, opens away from you. twenty words that cannot be misread beat one letter that can. a useful test that needs no convention at all: stand where the key goes. if the hinge knuckles are on your left, it is left-handed in the american sense; if the door swings towards you from there, it is "reverse". say which side you stood on and the sentence survives translation. some hardware does not care. a tubular latch with a symmetrical bolt, most euro-profile cylinders, hinges themselves, and any lever on a sprung rose are non-handed (universal, marked u) and the field can honestly say so. reversible latches are a middle case: the bolt can be turned on site, which is a real convenience and also a real opportunity for it to be turned wrong and never checked. what is genuinely handed, and where the cost lands: mortise cases with an asymmetric follower, rebated pairs, and anything with a deadlocking latch whose auxiliary bolt has to meet the keep. on those, a wrong hand is not adjustable with a file, it is a different part number, and on a container quantity it is a different shipment. the practical rule for a schedule: give every opening a hand or the word universal, and never leave the column empty. an empty column reads as "not decided yet" to the person filling the order and as "universal" to the person in a hurry, and only one of those is safe. ## the four north american terms, spelled out the european convention gives two answers; the north american one gives four, because it adds a second axis. stand outside the door. note which side the hinges are on and whether the door swings away from you or toward you. the four combinations are the four terms: | hinges, seen from outside | swings away from you | swings toward you |
| --- | --- | --- |
| left | lh: left hand | lhr: left hand reverse |
| right | rh, right hand | rhr, right hand reverse | "reverse" does not mean the door is unusual or that anything has been flipped. it only means the leaf swings toward the person standing outside, which is normal on an outward-opening exit door, and therefore very common on exactly the doors that carry panic hardware. ## din, and what a european product code is telling you european codes carry the hand as din left or din right, and din follows the european convention: look at the door from the side it opens toward you, and name the hand by the hinge side. a code ending in a din designation is describing the lock case, not the door, which matters, because a din-left case fitted into a door somebody has described as right-handed in the american sense is not necessarily a mistake. that is the trap in one sentence: a door correctly called left hand in one convention can be correctly called right hand in the other, and nobody has made an error. it is why "lh" written alone on an international order is a coin toss, and why the convention has to be named next to the hand every single time. ## reversible, universal and field-reversible are three different claims these three words get used interchangeably in catalogs and they promise different things. the difference decides whether your fitter can solve a problem on site or has to order another part. | claim | what it actually means | what the fitter does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| non-handed / universal | the part is symmetrical or hand-independent as shipped | nothing. fit it either way |
| reversible | the part can be converted, usually with the lock out of the door | bench work, tools, sometimes a spring moved |
| field-reversible | converted in place, typically one screw or a lever flip | a minute at the door, no dismantling | when a supplier says "reversible" and means the first row, everyone is happy. when they say it and mean the second row, a fitter on a ladder discovers it at the worst possible moment. ask which of the three it is, in those words, and ask whether the conversion needs the lock removed. ## what our own catalog actually says we should be concrete about this rather than general, because the answer surprised us when we counted it. 184 of our products publish a handing row. of the 188 handing rows across them, 187 say the product is fully reversible or non-handed. exactly one names a handed left-or-right choice. so for almost everything we sell, the honest answer to "what hand do you need?" is: we do not need one. the lever, the latch, the rim lock, the cylinder, they go either way. that is not a reason to stop recording the hand, and this is the part worth saying plainly rather than quietly. the hand is not a property of the hardware; it is a property of the opening. it still decides which way the door is hung, which side the frame is rebated, where the closer arm goes, which leaf of a pair is active, and which way round the strike is cut. reversible hardware removes one of those decisions and leaves the rest untouched. ## where handing still bites, even with reversible hardware the frame and the strike: a keep is cut into one side of the frame. reversible hardware does not move it. the closer: a closer arm, a backcheck setting and a parallel-arm bracket are all handed by the opening even when the lock is not. pairs of doors: which leaf is active is a handing decision, and it determines where the astragal, the flush bolts and the coordinator go. anything with a thumbturn, an indicator, or a lettered face: symmetry ends where text or an icon begins, an occupied/vacant indicator read upside down is a defect, not an orientation. anything bought elsewhere: the ironmongery on the same door from another supplier may be genuinely handed, and it will be handed in whichever convention that supplier writes in. so record the hand on the schedule, name the convention beside it, and then enjoy the fact that on our side of the order it usually will not change what we ship. ## why there are two conventions at all neither convention is wrong, and knowing why they differ makes them easier to keep straight than memorising them does. they were written by two different trades solving two different problems. the european convention was written from the leaf. a joiner hanging a door cares which edge the hinges go on, and answers that standing where the door opens toward him. one axis, two answers, and it maps directly onto the work. the north american convention was written from the lock. a locksmith cares where the key goes, so the observer is planted on the outside face, and once you are standing outside, the swing direction becomes a second thing you can see and therefore a second thing worth naming. one axis became two, and two terms became four. so the conventions are not rivals; they are answers to "which way does this door work?" asked by a carpenter and by a locksmith. that is also why the disagreement is so stubborn: each one is the shortest correct answer to its own question. ## when the order already says "lh" and nobody knows whose lh it is this happens constantly on a re-order, where the original schedule is gone and all that survives is two letters. do not guess, and do not assume the previous supplier used your convention. go back to the physical evidence in this order. look at an installed door from the original batch, if one exists, and record the three plain observations, hinge side, swing direction, which face is outside. those three survive any convention. failing that, look at the part itself: a handed lock case shows its latch bevel, and the bevel always faces the direction the door closes in. failing that, ask what the original supplier's catalog said, because the convention is usually printed in its front matter even when the order is not. if none of the three is available, say so on the order rather than picking one. on our catalog it will almost certainly not matter (see the count above) and on a genuinely handed item, an honest "hand unknown, please confirm" costs one email. a guess costs a container. where a model is handed, our specification tables state it as a row rather than burying it in the description, and the guided selector asks for it before it offers a model number, because the answer changes which models can be offered at all, not just which variant of one. lc07 85×45mm lc14 85×50mm 9001 587 pbet

title: 200,000 Cycles: What the LH Lever Range Is Actually Rated For
subtitle: Insight
text:
