200,000 cycles: what the lh lever range is actually rated for lh852, lh853, lh855, 808 and 6491 share a published cycle life of 200,000 operations, a 60/70mm backset, a 35–45mm (1-3/8" to 1-3/4") adjustable door thickness and a solid steel zinc-plated chassis behind a zinc-alloy lever. what separates them is the function set and the shape, and only one of the five offers a dummy. five lever sets in our selected range (lh852, lh853, lh855, 808 and 6491) publish the same cycle life: 200,000 operations. that number is the most useful thing on their specification sheets and also the most easily misread, so it is worth being precise about what it describes and what it does not. a cycle is one full operation: lever down, latch retracted, lever released, latch returned. two hundred thousand of them is a service expectation for a door in normal use, not a warranty and not a grade in the ansi sense, a156 grades exit devices and locks on cycle counts, and we hold no ansi/bhma certification, so this figure is our own published expectation rather than a graded result. stating it that way is the difference between a specification and an advertisement. what makes the number credible is the construction behind it, and that is published too. the lever itself is zinc alloy. the chassis is solid steel, zinc plated for corrosion resistance. that division is deliberate: the lever is the visible part and zinc casts into shapes steel cannot, while the chassis is the part that carries the load every one of those 200,000 times, and it is steel. a lever set that is zinc all the way through wears at the spindle, and it does it long before the finish shows any sign of it. the dimensions are shared across all five: a 60/70mm backset and a door thickness of 35mm (1-3/8") to 45mm (1-3/4") adjustable, with the lh853 also published at 60mm (2-3/8") on some variants. all five are fully reversible, left or right hand, so handing is an assembly matter rather than a separate part number, which is worth knowing when a schedule arrives with the handing column empty, as they often do. where they separate is function. the lh855 is published with the widest set: entrance, privacy, passage or dummy. a dummy is a lever fixed to the door with no mechanism at all, used on the inactive leaf of a pair or on a cupboard, and it is the one function buyers routinely forget to order and then improvise on site with a working set. if your schedule has inactive leaves on it, that is the model to ask about first. the 808 is the one to look at where the finish is doing the work. it is published in antique brass (us5) and matt black, and antique brass is a relieved finish (color worked back off the high points) rather than a plating with one uniform tone. that is why it is not translatable to a single bhma number, as our finish-code article explains, and also why it looks different on a lever than on a flat rose. order a sample of the actual lever rather than a finish chip. all five are published as keyable alike with deadbolts, or master keyed. that is the row that turns a lever range into a project specification: the lever set, the deadbolt above it and the cylinder in the door next to it can be one keying group, which is what a building manager is actually buying. the number of levels that group needs is a separate decision and usually a smaller one than the inquiry assumes. the trim material is published as zinc die-casting electro-plated, or solid brass. that is a genuine choice rather than a grade, solid brass is the option where the door is exterior or coastal, and the electro-plated die casting is the option everywhere else. say which one you want at inquiry, because it is not a finish decision and cannot be changed by picking a different finish code. ## what the 62 lever entries on this site are the five sets above are not a sample of a varied range; they are typical of it. of the 62 lever-handle entries on this site, 56 are tubular lever sets that publish the same core rows described above: a 60/70mm backset, a 35–45mm door, 200,000 cycles, a solid steel chassis, full reversibility and keying alike with deadbolts. so the choice between them is function, finish and trim material, not construction, and a buyer comparing two of them on cycle life or backset will find nothing to separate them. the other six publish no specification rows yet: 819 pbet, 8803 snbk, 8803 snet, 8806 ssbk, 8806 sset and lh851. several carry the same function suffixes as the rest of the range (bk for privacy and et for entrance, as on our cylindrical locks), but a suffix is not a specification. we are not going to give those six the rows of their neighbors. ask, and we will confirm them against the drawing. ## choosing between the five, by what each is published in since construction does not separate them, here is what does: the functions and finishes each family is actually published in, counted from its variants on this site. | family | variants | functions published | finishes published |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| lh852 | 5 | entrance, privacy, passage | black nickel, gun metal, satin stainless (us32d) |
| lh853 | 8 | entrance, privacy, passage | chrome, satin nickel, black nickel |
| lh855 | 4 | entrance, privacy (the base record also lists passage and dummy) | satin nickel, black nickel |
| 808 | 4 | entrance, passage | antique brass (us5), matt black, satin nickel |
| 6491 | 2 | entrance | satin nickel, satin stainless (us32d) | two practical readings follow. for a building that needs every function in one finish, the lh853 is the widest published set, with entrance, privacy and passage all three in satin nickel (its chrome versions cover privacy and passage only). for a darker scheme, the lh852 is the family published in black nickel across all three functions, and the 808 adds matt black on the entrance function. and if the schedule has inactive leaves, the lh855 is the one family whose record names a dummy function, which is worth confirming for the finish you need before ordering. ## a tubular set is the whole lock it is worth being clear about what a tubular lever set is, because it decides the door preparation. the set carries its own latch in a bored hole: a round hole through the face of the door and a smaller one into its edge. the levers, the latch and the keyed cylinder are one product, which is why the specification talks about backset, cycle life and function. a door with a rectangular pocket cut into its edge for a mortise lock case is a different door, and a tubular set is not the right part for it; tell us which preparation you have before choosing. the 35–45mm door range is the other row to check early. it covers most internal timber doors. a heavier or thicker leaf needs a lever with a wider range, and on this site that means the stainless 9000 series, published for doors of 35–50mm (1-3/8" to 1-15/16"). our article on the stainless 9000 levers compares that family model by model. ## projection and lever length: the numbers that meet the wall the lh sets do not publish projection or lever length, and those are the two figures that decide what the lever hits. for reference, the stainless levers on this site that do publish them sit at a lever length of 130 to 135mm (5-1/8" to 5-5/16") and a projection of 60 to 68mm (2-3/8" to 2-11/16"), which is the ordinary range for a commercial lever. if a door opens against a return wall or sits close to the next door in a corridor, ask for the projection of the lh set you are considering before ordering it. projection is the figure to carry across to the rest of the door. it sets how much clearance the lever needs from a wall when the door is fully open, and it is the number our article on door stops tells you to choose a stop against: a stop shorter than the lever's projection lets the lever reach the wall first. ## replacing levers on existing doors on a replacement, three things from the old set decide the new one, and none of them is the finish. the backset, measured from the door edge to the center of the bored hole, which on these sets has to be 60 or 70mm. the door thickness at the lock position, not at the edge of a panelled door. and the marks the old rose left on the door: a new rose has to cover the screw holes and the paint line of the old one, so measure what the old one covered before choosing. a like-for-like replacement that leaves a crescent of bare timber round the new rose is the most common reason a re-handling job turns into a decorating job. ## keying a building's worth of lever sets because every published set in the range keys alike with our deadbolts or into a master key system, the keying decision is the one that turns a list of lever sets into a building. decide which doors share a key, which sit under a master, and which must open to no other key, and send that with the order. cylinders are pinned before they are packed, so keying decided after the order means reopening it, and our article on master key systems sets out how many levels a building actually needs (usually fewer than the inquiry asks for). for a quotation on this range, four rows are enough: function per door, backset, leaf thickness, and whether any of it is keyed together. the cycle figure is the same across all five, so it will not choose between them; the function set and the trim material will. lh853 cpbk lh852 sset lh855 snet 808 abet 6491 sset

title: How Many Levels Your Master Key System Actually Needs
subtitle: Insight
text:
how many levels your master key system actually needs a master key system is a hierarchy, and the number of levels in it is a decision about who is allowed through which door, not a hardware specification. we build to five levels, ggmk down to the change key, with four tiers of management keying above the individual lock. most buildings need three. almost every inquiry we get about master keying opens the same way: "can you do master key?" the answer is yes, and it is not useful, because master keying is not a feature a cylinder either has or lacks. it is a plan (a map of who may open what) and the cylinders are cut afterwards to match the plan. the question that actually moves an order forward is how many levels that plan has. the vocabulary is worth getting straight, because the abbreviations are used loosely and they are not interchangeable. a change key (ck) opens one lock and nothing else, the key a tenant or an office occupant carries. a master key (mk) opens every lock in one defined group: a floor, a wing, a department. a grand master key (gmk) opens several groups. a great grand master key (ggmk) sits above those. between them sit the management levels a facilities team actually uses day to day, the cleaner who needs every room on two floors but no plant room, the maintenance contractor who needs plant rooms across the whole site and no offices. we build to five levels, from ggmk down to the change key, with four tiers of management keying between the top and the individual lock. that is the ceiling, not the recommendation. most buildings we quote need three: a change key per door, a master per floor or department, and one grand master for the building manager. specifying five levels for a building that needs three does not add security, it adds cross-keying complexity, and every additional level narrows the number of distinct key cuts available below it. that last point is the one most often missed, and it is arithmetic rather than opinion. a cylinder has a fixed number of pin positions and a fixed number of depths per position, so the total number of distinct keys is finite. every master level consumes some of that space, because a master key works by adding a second shear line in the pin stack, and each added shear line reduces how many change keys can remain unique underneath. a five-level system in a small building is not more secure than a three-level one; it is a three-level building with fewer available combinations and more keys that accidentally fit more than they should. so the design starts from the building, not from the hardware. what we need to draw a system is the door schedule with a line per door, and for each door: who must be able to open it, and which group it belongs to. that is usually a spreadsheet the facilities manager already has. from it we produce a keying chart (every door, every key that opens it, and the total key count) and that chart is what gets approved before a single cylinder is pinned. two practical constraints worth raising before the chart, because they change it. first, all cylinders in one system must be the same keyway, and that keyway has to be decided at the start, a system cannot be extended later with cylinders from a different profile. second, decide early how many keys each level needs, including spares held by the building owner. cutting additional keys to an existing system later is straightforward; discovering that the chart never allowed for the night cleaner is not. our cylinders are solid brass, in euro profile. the catalog carries them in nine overall lengths (45, 47, 54, 56, 60, 65, 70, 80 and 90mm (3-9/16")) and the length is the leading figure of the model number, which is how the factory names them. ask us to confirm the exact overall length for the model you settle on: only ten of the forty-five published cylinders state it as a specification row, and on the rest the model number is the only thing carrying it. overall length is also not the split: a 70mm (2-3/4") cylinder can be 35/35, 30/40 or 40/30, and which one fits depends on your door. that is a separate decision from the keying plan and it is explained in our note on cylinder length and split, but the two arrive together on the same order, so it is worth measuring while you draw the chart. ## the chart itself here is the hierarchy as a chart, because that is what people are actually looking for when they search for one. read it downward: each level opens everything below it and nothing above it. | level | abbreviation | opens | typical holder | how many exist |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | ggmk: great grand master | every lock in the system | owner, estates director | one, sometimes two |
| 2 | gmk: grand master | every lock in one building or one whole function | building manager, head of security | one per building |
| 3 | mk, master | every lock in one department, floor or wing | floor manager, housekeeping supervisor | one per group |
| 4 | smk, sub-master | a small named set of doors | team leader, contractor with limited access | one per sub-group |
| 5 | ck, change key | one lock, or a keyed-alike set | the person who uses that room | one per door | two labels sit outside the hierarchy and are constantly confused with it. keyed alike (ka) means several locks share one change key, two doors into the same office, or a run of identical store cupboards. it is not a level; it is a decision made at the bottom of the chart. keyed different (kd) is the default: every lock has its own change key. a maison key is the other one worth naming. it is a key that a lock accepts *in addition* to its own, the classic case being a main entrance that every flat key must open. maison working is a property of the lock, not of the key, and it is specified per door rather than per level. ## a worked example, so the chart has a shape take a four-storey office building with a ground-floor reception, three tenant floors, a plant room, and a cleaners' store on each floor. the system that fits it is four levels, not five: | who | level | opens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| building owner | gmk | everything |
| facilities manager | mk-a | plant room, risers, all cleaners' stores |
| cleaning contractor | smk-1 | the three cleaners' stores only |
| floor 2 tenant | ck ×9 | their own nine doors, keyed different |
| main entrance | maison | accepts every tenant ck plus gmk | nobody in that building needs a ggmk, because there is only one building. adding the sixth line (a ggmk above the owner's gmk) costs pin space on every cylinder in the system and buys nothing until there is a second building. that is the whole argument for designing down rather than up. ## what each level costs you in pin space the arithmetic in the previous section is not abstract, and it is worth stating as a rule of thumb rather than a formula. every level above the change key needs at least one extra split in the pin stack of every cylinder that the level must open. splits are what make a cylinder pickable and what make it wear unevenly, so the count matters to security and to service life, not only to whether the system can be drawn at all. the practical consequence: a five-level system on a six-pin cylinder leaves very little room for future doors. if the building will grow, the honest move is to use fewer levels now and leave depth unspent, rather than to design the maximum system and discover in year three that no more keys can be cut in it. this is also why we ask for the schedule before quoting rather than after. a system is not a product we take off a shelf; it is a chart drawn against a specific building, and a chart drawn against the wrong building cannot be corrected later without recutting every cylinder in it. ## what you get back, and why it has to be kept the deliverable is not a box of cylinders. it is a key schedule: one row per door, naming the door, the cylinder, which levels open it, and how many change keys were cut. alongside it sits the bitting list, the actual pin depths behind every key in the system. keep both, and keep them somewhere that survives a change of facilities manager. a master key system whose chart has been lost is not a master key system any more; it is a set of cylinders nobody can extend, because the next key has to be cut into a scheme that no longer exists on paper. rebuilding a lost chart means pulling and reading cylinders one at a time, and on a large building that costs more than the original system did. send the door schedule and say how many levels you think you need. if the schedule suggests fewer, we will say so: a system with one level more than the building uses is a cost and a complication that shows up years later, when somebody has to explain why a key opens a door it should not. and if the building is likely to grow, say that too, because spare capacity has to be designed in at the start. 70sn 65sn 80sn 45bn

title: Backset and Center Distance: How to Read a Mortise Lock Case Number
subtitle: Insight
text:
backset and center distance: how to read a mortise lock case number two numbers decide whether a lock case fits the door in front of you. they are printed in the model number, and getting them wrong is the most common reason a container of hardware cannot be installed. a distributor sends a purchase order for four hundred mortise lock cases. the model number is right, the finish is right, the price is agreed. eight weeks later the cases arrive on site, the installer offers one up to a prepared door, and the handle spindle sits fifteen millimeters from where the hole is. nothing is defective. the cases were simply made for a different door preparation, and the only clue was two digits in the model number that nobody read. this happens often enough that it is worth spelling out exactly what those digits mean, because once you can read them you can specify a lock case from its name alone. center distance is the gap between the center of the cylinder hole and the center of the handle spindle, measured along the face of the lock. backset is the distance from the front edge of the faceplate back to the center of that spindle. center distance has to match the handle plate or escutcheon you are fitting. backset has to match how far in from the door edge the door was bored. they are independent of each other, and a lock case is only usable when both agree with the door. across the euro-profile range those two figures are the model number. lc08 85×55 is an 85 mm (3-3/8") center distance with a 55 mm (2-3/16") backset. lc21 85×50 is the same 85 mm (3-3/8") center distance on a 50 mm (1-15/16") backset. lc8520 compresses the same information without the separator: 85 mm center distance, 20 mm (13/16") backset. once you know the convention, a packing list becomes readable at a glance. eighty-five millimeters is the figure you will meet most often. it is the standard center distance for euro-profile cylinder locks, and it is why a european handle plate drops onto a case from almost any manufacturer without drilling. seventy-two millimeters is the other one worth knowing, it is common through latin american markets, and it is why lc34 50×72 puts the backset first: at 72 mm (2-13/16") center distance the numbers read in the reverse order, so the model name follows the market's own convention rather than ours. backset is where the real variation lives, because backset follows the door rather than the standard. narrow aluminum stiles cannot take a deep case, so 16 mm (5/8"), 17 mm (11/16") and 20 mm (13/16") backsets exist for them, that is what lc8520 at 20 mm and the 16 mm (5/8") sliding-hook cases are for. timber doors take more, and 45 mm (1-3/4"), 50 mm (1-15/16"), 55 mm (2-3/16") and 60 mm (2-3/8") are the usual span. a 70 mm (2-3/4") backset like the lc7065 puts the handle a long way in from the edge, which is what a wide entrance door with a heavy rail needs. two suffixes are worth recognizing while you are reading the number. ps marks a passage case: latch only, no cylinder, for a door that closes but does not lock. and where the model carries a bolt count (lc04 85×60 and lc14 85×50 both run four round bolts alongside the latch) you are looking at a multi-point case meant for a security or entrance door rather than an interior one. the practical sequence when you specify is short. measure the door first, not the lock: how far in is the spindle hole bored, and what center distance does the handle plate you intend to use require. then read those two figures out of the candidate model numbers. then confirm handing and faceplate dimensions, which the model number does not encode. if you are replacing existing hardware rather than fitting new doors, take the old case out and measure it, a door that was prepared once has already made both decisions for you, and matching it is cheaper than re-boring four hundred doors. ## the backsets this catalog actually carries general advice about backsets is easy to find and not much use. here is what our own range publishes, counted from the records rather than described: 180 of the 588 records in our catalog publish a backset. of those, 116 are 60mm / 70mm adjustable, a single case that can be set to either. fixed 60mm accounts for 23 more. the rest are specials, from 20mm narrow-stile cases to 90mm deep ones, each in single figures. | backset | records | what it is for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 60 / 70mm adjustable | 116 | the default. one case covers both common door preparations |
| 60mm fixed | 23 | where the preparation is known and fixed |
| 70mm fixed | 5 | thicker leaf, or a deeper handle set |
| 50mm | 7 | narrower stile |
| 45mm | 5 | narrower again |
| 40mm | 3 | narrow timber or steel stile |
| 30mm | 4 | very narrow aluminum stile |
| 65mm | 2 | one-off preparations |
| 90mm, or adjustable to 90mm | 4 | deep backset, wide stile |
| other: 16, 20, 25, 35 and 55mm | 11 | specials, one to three records each | the practical reading of that table is one sentence: if your door is prepared to either of the two common backsets, the adjustable case almost certainly fits, and you do not need to decide before ordering. it is the narrow-stile end of the range (30, 45 and 50mm) where the choice is real and where getting it wrong means a new door. ## the imperial trap, which is the one that actually costs money 60mm and 70mm are not arbitrary. they exist because they sit next to the two north american standards, and the near-miss between the two systems is where four hundred lock cases go wrong. | inch | exact mm | nominal metric | same thing? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2-3/8" | 60.3mm | 60mm | close enough to interchange in most preparations |
| 2-3/4" | 69.9mm | 70mm | close enough to interchange in most preparations |
| 2-1/2" | 63.5mm | none | no metric equivalent. neither 60 nor 70 | the first two rows are why an adjustable 60/70 case is usually the right answer for a north american door as well as a european one. the third row is the trap. a 2-1/2" backset is common on older north american mortise locks and has no metric neighbor; a 60mm case leaves the lever 3.5mm off the existing hole and a 70mm case is 6.4mm the other way. neither is a fit, and neither failure is visible until the lock is in the door. so when a schedule quotes backset in inches, convert it before you order and check which side of the two metric sizes it falls on, rather than assuming the fractions map onto the millimeters. ## center distance: what we publish, and what we do not we should be straight about this, because it is a gap rather than a strength. only 34 of the 588 records in our catalog publish a lock center distance, and 22 of those 34 say 85mm. the others are 72mm, 65mm, and a handful of one-offs. that count is smaller than it looks at first glance, and the reason is worth recording because it caught us out. the same label, `centre distance`, was also used on pull handles, where the figure is the fixing pitch between the two mounting points, written as `p=425mm` and similar. one label, two completely different measurements. we have since split them apart in our own data, and the count above is locks only. the consequence for you: if you are cross-referencing a lock case and center distance decides the fit, assume we have not published it and ask. on most of the euro-profile range the figure is 85mm, which the model number carries anyway; outside that range, it needs a drawing or a sample. ## measuring a lock you cannot take out of the door on a refurbishment the case is usually still in the leaf, and both figures can be taken from the face without removing anything. backset is from the front edge of the door to the center of the spindle. put a rule on the face of the leaf, hook it on the lock edge, and read where the center of the handle spindle falls. take it on the lock edge, not the frame, and do not measure to the edge of the escutcheon, which is a different and always larger number. center distance is from the center of the spindle to the center of the cylinder, both of which you can see on the face. measure between the centers, not between the nearest edges of the two holes, the difference is half a cylinder diameter and it is enough to order the wrong case. write both down together with the model number you are replacing, and photograph the lock edge with a rule in frame. two dimensions plus a photograph will resolve almost any cross-reference; a model number on its own frequently will not, which is where this article started. one line on the purchase order closes almost all of this: backset in millimeters, center distance in millimeters, and the model you are replacing. three fields, no fractions, no assumptions about whose standard anybody meant. where a dimension is not printed on our product pages, it is because we have not verified it for that model rather than because it does not matter. ask for the drawing before you order and we will send the one that covers the model on your schedule, or say plainly that it is still being prepared. lc08 85×55mm lc04 85*60 lc8520ps lc34 50×72mm lc7065

title: Why Aluminum Doors Drop, and What the Lock Case Has to Do With It
subtitle: Insight
text: why aluminum doors drop, and what the lock case has to do with it a narrow-stile aluminum door that no longer latches has almost never got a broken lock. it has dropped a few millimeters at the far edge, and the lock is simply the first place anyone notices. here is what actually moves, and which of it is a hardware decision. the complaint arrives in the same words every time: the lock has failed, the door will not latch, the key turns but the bolt misses the strike. in a narrow-stile aluminum door the lock is almost never the fault. the leaf has dropped (often by two or three millimeters at the lock edge) and the latch is now presenting itself below the hole it is supposed to enter. replacing the lock case fixes nothing, and it is the most common wasted purchase in this category. ## five minutes with a tape measure, before anything is ordered four checks separate a dropped leaf from an actual lock fault, and all four can be done by whoever is already standing at the door. read the gap along the lock edge, top and bottom: on a square door that reveal is parallel. if it is wider at the top than at the bottom (or the reverse) the leaf is no longer square to the frame, and that taper is the fault. two millimeters of difference over the height of the leaf is enough to make a latch miss. look for the witness mark on the strike: a latch that has been striking the plate instead of entering the hole leaves a bright scuff, and that scuff sits exactly where the latch now arrives. if the bright mark is below the hole, the leaf has dropped; if it is beside the hole, the frame has moved in or out. this is the single most direct piece of evidence available and it costs nothing to look at. open the leaf to ninety degrees and lift the free edge: take the weight on your hands and raise it gently. any perceptible lift (a millimeter is perceptible) is wear in the pivot or hinge, not in the lock. a door that lifts and then drops back is telling you where its next repair is. check the frame diagonals if the door is in a frame you can reach. corner to corner, both ways. a difference between them means the frame itself has racked, and no amount of hardware will fix a frame that is out of square; the strike can be moved to follow it, which is a repair, or the frame can be re-squared, which is the fix. the order in which these fail is the order of the repair. pivot first, strike second, lock case last, and in most of the calls that reach us, the job stops after the second. understand what a narrow stile is and the reason becomes obvious. the stile is the vertical member at the edge of the leaf, and on a commercial aluminum door it is often only 30 to 50mm (1-3/16" to 1-15/16") wide, because the client wanted glass and not frame. that leaves a 30mm (1-3/16") section of extruded aluminum to carry the entire weight of a large glazed leaf, resist the leverage of someone pulling on a handle a meter from the hinge, and house a lock cavity cut into the middle of it. the lock pocket removes material from the one part already doing the most work. three things move, in this order. the hinge or pivot side wears first, because every opening is a lever with the leaf as its arm, a 2.2 meter glazed door concentrates a great deal of moment onto a top pivot. second, the corner joints of the frame open slightly; a mitred aluminum corner held by cleats and screws is stiff but not infinitely so, and once it racks by a fraction of a degree the diagonal shortens and the free corner falls. third, and only third, the door furniture shows it, because the latch is a precision fit into a strike with perhaps 2mm (1/16") of tolerance, and it is the first component in the assembly with no slack left to absorb the movement. this is why the hardware choice that matters most on a narrow-stile door is not the lock at all: it is what carries the leaf. a floor spring set into the slab takes the weight into the structure rather than into the frame corner, which is why a heavy glazed door on a floor spring stays square for years while the same leaf on butt hinges racks its frame. if you are specifying a door that is tall, wide, glazed, or used hundreds of times a day, the pivot decision is the anti-sag decision, and it has to be made before the floor is poured. ## floor spring, pivot or hinge, what each one actually does to the frame since the anti-sag decision is the carrying decision, it is worth setting the four options side by side. they are not four grades of the same thing; they route the load to four different places. floor spring: a closer body set into the slab, with the leaf turning on a spindle above it. the weight of the leaf goes down into the structure, and the frame carries almost nothing. this is why a heavy glazed door on a floor spring stays square for years. the costs are real and they are not hardware costs: a recess has to be formed in the floor before it is poured, the cement box must be sealed against water, and replacing the unit later means opening the floor. specify it early or do not specify it at all. top-centre and bottom pivot, no closer: the same load path (weight into the threshold and the head) without the closing function. cheaper, thinner, and the right answer for an internal leaf that does not need to self-close. it is also the arrangement most often found sagging, because the bottom pivot is a small bearing under a large load and nobody inspects it. offset pivots: the pivot sits inboard of the door edge, which lets the leaf clear an adjacent wall and keeps the load close to the frame member rather than out at the corner. common on aluminum entrances with an overhead closer. butt hinges: load enters the frame as a pair of horizontal forces at the top and bottom hinge, and the top hinge pulls outwards on a jamb that in an aluminum system is an extrusion a few millimeters thick. this is fine on a small, light leaf and it is the mechanism behind most racked aluminum frames. if you have a wide glazed leaf on butt hinges, the sag is not a defect; it is the system working as designed, at a size it was not designed for. the rule that falls out of this: anything tall, wide, glazed or high-traffic goes on something that puts the weight into the floor, not into a frame corner. everything else is a preference. now the part that genuinely is a lock-case decision. in a 30mm stile there is very little metal either side of the lock pocket, so the case has to be narrow, and its backset (the distance from the door edge to the center of the follower) is fixed by the profile rather than chosen. our narrow-stile cases run at 30, 40 and 45mm (1-3/4") backsets for exactly this reason; a 60mm (2-3/8") backset case simply will not fit a narrow stile, and forcing a wider pocket into the extrusion removes the material the stile needs to stay stiff. ordering by backset first, and by everything else second, is the correct sequence for aluminum. two more details decide whether the installation survives. the first is latch throw. a door that has moved a millimeter still latches if the bolt is long enough to find the strike, and fails if it is not, which is why a hook bolt or a longer deadbolt throw is worth specifying on a wide leaf, and why our sliding hook-lock cases exist for aluminum sliders where a straight latch has nothing to bite. the second is the strike itself: an adjustable or slotted strike gives the installer a millimeter or two of vertical adjustment, and that is often the entire repair on a door that has dropped slightly. it costs almost nothing at order time and saves a site visit. so the checklist, in the order that prevents the problem rather than chases it. decide how the leaf is carried, floor spring for anything heavy, tall or glazed. measure the stile and pick the backset from it, not from a catalog habit. choose a bolt with enough throw for the leaf width, and a hook rather than a latch on sliders. specify an adjustable strike. and when a door does drop, adjust the pivot and the strike before ordering anything: the lock case is the symptom, and replacing a symptom is how the same fault comes back next season. ## six measurements that let a supplier answer in one reply almost every slow quotation on a narrow-stile door comes from the same place: the inquiry described the door in words and the supplier had to ask for numbers. these are the numbers. stile width: the face width of the vertical member at the lock edge, in millimeters. this is what decides whether a case fits at all, and it is measured on the door, not read off the system's brochure, the same profile family is sold in several widths. backset: on an existing door, from the face of the forend in the door edge to the center of the handle spindle hole. if the door is new, the backset comes from the stile and not from preference. center distance: handle spindle center to cylinder center. it is the measurement that decides whether a lever plate or escutcheon lines up with the case, and it is the one most often left out. leaf size, and glazed or solid: width and height, and whether the infill is glass. this is what determines how the leaf should be carried, which (per everything above) is the decision that actually prevents the fault. which cylinder the case is to take: euro profile, oval or something else, and the length once that is settled. a euro cylinder also needs its split, not just its total length, and that is a separate subject with its own article on this site. handing, and the profile system name: handing decides the latch orientation. the system name (the extrusion family the door is built from) tells an engineer more about the pocket than a paragraph of description will. six lines in an email. a supplier who has all six can quote a model number; a supplier missing two of them is guessing, and on aluminum a guess arrives as a case that does not fit a pocket already cut. one honest note on what we publish. our lock cases carry backset, center distance, case size and bolt throw on the product pages, because those are the numbers this decision turns on and several of them came off our own production drawings rather than out of marketing copy. what we do not yet publish is a load rating for the doors these cases suit, that depends on the leaf, the glazing and the pivot far more than on the lock, and a number invented for the lock alone would be worse than no number. send the leaf size, the stile width and the profile system, and the export team will tell you which backset fits and what to carry it on. ai8530 lc02 85×40mm lc03 85×45mm lc33-5572 lc7065 ju-071

title: Occupied or Vacant: What a Washroom Indicator Actually Has to Do
subtitle: Insight
text: occupied or vacant: what a washroom indicator actually has to do an indicator bolt is a lock and a sign in one part, and the sign is the half that gets specified badly. it has to be readable from standing distance, it has to be releasable from outside in an emergency, and on a public washroom it has to survive being operated several hundred times a day by people who are not being careful. an indicator bolt is the part on a toilet cubicle door that both locks it and tells you it is locked. that is two jobs in one casting, and the two are specified by different people: the ironmonger buys the bolt, and the person who complains about it is whoever could not tell from six feet away whether the cubicle was free. the second job is the one that decides whether the product was a good choice. mechanically it is a slide bolt. turning the inside knob drives a bolt into a keep on the frame and simultaneously rotates a colored element behind a window on the outside face, so the state of the lock and the state of the sign cannot disagree. that is the whole design argument for an indicator over a plain bolt plus a sign: a separate sign can be wrong, and this one cannot, because it is the same movement. the feature that matters most is the one nobody looks at in the catalog photograph: the emergency release. a cubicle door has to be openable from outside by a member of staff, without a key, when somebody inside cannot open it. on a well-made indicator that is a coin-slot or a screwdriver slot in the outside face which overrides the bolt. if you are comparing two indicators and only one states an override, you are comparing a washroom fitting with something that will eventually require the door to be taken off. the word to search for, and the reason this article exists, is that different markets call it different things. indicator bolt, indicator lock, occupied-vacant bolt, vacant-engaged bolt, washroom turn, and in a specification often just "privacy set with indicator". they describe the same part. our own catalog calls the category indicator, and lists the function on the 200 as "vacant & occupied indicator" with the structure named plainly as a slide bolt lock. our 200 is zinc alloy, surface mounted, in a satin or plated finish, and it is scheduled for toilet cubicle doors, restroom doors, hotels, offices, hospitals and public washrooms. surface mounted matters more than it sounds: it means the door needs no mortise and no through-preparation beyond the fixings, so an indicator can be retrofitted to a cubicle that already exists, which is most of them. the 400 and the 500 are the same idea in different metals. the 400 is zinc alloy. the 500 is stainless steel, and it is the one to specify where the washroom is cleaned with anything aggressive or where the building is coastal, a zinc casting with a plated finish and a stainless part are not the same product after two years of that. the 500 is also the one that carries a full finish range: antique brass, antique copper, polished brass, satin brass, stainless steel, bright polished, satin chrome and satin nickel. two things we do not state, and they are the two most likely to matter on a public building. we do not publish a cycle-test figure for these, so if your specification calls for a tested bolt at a stated number of operations, ask before you quote rather than assume. and we do not publish a door-thickness range on the 200 the way we do on our night latches. both are questions for our factory rather than answers we are willing to estimate, and both are on the list. for a straightforward commercial washroom the honest answer is that the indicator is rarely the expensive decision and often the visible one. get the override, get the metal right for the cleaning regime, and check that the window reads from the far end of the room rather than from arm's length, a window that is technically two-state and practically unreadable is the most common complaint about this product category, and it is never a manufacturing defect. ## surface indicator or indicator on a bathroom lock there are two ways to get an occupied-vacant sign onto a washroom door, and they suit different doors. the first is the one described above: a surface-mounted indicator bolt, like our 200, 400 and 500, which is its own lock and needs no preparation beyond its fixings. it belongs on cubicle doors and on existing doors being upgraded. the second is an indicator turn fitted to a bathroom lock: a mortise or tubular privacy lock whose inside turn operates the bolt, with an indicator on the outside in place of a plain emergency release. that arrangement belongs on a full-height washroom door in a hotel, an office or a hospital, where the door already has a lever set and a lock case and a separate slide bolt would look like an afterthought. our cylindrical locks with the bk (privacy) function are the starting point for that route, and the indicator is then a matter of the matching outside trim. the choice follows the door rather than the budget. a cubicle partition does not take a lock case; a solid washroom door with a lever set usually should not carry a surface bolt as well. ## reading the indicator from the far end of the room the complaint about unreadable windows comes from three things, and each can be specified. size: the window has to be large enough to read at the distance people actually decide from: the entrance of the washroom, not the cubicle door. contrast: red and green are the convention, but a significant share of people cannot easily tell them apart, so an indicator that also shows a word or a symbol is more legible than color alone. wording and language: "occupied" and "vacant" in the local language, or a symbol that needs no language, matters in an airport or a hotel far more than in an office where everyone knows the building. none of those is a manufacturing claim we can make about the 200, 400 or 500 from the records, which publish the metal, the finish and the mounting but not the window size or the legend. ask for a photograph of the outside face at actual size, and hold it up at the distance people will read it from. it is the cheapest test in this article. ## accessible washrooms an accessible toilet puts extra demands on the same small part. the inside control has to be operable by someone with limited grip or strength (a large turn or a lever rather than a small knob) and the emergency release outside matters more, not less, because the person inside is more likely to need help. accessibility codes differ by country on the details, so treat the local code as the specification and the product page as the starting point, and confirm the inside control shape before ordering for an accessible cubicle. ## what to write on the order for an indicator, the useful order line is short: the door type (cubicle partition or full door), the metal chosen for the cleaning regime, the finish, whether an emergency release from outside is required (it almost always is) and whether the cubicle is accessible. our 500 is published in eight finishes, from antique brass to satin nickel, and in stainless steel; the 200 and 400 in zinc alloy. if your specification also calls for a cycle figure or a panel-thickness range, say so at inquiry: as noted above, those are not published on these records, and we would rather ask the factory than estimate them. ## the keep, and why cubicle bolts stop working an indicator bolt fails in use far more often at the keep than in the bolt. the keep is the part on the partition or pilaster that the bolt slides into, and on a cubicle it is screwed into a panel that is thinner and softer than a door frame. two things go wrong. the first is sag: cubicle doors are hung on light hinges and used hard, and after a few months the door drops a few millimeters, the bolt no longer lines up with the keep, and people slam the door or force the knob to make it engage, which is when the knob breaks and the complaint arrives about the indicator. the second is fixing: screws driven into the edge of a laminate or chipboard panel pull out long before screws into timber would. both are installation matters rather than product defects, and both are cheaper to prevent than to repair. check the hinge and door alignment at handover, so the bolt meets the keep without effort. use fixings made for the panel material (through-bolts or inserts where the panel allows) rather than wood screws into an edge. and if a washroom has a history of broken indicators, look at how far the bolt is traveling into the keep before blaming the bolt. ## replacing indicators in an existing washroom most indicator orders are replacements, and the surface-mounted design is what makes them easy, with one catch. the new bolt and keep will rarely have exactly the same fixing-hole positions as the old ones, so the new holes land close to the old ones, and a panel that is already worn around its screw holes may not hold a second set nearby. before ordering replacements for a whole washroom, take one old indicator off and look at the panel behind it. if the fixing holes are sound, a like-for-like surface indicator is a ten-minute job per door. if they are not, the answer may be a cover plate, a repair to the panel, or a model whose fixings fall on fresh material. it is also the moment to fix the problems the old ones had. if they were unreadable, choose on legibility. if they corroded, change the metal: the 500 in stainless steel rather than a plated zinc casting in a washroom cleaned with anything aggressive. if staff could not open them in an emergency, make the outside release the first row of the order, not the last. 200 400 500

title: Push Bar or Touch Bar: Which Panic Device Your Door Needs
subtitle: Insight
text:
push bar or touch bar: which panic device your door needs a push bar pivots and travels; a touch bar depresses flush into its own housing. they cost differently, they fail differently, and only one of them survives a corridor that gets hit by trolleys. canton hyland builds the push-bar type across all 42 devices in the range. ask a supplier for a panic exit device and you will be offered two shapes without being told they are different products. one is a bar that stands off the door on two arms and swings toward the leaf when you push it. the other is a bar that sits almost flush in a full-width housing and sinks into that housing when you lean on it. the first is a push bar, sometimes called a crash bar or a panic bolt. the second is a touch bar, sometimes called a touch rail, or a box-style device because the working parts live inside a box. every one of the 42 devices in the canton hyland range is the push-bar type. both do the same job in the same way as far as the law is concerned. a person moving at speed, in the dark, possibly carrying someone, hits the bar anywhere along its length and the door opens. neither requires a key, a code, or a second action, and that single-motion release is the whole point: en 1125 exists because doors that need two hands or a conscious decision have killed people in fires. what separates the two is not compliance. it is mechanism, and mechanism is what determines cost, wear and how the door behaves after five years of abuse. a push bar carries its load on two pivoting arms bolted through the door. when you push, the bar travels three or four centimeters toward the leaf and rotates those arms, which retract the latch. that travel is the mechanical advantage: the arms are levers, so a light hand anywhere along a meter of bar produces enough force at the latch to pull it clear of a strike the door is pressing against. the travel is visible and the mechanism is exposed, which sounds like a disadvantage and is mostly the opposite: you can see what is worn, the moving parts are reachable without dismantling a housing, and a bent arm can be replaced on site. the exposed geometry is also why a push bar shrugs off the thing that destroys hardware in real buildings, a trolley, a bed, a pallet truck hitting the door at hip height. it hits the bar, the bar retracts, nothing binds. a touch bar hides its mechanism inside a housing that runs the full width of the door, and the bar depresses into that housing rather than traveling away from it. it looks better. on a hotel corridor or a gallery it looks considerably better, because there is no gap between bar and door collecting dust, and the profile is a clean horizontal line. it trades the lever for a cam, so the mechanical advantage comes from the shape of the cam rather than from the length of an arm, and the whole of it is inside a sealed extrusion. a distorted housing after an impact is not a part you swap; it is a device you replace. touch bars are also, as a class, more expensive to manufacture, which is why they dominate specification-led european projects and are rare on the price-sensitive end of the market. the choice usually makes itself from the building rather than from the door. a school corridor, a warehouse, a back-of-house route in a hotel, a hospital service door (anywhere carts move) takes a push bar, and takes it in stainless steel rather than a coated finish. a front-of-house fire exit in a building where the exit is visible to the public, and where nothing wider than a person passes through it, is where a touch bar earns its price. between those two cases sits most of the world, and most of the world buys push bars. one more word, because north american specifications are written in it and european catalogs often are not. exit devices are grouped by how the latching happens, not by the bar: a rim device latches against a strike on the frame and mounts on the face of the door; a mortise device drives a lock case let into the edge of the leaf; a vertical rod device throws bolts into the head and the threshold, surface-run (svr) or concealed in the leaf (cvr). the bar shape and the latching family are independent choices, which is why "push bar" answers less of a specification than it appears to. our records state the lock body and the bar length for each model rather than a family label, so if your specification names one of these four, quote the model number back to us and ask which it is, a straight answer against the drawing is worth more than a category on a web page. the same applies to dogging, the mechanism that holds the latch retracted so a door stays push-open during trading hours: it is listed on the models that have it, as an optional function, and it is not a property of the bar. two questions matter more than the bar shape and are asked less often. the first is what happens on the outside face. a panic device is an exit device: it guarantees you can get out, and says nothing about getting in. if the door is also an entrance, it needs outside trim (a lever, a knob or a pull, keyed or not) and that trim is a separate order line with its own finish and its own handing. our range carries exterior trim as its own sub-type for exactly this reason, because a device ordered without it arrives as a door that opens one way only, and that is discovered on site. the second is the double door. two leaves meeting in the middle need a decision about which leaf is active and what holds the inactive one shut. a device with top-and-bottom bolts (a multi-point or two-point locking version) pins the inactive leaf into the frame and the head, and the active leaf latches against it. ordering two single-point devices for a pair of doors produces a pair that rattles, does not seal against smoke, and will not pass an inspection. our multi-point and double-door versions exist as distinct models rather than as an option on the standard one. so compare them where the difference actually lives, which is in the load path. on a push bar the force you apply travels down two arms into two pivot points, and those pivots are bolted through the leaf. everything the bar experiences (a shoulder at running speed, a trolley, a decade of feet) arrives at those two points. they are serviceable, visible and greasable, and they are also the two places the device will eventually loosen. a touch bar spreads the same force along a pad that is supported across the full width of the housing, so no single point carries the whole event. that is the mechanical advantage people ask about, and it is real: the touch bar is the better device in a corridor where the same door is hit thousands of times by people who are not looking at it. the push bar's advantage is the opposite of subtle. its mechanism is outside the housing where a maintenance person can see it, and a bent arm is obvious from across the room. when a touch bar goes wrong, the fault is inside a sealed extrusion and the usual repair is a new device. on a site with its own maintenance team, that visibility is worth more than the smoother action. | | push bar | touch bar |
| --- | --- | --- |
| force path | two pivot arms through the leaf | spread along the full-width pad |
| projection from the leaf | larger, and it moves toward the door | smaller, the pad sinks into the housing |
| where it wears | the two pivots | the internal carriage |
| diagnosing a fault | visible from across the room | inside a sealed housing |
| usual repair | adjust or replace the arm | replace the device |
| suits | back-of-house, industrial, own maintenance | public corridors, high traffic, cleaner lines | neither row in that table is a reason on its own. read the whole column against the building: who walks through this door, how often, and who fixes it when it stops working. ## double doors: the coordinator, the astragal, and the order the leaves close in a pair of doors with exit devices raises a problem a single leaf never has. the two leaves must close in a specific order (the inactive leaf first, then the active one over it) because the astragal (the vertical strip that closes the gap between them) sits on one leaf and overlaps the other. close them in the wrong order and the active leaf lands on top of the astragal instead of behind it, and the door stands open by the thickness of that strip. a door coordinator is the small mechanical arm above the leaves that enforces that order. it holds the active leaf back until the inactive one has passed, then releases it. it is not optional on a pair with an astragal, and it is the single most frequently omitted item on a double-door schedule, usually because the schedule was written leaf by leaf, and a coordinator belongs to the pair rather than to either leaf. two more things get missed on the same opening. the inactive leaf needs flush bolts or a vertical rod device to hold it, and whoever specifies them has to decide whether they are manual (someone has to bend down) or automatic (released by the active leaf). and if the pair is fire rated, the coordinator, the bolts and both devices all have to be part of the rated assembly, a coordinator added afterwards from a different maker is a change to a tested assembly, which is exactly the situation our page on what a test report actually covers is about. on certification, we will be plain, because this is where catalogs are least honest. panic hardware sold into europe is expected to carry en 1125, and a compliant device is a tested assembly (bar, latch, trim, fixings) not a shape. so ask for the report against the specific model you are quoting, and read whose name is on it: a test another buyer paid for covers that buyer's product, and a report is only any use to you if it names the model you are buying. specify the model before the finish, because the finish never changes the test and the model always does. treat any datasheet quoting a standard number that does not exist as what it is. we have seen a competitor's page for a device in this category cite en 1205 compliance. there is no en 1205. it is a typo for en 1125 that has been copied from price list to price list for years, and it tells you how much of this industry's paperwork is transcription rather than testing. 001 015 023 et 027 301-s 310 316-d

title: What the Letters After a Model Number Mean
subtitle: Insight
text:
what the letters after a model number mean 607 pb, 607 ab, 607 sn and 607 bn are the same lock in four finishes. the letters are a finish code and a function code, read from the right, and once you can read them a price list of four hundred lines collapses into about sixty products. open any chinese hardware manufacturer's price list and you will find the same thing: four hundred lines that look like four hundred products, and are not. somewhere in there are 607 pbbk, 607 abet, 607 snet and 607 bnet, and a buyer new to the catalog reasonably assumes these are four different locks that happen to share a number. they are one lock. the digits are the product. the letters are the finish, and sometimes the function. nobody writes this down, because inside a factory it is too obvious to explain and outside one there is no way to find out. so here it is written down. the finish codes are two letters, and most of the set runs across the whole industry rather than being ours alone. pb is polished brass. ab is antique brass. ac is antique copper. sn is satin nickel. sc is satin chrome. cp is chrome plated. sb is satin brass. sp is bright polished. bn is black nickel. ss is stainless steel, and where a supplier distinguishes the two grades of it, sss is satin stainless and pss is polished stainless. two more are sprayed coatings rather than platings: w and wl are white paint, and f is a wood-grain spray. our own price list spells several of these out in its finish column (pb=polish brass on the 6094, sn=satin nickel on the 70710, sc=satin chrome on the 70610, bn black nickle on the 9211) and once you have seen the pattern once, the rest of the list reads itself. a second group of letters is the function rather than the finish. et is the entrance function, keyed from the outside. ps is passage: latch only, no cylinder, for a door that closes but never locks. bk is the privacy or bathroom function, with a turn button inside and an emergency release outside. so 607 pbbk is a 607 in polished brass, privacy function; 607 snet is the same lock in satin nickel, keyed entrance. read the letters from the right: the function comes last, the finish sits in front of it. 592 sset is ss plus et (stainless steel, entrance) not s plus set, which is why reading left to right gets this backwards. this matters commercially in a way that is easy to miss. a distributor who reads the codes stops quoting four hundred products and starts quoting sixty, each in the finishes their market actually buys. it shortens the range, shortens the conversation, and shortens the sample order, because a sample of the mechanism in one finish tells you what the other five feel like. it also changes what you check before ordering. if the letters are the finish, then the finish is the part of the order most easily got wrong, and the part a photograph settles fastest. ask for the finish you intend to order rather than accepting the one that happens to be photographed, and if a supplier sends the polished brass image against an antique copper line, treat that as a question rather than a detail. one honest caveat about our own list. where the finish column reads ab/ac/pb/sb/ss/sp/sc all available, that is the range the model can be produced in, not the finish of the piece in the photograph. a range in a specification is not a specification, and the two are worth keeping apart in your own records. a handful of older lines also carry a letter we have not confirmed the meaning of (s, e, d and a few others) and where we are not certain, our product pages say nothing rather than guessing. ## the whole table, in one place prose is a poor way to carry a lookup, so here is the set we use. most of it is industry-wide rather than ours; where a code is ours alone, it is marked. finish, the metal and its treatment | code | finish | | code | finish |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| pb / bp | polished brass | | sn | satin nickel |
| sb | satin brass | | np | nickel plated |
| ab | antique brass | | bn / nb | black nickel |
| ac | antique copper | | mb | matte black |
| cp | chrome plated | | bl / brn / orb | black |
| sc | satin chrome | | gm | gun metal |
| cb / bc | bright chrome | | gp | polished gold |
| ss | stainless steel | | wl | white |
| sss | satin stainless steel | | pvd | pvd coating |
| pss / sp | polished stainless steel | | bs | satin | function, what the lock does | code | function |
| --- | --- |
| et | entrance: keyed from the outside |
| bk | privacy: bathroom, turn button inside |
| ps | passage, latch only, no locking |
| cr | classroom, keyed outside, inside lever always free |

| el | exit latch |
| dk | double key, keyed both sides |
| s / d | single door / double door | ## the reversal trap, which is ours to own look carefully at the first table and you will find three pairs that are the same code written backwards: pb and bp both mean polished brass. bn and nb both mean black nickel. cb and bc both mean bright chrome. this is not a typo in one record; both spellings appear across the range, because they arrived from different sources over different years and nobody reconciled them. we are stating it here rather than quietly normalising it, because a buyer holding an old price list needs to know that `bp` and `pb` on two different lines are not two different finishes. the same applies to black. bl, brn and orb all resolve to black in our data, and only orb carries a distinct intent, oil-rubbed bronze, which is a black with a warm undertone rather than a neutral one. if black matters to the project, name the finish in words on the order and ask for a sample; the letters will not settle it. ## position beats letters here is the rule that makes the whole system readable, and it is the one nobody writes down. bs is a finish code meaning satin. bs is also an order code on one cylindrical lock in our range, where it means something else entirely. both are correct. the way to tell them apart is not the letters, it is where they sit in the string. finish codes sit at the end. function codes sit before them. digits (the actual mechanism) sit at the front. so the reading order is: | position | what it is | example from `5870-pbbset` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| front | the mechanism, in digits | `5870`: the lock case |
| middle | function | `et`: entrance, keyed outside |
| end | finish | `pbb`, a polished brass variant | read from the right and the string comes apart cleanly. read left to right and you will try to resolve `pb` as a finish while it is still part of the model number. this is why our own parser reads position rather than letters, and it is the same method that works on a competitor's code, see our finish codes page for what to do when nothing resolves at all. ## four codes we have not confirmed, and will not guess four letter codes appear in our own model numbers that we cannot yet explain from a source: n, kt, ik and pt. for each of them we have a plausible reading. kt beside dk looks like key-and-turn. ik appears on two cylinders only. we are not printing those readings as fact, because a plausible code definition is worse than a missing one, a buyer who orders against a guessed code gets the wrong part and has no way of knowing whose mistake it was. if one of these appears on a list you are working from, send us the model and we will confirm it against the production record rather than the catalog. that is a slower answer and it is the only one worth having. ## why we publish the ugly version of this it would be easy to print a clean table with one code per finish and no reversals, no duplicates and no unconfirmed rows. it would also be a table that stops matching the price lists people actually hold. the codes on this page are the ones in our records, including the three reversed pairs, the three spellings of black, and the four we cannot yet explain. a buyer cross-referencing an old list needs the messy version, because the messy version is what is printed on the paper in front of them. a tidy table that silently drops `bp` helps nobody holding a line that says `bp`. if you are building a purchase order from a list like this, the useful sequence is: identify the mechanism from the digits, choose the function from the third letter group, then choose the finish last and confirm it in writing against a photograph of that exact code. the first two decisions are engineering. the last one is the one that arrives in a container and either matches the door or does not. 607 pbbk 6094 pbbk 70710 sn 70610 sc

title: The Rim Night Latch: What 564 and 1073 Actually Measure
subtitle: Insight
text: the rim night latch: what 564 and 1073 actually measure a rim night latch sits on the face of the door rather than inside it, which changes every dimension that matters: backset, door thickness range, latch extension and deadbolt throw. the 564 and the 1073 answer the same job in two different metals, and the difference between single-side and double-side is a security decision rather than a convenience one. a rim lock is a lock that does not go inside the door. the case screws to the inside face of the leaf, the cylinder passes through a single hole, and the latch engages a keep screwed to the frame rather than a mortised strike. everything that follows from that is why a rim night latch is dimensioned differently from a mortise case, and why the numbers a buyer asks for are not the same numbers. start with backset, because it is the one that gets confused. on a mortise lock the backset is measured from the edge of the door to the center of the spindle. on a rim night latch it is measured from the edge of the door to the center of the cylinder hole, and on both our 564 and the 1073 it is 60mm (2-3/8"), 2-3/8 inches in the form a north american buyer will write it. that single hole is the whole of the door preparation, which is why a rim lock is the lock people fit to a door that already exists. door thickness is the next constraint, and it is a range rather than a figure: 35mm (1-3/8") to 55mm (2-3/16") as standard on both models, and 30mm (1-3/16") to 60mm (2-3/8") on request. the range exists because the cylinder tail bar has to reach the mechanism, and a cylinder too long for its door leaves the lock proud and the fixing loose. if your leaf is outside 35 to 55, say so in the inquiry rather than at the packing stage. two throws matter and they are not the same throw. the latch extension is 13mm (1/2") (that is the sprung latch that closes the door behind you) and it carries an inside deadlocking button, which is the part that turns a night latch from a door-closer into a lock. the deadbolt throw is 25mm (1") on the rim deadbolt versions, and 25mm (1") is the figure a specification usually means when it asks for a full-throw deadbolt on a rim lock. handing is the question a rim lock mostly does not have. both models are fully reversible, left or right hand, which on a lock that mounts to the face rather than into the edge is a matter of assembly rather than of a different part number. what is not reversible is the strike: an angle strike is standard for an inward-opening door, and a flat strike is available. ordering the wrong one is a site problem, not a factory one, so it belongs in the schedule. the 564 and the 1073 differ in the metal, and the difference is stated rather than implied. the 564 is a zinc die-cast case with zinc-plated steel internals, a brass thumbturn button, a brass cylinder core and an aluminum cylinder housing. the 1073 is an iron case with zinc-plated steel internals, a brass rolling latch, a brass cylinder, and it ships with three brass keys. both are residential-to-light-commercial locks; neither is presented here as a high-security product, and a project that needs one should be asking about a mortise case instead. the choice buyers actually have to make is 1073s against 1073d: single-side opening against double-side. a single-side night latch is opened by key from outside and by knob from inside, always, with no key required to get out. a double-side version needs a key on both faces. that second arrangement is more secure against somebody reaching through broken glass and less safe in a fire, and in many jurisdictions it is not permitted on a final exit door at all. it is a decision about the building, and we will supply either, but it is not a preference. one feature is worth naming because it is easy to skip in a specification: an anti-picking slide gate on the single-cylinder deadlock. that is a mechanical obstruction in the case rather than a property of the cylinder, so it is independent of whichever cylinder you key the lock with, and it is the kind of thing that does not show up in a photograph. if you are comparing our 564 against a competitor's night latch, that row is worth comparing directly, because catalogs tend to state it only when they have it. ## the rest of the family, and what actually differs the 564 and the 1073 are the two most asked-about, but they sit in a family of rim locks that share far more than their model numbers suggest. across the 260, 556, 558, 559, 5681, 5682, 5683 and the two models above, the published core is the same: a 60mm (2-3/8") backset, a 35–55mm (1-3/8" to 2-3/16") door as standard and 30–60mm (1-3/16" to 2-3/8") on request, a 13mm (1/2") latch with an inside deadlocking button, a 25mm (1") deadbolt throw on the rim deadbolt versions, an angle strike as standard, full reversibility and the anti-picking slide gate. that common core is useful: it means a door prepared for one of them is prepared for the others. what separates them is published in the rows that are not shared. the case metal: iron on the 260, 556, 558, 559, 5683 and the 1073, zinc die-cast on the 564. the latch metal: brass on the 5681, zinc alloy on the 5682, both otherwise in iron cases with three brass keys. the latch form: the 558 and the 564 are published with a bevelled latch structure. and the opening: the 1073s is single-side, while the 1073d, 5681, 5682 and 5683 are published as double-side. the 5688 is the odd one out, an iron case published at 100 × 100mm (3-15/16" square) as double cylinder, double throw. three functions are published across the family: single cylinder, double cylinder and self-locking. the first two are the single-side and double-side choice described above. self-locking is the listing's term, and it is exactly the kind of word that means slightly different things in different markets, so if it matters to your door, ask what it does on the specific model rather than assuming the behavior of a lock you have fitted before. ## fitting: the tail bar and the screws a rim lock is the lock people fit to a door that already exists, and two things decide whether that fitting is solid or merely attached. the first is the tail bar, the flat bar on the back of the cylinder that passes through the door and turns the mechanism in the case. it is supplied long and cut to the door. cut it too short and it does not engage; leave it too long and it pushes the case away from the door face. this is the practical reason the door-thickness range exists: 35 to 55mm is the span over which the standard parts work without special lengths, and the 30–60mm range on request is the same lock with a different tail bar and fixing length. measure the leaf at the lock position, not at the edge, because a panelled or rebated door is often thinner where the lock actually sits. the second is the fixings. the case screws into the face of the leaf and the keep screws into the frame, and neither is stronger than the timber it sits in. on a softwood frame the keep is the weak point of the whole installation, so use the longest screws the frame will take, and on a hollow or metal door confirm what the fixing will bite into before the order, because the answer changes the screws rather than the lock. ## the strike decides the door's opening as noted above, the angle strike is standard for an inward-opening door and a flat strike is available. the consequence is worth spelling out: a rim night latch is at home on an inward-opening door, where the angle strike wraps the frame edge and the latch engages it cleanly. on an outward-opening door the geometry changes, and the strike, the fixings and sometimes the lock choice itself change with it. state the opening direction on the schedule next to each rim lock, it costs a word and saves a site visit. ## when a rim lock is the right answer a rim lock is the right answer more often than its price suggests. it suits a timber door that already exists, a door where cutting a mortise pocket would weaken a thin stile, a secondary lock added to a door that already has a latch, and any job where the installer has one hole's worth of time rather than a mortise's. where the family publishes an application at all, it is residential, the 1073 and 5683 say so directly, and the 564 mb is published for wooden and metal doors in homes. it is the wrong answer where the door needs a rated lock, where the specification asks for a particular security grade, or where an authority wants a single-action exit on a final escape door and the proposed version is double-side. in those cases the conversation is about a mortise case or an exit device, and it is better to have it before the rim locks are on a container. ## ordering in quantity one commercial row is published for the 564 and worth knowing early: a minimum order of 1,000 pieces. other models in the family do not publish a minimum, which is not the same as having none, so if you are pricing a small project, ask for the minimum on the models you are considering in the same email as the price. mixing finishes or functions within one order is a common question, and the answer depends on the model; say what mix you need and we will tell you what is possible rather than what is convenient. 564 564 mb 1073d 1073s

title: The Six Values a Hardware Order Actually Needs
subtitle: Insight
text: the six values a hardware order actually needs most inquiries arrive with a model number and a quantity, and most of those go back with a question. six values decide whether a part can be installed, and an inquiry carrying all six can be quoted the same day. a model number is not an order. it names a family and a form; it does not say which of the variants inside that family fits the door in front of you. the gap between the two is where a week goes, because the questions are asked one at a time by email across an eight-hour time difference. six values close the gap: model, finish, backset, center distance, handing, door thickness. written in that order they read as one reference (9001-sss-60-72-l-45) and every one of them is a fact about the opening rather than a preference. nothing on that line is negotiable after the mortise is cut. model is the family. finish is the code, not the word: sss and pss are both "stainless", they are a satin and a mirror, and they do not sit next to each other on the same floor. where a us equivalent exists we publish it beside the code, because a schedule written to us32d and a factory reading sss are describing the same part and should not have to discover that by correspondence. backset is the distance from the face of the door edge to the center of the spindle, and it is set by the door, not by the lock. a 60mm (2-3/8") backset lock in a door prepared for 45mm (1-3/4") does not go in. center distance is the gap between the spindle and the cylinder, and it is what decides whether the handle and the key hole line up with the holes already drilled in the plate. handing is a letter (left, right or universal) and it is discussed in its own article because the two conventions in use disagree. door thickness is the one people assume is standard and is not: our records carry ranges like 35–45mm (1-3/8" to 1-3/4") adjustable and 35–50mm (1-3/8" to 1-15/16"), because the spindle and the fixing screws have a working travel and a 60mm (2-3/8") door is outside it. what happens when a value is missing depends on which one. a missing finish delays a quotation. a missing backset delays a shipment, because it is not visible until the case is offered up to the door and by then the container has landed. that asymmetry is the argument for writing all six at inquiry rather than the ones that feel important. two of the six are frequently unknown at inquiry, and saying so is a valid answer. "door thickness to be confirmed" is a line an export engineer can work with, it flags the risk and keeps the rest of the quotation moving. a blank is not the same thing: a blank gets filled in by whoever is in the most hurry. our guided selector asks four of the six and returns a published model with its specification rather than a category, so the reference can be pasted straight into a schedule. where a figure is not published for a model, the specification table shows a dash rather than a plausible number, the dash is a question for us, and it is cheaper to ask it now than to answer it on site. ##
