who actually knows each value part of the reason orders arrive with gaps is that no single person holds all six. knowing who does makes the missing one quick to get. model is usually the specifier's or buyer's choice. finish comes from the architect or the client, often from a general note rather than the row. backset belongs to the door: the door manufacturer knows it for new doors, and the existing door shows it on a replacement. center distance belongs to the lock case and the lever plate together, so it comes from whoever chose the lock body. handing comes from the drawings: the door's swing and which side is "outside". door thickness comes from the door schedule or the door maker. so when one value is missing, the fastest route is rarely to ask the person who sent the inquiry. it is to ask whoever owns that value, and to say so in the reply: "backset to be confirmed by the door manufacturer" is a line that gets answered. ## the mistakes each value attracts every one of the six has a characteristic way of being measured wrong. backset is measured to the case instead of to the face of the faceplate, which puts it a few millimeters out, enough to put a lever off-center on its rose. center distance is confused with other distances called by the same name: on a pull handle, the p= figure is the distance between the two fixing points, which has nothing to do with the spindle-to-cylinder distance on a lock. door thickness is taken at the edge of a panelled door rather than at the lock position, where the leaf may be thinner. handing is read from the wrong side of the door, or in the wrong convention, as our article on handing explains. finish is written as a word that two factories understand differently. and model is written without its suffix, so the function goes missing. none of these is exotic. they are the ordinary errors of a busy site, and each one is caught by the same habit: write the value together with how it was measured ("backset 60, measured from faceplate face") at least on the first order with a new supplier. ## the seventh value for anything with a key for any product with a cylinder, there is effectively a seventh value, and it is the one most often added late: keying. keyed alike, keyed to differ, or part of a master key system, and if the last, which level. cylinders are pinned before they are packed, so keying is part of the order, not a detail to settle on delivery. our articles on master key systems and on the euro cylinder range cover how to specify it. ## writing the values for a whole project for more than a handful of doors, a spreadsheet beats prose. one row per variant, with columns in the same order as the reference: model, finish, backset, center distance, handing, door thickness, then quantity, keying and remarks. two rules make it work. a value that is not yet known is written as "tbc" with the name of whoever will confirm it, never left blank. and a variant that differs in any one of the six gets its own row, even if every other value matches, because to the factory, a lock with a different backset is a different product. a sheet written that way can be answered row by row, with a model and a price against every line or a question against the one that cannot be answered yet. it also becomes the checklist at goods-in, when the cartons arrive and somebody has to confirm they contain what the doors need. ## when a value does not apply the six values are written for the product they come from (a mortise lock) and not every product has all six. a tubular lever set has a backset but no center distance, because the latch and the lever share one bored hole. a euro cylinder has neither; its equivalents are overall length and split. a pull handle has no backset at all, and its p= figure means something else entirely. the rule for those is simple: write "n/a" in the column, never leave it blank. a blank looks like a value somebody forgot; "n/a" says somebody checked. ## three references, written out here is how the reference reads for three different kinds of product, using the conventions above. a mortise lock case: our lc07 85×45mm publishes a center distance of 85mm and a backset of 45mm, so its reference carries both: *lc07 (finish per project) backset 45, center 85, handing per door, door thickness per door*. the two figures in the name are only a convenience; they still belong in their own columns. a tubular lever set: a 607 pbet is published in polished brass (us3) with the entrance function, a 60 or 70mm adjustable backset and a 35–45mm door. its reference: *607 pbet (us3) backset 60, center n/a, reversible, door 44*. the center distance is not applicable, and handing is written as reversible because the product is published that way, which is information, not an omission. a euro cylinder: our 70sn is a 70mm cylinder whose record lists a set of finishes rather than one. its reference replaces backset and center distance with length and split, and names the finish from that list: *70sn (finish as ordered) length 70, split to be confirmed against the door, keying per schedule*. the split is the value that most often goes missing on cylinders, for the reason set out in our article on euro cylinder length and split. ## why the order of the columns matters it might seem fussy to insist on the same order every time. the reason is that people read references quickly and pattern-match, and a consistent order is what lets an export engineer see at a glance which value is missing or odd. a backset in the finish column is a mistake that survives three readings when the columns move around, and is caught in one when they do not. write the values in the same order on every line and on every order, and your supplier's first reply will be about the product rather than about the form. one reference per line, in one order, with nothing left blank: it is a small discipline, and it is the one that most reliably turns a first inquiry into a first shipment. 9001 lc07 85×45mm 70sn 587 pbet

title: Lever Length, Rose Diameter, Projection: The Stainless 9000 Levers
subtitle: Insight
text:
lever length, rose diameter, projection: the stainless 9000 levers the 9014, 9007 and 9008 are stainless lever sets on a 53mm (2-1/16") rose for a 35–50mm (1-3/8" to 1-15/16") door. the 9014 publishes a 135mm (5-5/16") lever, 60mm (2-3/8") projection and a 9mm (3/8") rose; the 9007 a 132mm (5-3/16") lever, 63mm (2-1/2") projection and an 8mm (5/16") rose. the 9008 publishes six rows in total, and this article says so rather than filling the gap in. a lever handle is specified by three measurements that most catalogs bury under a photograph: how long the lever is, how wide the rose is, and how far the assembly stands off the door face. those three decide whether it fits, whether it clashes with the frame, and whether a hand can get behind it. the stainless 9000 levers in our selected range publish all three, so this is a comparison that can be made from the page rather than from a sample. the 9014 publishes a lever length of 135mm (5-5/16"), a rose diameter of 53mm (2-1/16"), a rose thickness of 9mm (3/8") and a projection of 60mm (2-3/8"), in satin stainless steel, 630 in bhma numbers, us32d in the older convention, and one of the few finishes on this site that translates to a number without a caveat, because solid stainless is a base group in a156.18 and the finish is worked into the metal rather than plated onto it. the 9007 is the same idea a few millimeters apart: a 132mm (5-3/16") lever, the same 53mm rose but 8mm (5/16") thick rather than 9mm, a 63mm (2-1/2") projection and a published lever section of 19mm (3/4") with an 8mm spindle. three millimeters more projection and three less lever is not a styling difference; it changes how the handle sits in a hand and how close the lever end comes to the frame on a narrow stile. projection is the measurement that causes site problems and the one buyers check last. it is the distance from the door face to the outermost part of the assembly, and it decides whether the door can open against a wall, whether a lever clears an adjacent door in a pair, and whether the handle catches a coat. sixty millimeters is normal for a commercial lever; the point is that both of these publish it, so it can be checked against the reveal before anything is ordered. the rose diameter matters for a different reason: it decides what the lever can cover. a 53mm rose will not hide the preparation left by a lock with a larger rose, so on a refurbishment where existing doors are being re-handled, the old rose diameter is the number to survey. it is a common way for a straightforward like-for-like replacement to turn into a joinery job. all three take a 35–50mm (1-3/8" to 1-15/16") door, which is a wider range than most of our zinc-alloy lever sets and the reason these are the ones to reach for on a heavier leaf. the cylinder in all three is brass. the bodies are stainless steel, which is what puts them in a different conversation from the zinc-alloy lh range: stainless is the specification for an exterior door, a coastal building or a washroom that gets cleaned aggressively, and zinc alloy is the specification for everywhere else. the 9008 is in this selected range and publishes six specification rows in total across its two variants: stainless steel, a brass cylinder, a 35–50mm door thickness. no lever length, no rose diameter, no projection. we are not going to infer them from the 9007 sitting next to it in the same series, because a projection copied from a neighboring model is exactly the number that causes a door not to open against a wall. it is on the list of measurements we have asked the factory for. if you are choosing between them, the practical order is: door thickness first (all three take 35–50mm, so this rarely decides it) then projection against the reveal, then lever length against the stile width, then finish. and if the answer is the 9008, ask us for the three missing figures before the order rather than after, because those are exactly the three that cannot be fixed on site. ## which stainless, exactly everything above calls these levers stainless steel, and with one exception that is all the records say: "stainless steel", with no grade. the exception is the 9088 ss, whose record states sus 304, stamped on the plate. that is worth flagging rather than glossing over, because the grade is precisely what decides whether stainless behaves as a buyer expects. grade 304 is the usual choice for interior and general exterior use; 316, with its added molybdenum, is the grade for coastal air, swimming pools and aggressive cleaning; and 201 is a cheaper grade that can mark and stain in conditions 304 shrugs off. our article on stainless steel grades 304, 201 and 316 sets out the differences properly. because the grade is not on most of these records, ask for it in writing against the model before ordering anything for an exterior, coastal or washroom door: the very places where a stainless lever is chosen over zinc alloy in the first place. a satin 630 finish looks the same on every grade. it does not last the same on every grade. ## the whole stainless lever family, side by side the 9014, 9007 and 9008 are three of a larger family. every stainless lever on this site that publishes its geometry is in the table below, taken from the specification rows, so the comparison can be made in one place rather than across nine product pages. | model | lever length | rose diameter | projection |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 9003e | 133mm | 53mm | 62mm |
| 9004s | 135mm | not published | 63mm |
| 9005e | 130mm | 53mm | 62mm |
| 9007s | 132mm | 53mm | 63mm |
| 9014 | 135mm | 53mm | 60mm |
| 9082e | 135mm | not published | not published |
| lh1016 | 130mm | 53mm | not published |
| lh1033 ss | 135mm | 53mm | 68mm |
| nc182 | 86mm | not published | not published | read across the table and the family is tighter than the model numbers suggest. lever lengths sit between 130 and 135mm (5-1/8" to 5-5/16"), the rose is 53mm (2-1/16") wherever it is published, and projection runs from 60mm on the 9014 to 68mm on the lh1033 ss. the one clear outlier is the nc182, with an 86mm (3-3/8") lever: a short lever for a narrow door or a cupboard rather than a passage door. that tightness is useful on a project. levers from this family can be mixed across a building without a hand noticing a change, and the choice between them comes down to shape, finish and function rather than size. it also means projection is the figure worth checking model by model: eight millimeters between the 9014 and the lh1033 ss is the difference between a lever that clears a return wall and one that marks it. ## where a pull handle is the better answer a lever on a rose goes with a latch or a lock, on a door that has to stay shut until someone operates it. a pull handle goes on a door that is held shut by a closer or a magnet, or not held at all, and is simply pushed from one side and pulled from the other. on a shop entrance, a corridor door on a closer or a washroom lobby, a pull handle and a push plate are often the better answer: nothing to turn, nothing to catch, and easier for someone carrying something. on a door that must latch, a pull handle alone is not a lock and should not be specified as one. pull handles are not part of this lever family, so if a door needs one, ask separately. ## functions: two published, the rest to ask about on the 9014, two variants publish a function in plain words: the 9014 sset is entrance (keyed outside) and the 9014 ssbk is privacy (the bathroom function, with a turn button inside), both in satin stainless steel (us32d). those follow the same suffix logic as our cylindrical locks, where et is entrance and bk is privacy. the other variants in the series (9007, 9007e, 9007s, 9008e, 9008s and 9014s) carry an e or s suffix that the records do not explain. it would be easy to guess, and a guess on a function code is exactly how a whole order arrives unable to lock. so we will not decode those suffixes here: tell us the function you need on each door, in words, and we will match it to the right variant rather than the other way round. ## lever shape is a safety choice as well as a style one two things about the form of a lever matter beyond how it looks. a lever whose end returns towards the door is less likely to catch a sleeve, a bag strap or a hospital gown than one that ends in a straight, open tip, which is why return-end levers are common in healthcare and schools. and a lever of any kind is easier to operate than a knob for anyone with limited grip, which is why accessibility guidance generally favors levers on doors people with disabilities will use. the 9000 levers publish their length, section and projection, so both points can be checked against the drawing rather than a photograph. the lever section is the other number a hand notices. the 9007 publishes a 19mm (3/4") section on an 8mm spindle. a section that is too thin feels sharp under load; one that is too thick is awkward for a small hand. nineteen millimeters sits in the ordinary range for a commercial lever. it is worth comparing directly if you are weighing it against a competitor's handle, because it is a row catalogs often leave out. 9014 9007s 9008s 9008e

title: 304, 201 or 316: Which Stainless Steel You Are Actually Buying
subtitle: Insight
text: 304, 201 or 316: which stainless steel you are actually buying three grades look identical in a photograph, cost differently, and behave nothing alike within sight of the sea. 201 substitutes manganese for nickel and rusts where 304 does not; 316 adds molybdenum and survives where 304 pits. here is how to tell which one you have been quoted. a stainless handle costs anywhere between four and eleven dollars from chinese factories that are all photographing the same shape against the same white background. the photographs are not lying. the metal is different, and the difference does not appear until the hardware has been on a building for a year, which is long after the container cleared, the retention was released and the buyer moved on. there are three grades in ordinary circulation. 304 is the default architectural stainless: roughly 18% chromium, 8% nickel, no deliberate molybdenum. it is what most people mean when they say stainless steel, it is what most specifications intend, and in a normal inland building it does not corrode. 201 is a substitution alloy invented when nickel got expensive, it drops the nickel to around 4% and makes up the austenite with manganese and nitrogen. it is cheaper by a fifth to a third, it polishes to a finish indistinguishable from 304 across a showroom, and it carries noticeably less corrosion resistance. 316 goes the other way, adding 2 to 3% molybdenum specifically to resist chloride attack, which is the failure mode that pits 304 near salt water and in swimming pools. ## why one rusts and the other does not stainless steel is not a metal that cannot rust. it is a metal that repairs itself. chromium above roughly 10.5% reacts with oxygen in the air to form a passive layer a few atoms thick, and when that layer is scratched it re-forms within seconds, provided there is oxygen available and nothing is attacking it chemically. everything in this article is a question about how well that film holds and how quickly it comes back. chloride is what breaks it. a chloride ion attacks the passive film at a single point, the film cannot re-form fast enough at that point, and corrosion goes downwards into a pit rather than spreading across the surface. this is why marine failure looks like freckles rather than a rusty sheet, and it is why a handle can be perfect over 99% of its area and still be rejected on site. molybdenum is a direct answer to that mechanism: the 2 to 3% in 316 stabilises the passive film specifically against chloride attack, which is the whole reason 316 exists and the reason it costs more. it is not a general upgrade, it is a targeted one. the nickel story about 201 is only half the story: substituting manganese and nitrogen for nickel keeps the alloy austenitic, which is what allows it to be formed and polished like 304. but 201 also sits lower on chromium: astm a240 lists 201 at 16.0 to 18.0% chromium and 304 at 18.0 to 20.0%. chromium is the element that makes the passive film in the first place, so the grade with less of it has a thinner margin before the film stops re-forming. the manganese does not compensate for that, because manganese was never doing that job. anyone comparing grades on paper will eventually meet the pitting resistance number, pren, calculated as the chromium percentage plus 3.3 times the molybdenum plus 16 times the nitrogen. it ranks the molybdenum grades sensibly and it is worth knowing. it also flatters the nitrogen-bearing 200 series, because that nitrogen term was derived for a different family of alloys, so a pren that puts 201 alongside 304 is arithmetic, not service experience. use it to compare 304 with 316. do not use it to argue that 201 is coastal. the practical consequence is narrow and sharp. inland, in a dry or temperate climate, 201 is usually fine for the life of the fit-out, which is why it exists and why it is not a scam. within a few kilometers of the sea, in a coastal hotel, on a pool enclosure, or anywhere the air carries chloride, 201 develops rust freckles in a single season and 304 develops them eventually. that is the specific case where 316 stops being an upgrade and starts being the only correct answer. it is also the case that produces the most warranty arguments in this industry, because the hardware did not fail, it was the wrong grade for the exposure, and nobody wrote the exposure down. ## the rust that is not the metal's fault before anyone argues about grade, it is worth separating three things that all look like the same complaint in a photograph sent from site. tea staining is a brown discolouration over a wide area, most of it shallow. it is a cosmetic failure and the part underneath is usually sound. it is also the one that gets hardware rejected, because a client does not accept a discoloured handle on the grounds that it is structurally fine. pitting is small, dark, localised and goes downwards. this is the chloride mechanism described above, and it is the one that eventually becomes a real failure. free-iron contamination is neither, and it is the one worth knowing because it gets blamed on the supplier when it was caused on site. stainless steel picks up particles of ordinary carbon steel very easily: from steel wool, from a wire brush that has been used on mild steel, from grinding dust drifting across a building, from a blade that cut something else first. those particles rust, and they rust sitting on a perfectly good stainless surface, so the part appears to be rusting when in fact something on it is. grade makes no difference whatsoever to this. it looks identical on 316. the distinction has a commercial consequence. rust freckles appearing within days of installation, in a pattern that follows where somebody worked, are almost never the alloy. rust appearing over a season, concentrated on the seaward face, usually is. three habits prevent most of it and none of them cost anything. never clean stainless with steel wool, use a nylon pad or a cloth. do not use chloride-based cleaners on it, which quietly rules out a large share of bathroom and kitchen products, and rinse anything that has been on it. rinse coastal hardware with fresh water periodically; the salt film is what sustains the attack, and rain does not reach a sheltered face. a building that does these three things will get more out of 304 than a building that does none of them will get out of 316. you can narrow it down on a sample without a laboratory, provided you know what the test does and does not prove. take a magnet to it. properly annealed 304 is essentially non-magnetic, and a fridge magnet slides off; 201 is usually weakly magnetic and the magnet drags or tugs. this is a useful screen and it is not proof: cold working (the stamping and forming that makes a rose or a plate) induces magnetism in 304 too, so a magnetic edge on a pressed part means nothing on its own. test the flat, unformed area, compare against a sample you trust, and treat a strong pull as a reason to ask rather than a verdict. if the answer matters commercially, the only thing that settles it is a material certificate or a positive material identification test on the delivered goods, and both are things you are entitled to ask for before you place the order rather than after. two more things travel under the same word and are not grades at all. the first is finish: sss is satin stainless, pss is polished stainless, and both codes describe the surface treatment, not the alloy underneath. a polished 201 handle and a polished 304 handle carry the same finish code. the second is construction. a great deal of hardware sold as stainless is stainless-clad or stainless-plated over zinc alloy or steel, which behaves like the substrate as soon as the skin is scratched. if a lever is priced far below the others in a comparison, the interesting question is usually not the grade but whether it is solid at all. we will be direct about our own catalog, because the audit that prompted this article was of our own data. of the 165 canton hyland records whose material field mentions stainless steel, 21 state a grade explicitly, some as 304, some as 201, several as "304/201" where the model is genuinely offered in both. the remaining records say "stainless steel" and stop. that is a gap in our published data, not a gap in the factory: the grade is known at production and is confirmed on request against a specific model and order quantity. we are filling it in as the records are revised, and in the meantime the honest instruction is to ask, and to get the answer in writing on the proforma rather than in a chat message. ## what a material certificate is, and what it is not if the grade matters commercially, the document that settles it has a standard behind it. en 10204 defines four types of inspection document, and the difference between them is the whole point. type 2.1 is a declaration that the material complies with the order. no test results. type 2.2 is a test report with results, but from non-specific inspection, results from the mill's routine production, not from your material. type 3.1 is an inspection certificate with results from specific inspection on the material actually supplied, validated by the manufacturer's authorized inspection representative, independent of the manufacturing department. type 3.2 is the same, countersigned by an inspector acting for the purchaser or named in regulations. in practice a specifier who writes "stainless" gets nothing, one who writes "304" gets an assertion, and one who writes "304 with en 10204 3.1" gets a document naming a heat number that can be checked against a mill. now the limits, because this is where the paperwork stops being magic. a mill certificate covers a heat of raw material, not a finished handle. it says what came out of the furnace; it does not by itself prove that the bar in your lever came from that heat. what connects the two is traceability through the factory, and traceability is a process, not a piece of paper. ask for both or accept that you have one. and a certificate for the shell says nothing about the parts inside it. a lever can be 304 and run on a mild steel spindle in a zinc rose. if the exposure is coastal, the fixing screws and the spindle are as much of the specification as the alloy of the visible part, and they are the components most often left out of the conversation. for our own goods, the honest statement is the one in the section above: the grade is known at production and we confirm it against a specific model and order quantity, in writing on the proforma. where a project needs mill documentation for the material used, that is a question to raise before the order rather than after, because whether it can be passed through depends on the mill and on the quantity, and a supplier who promises a certificate without asking either of those questions has not checked. the question to send a supplier is not "is this stainless steel?", because the answer is always yes and it settles nothing. ask three things in one line: which grade, solid or plated, and will you state it on the invoice. a supplier who answers all three specifically is quoting you a real product. a supplier who answers "high quality stainless" is quoting you a photograph. one last note on where grade genuinely does not matter. interior door furniture in a dry building (a bathroom hook in a private house, an indicator on an office door, a hinge in a corridor) is not an environment that distinguishes these alloys within any reasonable service life. specifying 316 there is money spent on a certificate. the grade conversation is worth having on external doors, coastal and marine projects, pool and spa areas, commercial kitchens and anywhere cleaning is done with chloride-based products. everywhere else, buy 304 and spend the difference on the lock. lh1033 ss lh1016 ncb 301-s gl125 ss

title: Trim Handle or Panic Bar: What the Outside of a Fire Exit Door Needs
subtitle: Insight
text: trim handle or panic bar: what the outside of a fire exit door needs a panic bar opens the door from inside. it does nothing for the person outside. the part that lets them in is a separate order line, and getting the two confused is the most common way an exit-door schedule arrives incomplete. a panic exit device is a one-way instrument. somebody inside falls against the bar under load, the latch retracts, the door opens. that is the whole specification, and it is deliberately the whole specification: en 1125 exists so that a person in smoke who has never seen the door before can leave without being taught anything. nothing about that mechanism helps the person standing on the other side. so the outside of the door is a second decision. on a pure escape route it may be nothing at all, a blank face, no handle, no keyway, and anyone who wants in goes round. on a door that is also used every day, or that a caretaker has to enter, it needs a trim handle: a lever and escutcheon that fits the same door preparation and, with a cylinder, retracts the same latch from outside. the two are not variants of one product. they are two products that are fitted to the same door, share the same spindle and the same fixing centers, and are ordered on separate lines. a schedule that says "panic device, single door, ×12" is a schedule that will arrive with twelve bars and no way in. the confusion is easy to explain. trade catalogs (ours included, until this month) file the trim under the range it works with, so the model number carries the panic device's family name and the listing photograph shows a lever. a buyer searching for a panic bar lands on a page showing a handle, decides the catalog is wrong, and leaves. the naming is the problem, not the part. what to check on a drawing, in the order it matters. first, whether the outside is specified at all: an omission and a deliberate blank face look identical on paper, so the schedule has to say which. second, the function of the trim, free entry, key-operated, or locked with the key retracting the latch. third, the cylinder: the trim's cutout diameter has to accept the cylinder the rest of the building is keyed to, and a 32mm (1-1/4") cutout will not take a plate drilled for something else. fourth, and the one that causes the most site returns, the fixing centers. the trim's screws pass through the door and into the panic device's own body, which means the two have to be designed for each other. a trim from one range on a bar from another will hold on the bench and work loose in service, and the door it is on is the door people leave by. the practical rule for a schedule: every exit door gets two lines, and one of them may legitimately read "no outside trim". writing that line down is what turns an omission into a decision. it costs nothing at specification and it is the difference between a container that installs and a container that waits. our exit range and the trims that work with it are published as separate records with their own dimensions, because that is how they are ordered. where a trim is listed under a panic-device model number, the specification table now names it as a trim handle on the first row, the model number keeps its history, and the page stops arguing with the person reading it. ## the trims we publish, by what they do reading the trims by function rather than by model number makes the choice short. on our range they fall into four groups. passage, always free from outside. the 023 ps is published with a passage function: the outside lever always retracts the latch, with no key. it suits a door that is an escape route from inside and an ordinary entrance from outside during the day. keyed, locked from outside, opened by key: the 016 is an outside lever with a key, key operated and reversible. the 028 is an external lever with key-operated locking and unlocking, published for doors of 35–55mm. the 039 includes a brass cylinder with key, for fire-rated metal or timber doors of 45–50mm. the x2 is brass, supplied with three brass keys, for doors up to 90mm, and the 015 is supplied with three brass keys for doors up to 80mm. these are the usual answer for a door a caretaker or staff member must be able to enter while everyone else can only leave. anti-pick keyed: the 023 etan is a keyed exterior trim published as anti-pick, for outside faces exposed to tampering (a service yard, a rear entrance on a street). plate sizes and levers: where the records publish geometry, the plates range from 178 × 52mm on the 030 to 300 × 75mm on the 001, and lever lengths from 122mm on the 027 to 140mm on the 030. the 027 also publishes a 60mm spindle length. those numbers matter when the outside face of the door already carries a kick plate, a sign or a vision panel near the lock height. ## door thickness belongs to the trim the most common reason a correctly chosen trim cannot be fitted is the door, not the trim or the bar. a trim's spindle and fixing screws pass through the leaf, so each trim has a range of door thicknesses it can reach. on ours that runs from 45–50mm on the 039, through 35–55mm on the 028 and 037, to up to 80mm on the 015 and up to 90mm on the x2. a trim chosen for a 45mm timber door will not reach through a 60mm steel fire door. write the leaf thickness on the trim's line of the schedule, not just on the device's. ## the outside face on a fire door on a fire-rated opening, the trim is part of the rated assembly as much as the device is. two points follow. first, a trim added to a rated door should be one intended for fire door use and for the specific device (several of ours are published for fire doors, and the 039 specifically for fire-rated metal or timber doors), because a trim that does not suit the device can loosen in service, as described above, and on a fire door a loose fitting is a failed fitting. second, whatever evidence covers the door assembly has to include the outside trim, or at least not exclude it. ask what the assembly was tested with before adding hardware to it. ## writing the second line here is what the two lines look like on a schedule, for three typical doors. *escape stair door, no entry from outside: device, rim, push bar, length to leaf; outside, none (blank face).* *rear staff entrance: device, rim, push bar; outside, keyed lever trim, key to building master, leaf 54mm.* *lobby door, open during the day: device, rim, push bar; outside, passage lever trim, leaf 45mm.* each of those second lines is a decision somebody has made. the first one especially ("none") is the line most often missing and most often needed, because without it nobody can tell whether the blank face was intended or forgotten. when the device and the trim arrive as two lines, in the right thickness, with the right function, the door is installed in one visit. ## the cylinder in the trim, and the building's keys a keyed trim is only as useful as the key that opens it, and that key usually has to belong to the building's system rather than to the trim. three rows on our trims decide how that works. some are supplied with their own cylinder and keys: the 030 includes a brass cylinder with two brass keys, the 039 a brass cylinder with key, the x2 and the 015 three brass keys each. some publish the cutout the cylinder has to fit: the 001 is published with a ø32mm (1-1/4") cylinder cutout, which is the number to check against the cylinders the rest of the building uses. and none of that is a substitute for a keying instruction on the order. the practical rule is to decide at order stage whether the trim's cylinder is keyed into the building's master system or supplied keyed to differ, exactly as for any other cylinder on the project. a trim that arrives with its own pair of keys on a building run on one master key is a trim that either gets a new cylinder on site or becomes the one door the caretaker cannot open. ## projection on the outside face the outside of an exit door is usually the side facing a corridor, a yard or a street, and whatever stands off that face is in the way of whatever passes it. two of our trims publish their projection: the 001 at 60mm (2-3/8") and the 030 at 40mm (1-9/16"). on a door opening into a narrow service corridor, or one where trolleys and bins are wheeled past, that difference is the difference between a handle that is knocked every day and one that is not. it is also the figure to check against anything else fixed to the outside face at the same height, and against the door stop if the door swings back against a wall on that side. none of this changes the principle of the article: the outside of an exit door is its own decision, on its own line. it simply means that line has a few more figures in it than "lever, keyed". two lines per exit door, each with its own thickness, function and keying: that is the whole of the rule, and it is the one that keeps a container of exit hardware installable on arrival. 015 016 027 305 310

title: UL 305 Is a Listing, Not a Grade
subtitle: Insight
text: ul 305 is a listing, not a grade en 1125 is a standard you test against. ansi/bhma a156.3 is a standard that grades you 1, 2 or 3. ul 305 is neither, it is the basis for a listing, which is an ongoing arrangement with a certification body rather than a document you hold. confusing the three is how a compliant-looking device fails a submittal. three numbers turn up in panic-hardware inquiries and they are usually treated as interchangeable: en 1125, ansi/bhma a156.3, and ul 305. they are not three grades of the same thing, and they are not even three of the same kind of thing. one is a performance standard, one is a grading standard, and one is the basis of a listing. getting the category wrong is more expensive than getting the number wrong, because a device can satisfy one and be irrelevant to another. en 1125 is the european standard for panic exit devices operated by a horizontal bar, on escape routes used by the public. you demonstrate compliance by testing, and what you end up holding is a report against a specific model. its companion en 179 covers emergency exit devices operated by a lever or a pad, for buildings where the occupants know the way out. we have written about the difference between those two elsewhere on this site. ansi/bhma a156.3 is the north american standard for exit devices, and it does something the european standard does not: it sorts products into grade 1, grade 2 and grade 3 on a cycle-test basis. grade 1 is tested to a higher cycle count than grade 3. both are graded exit devices; the grade is a durability classification, not a pass or a fail. this is the number a specifier means when they write "grade 1" on a schedule. ul 305 is the third kind. it is ul's standard for panic hardware, and the thing a manufacturer obtains against it is a listing, not a certificate in a drawer, but an ongoing arrangement in which the certification body inspects the factory periodically and the product carries a mark. that is the practical difference worth knowing: a test report is a photograph of one model on one date, and a listing is a continuing claim about production. they cost differently for that reason, and they lapse differently. which of them your project is under is decided by the building, not by the supplier. a door in a european member state under a public escape route is an en 1125 conversation. a door in a north american jurisdiction where the authority enforces the model code and the specification is written by an architect is an a156.3 conversation, and if that specification also says "ul listed" it is a ul 305 conversation on top. those are not alternatives, and a project can require two of them at once. now our own position, plainly, because this is where catalogs go quiet. our en 1125 evidence is a test report from intertek testing services shenzhen ltd., guangzhou branch, reference 130722068gzu-001, issued 7 november 2013, and it covers one model: kd070/30-290. there is also a ce certificate of conformity to en 1125:2008 from celab, italy. both issuers restrict redistribution, so we supply them against a named tender rather than as a download. there is no ansi/bhma certification, and no ul listing appears among the credentials this factory holds. we state that rather than leaving it to be discovered, because a north american specification that says "ul listed" cannot be met by us today, and the honest moment to find that out is before the quotation rather than at the submittal. if your project requires a listing, tell us at inquiry stage; it changes what we can offer and it changes it before anybody has spent money. a last note on the number itself, because it has cost us an inquiry already. our own catalog contains a panic exit device model 305, and a fire-door version of it. that is a model number in our own series and it has no relationship whatever to ul 305. if you are searching for one and find the other, the coincidence is exactly that. what our 305 does state is a fire rating, and a fire rating is a fourth axis again: it belongs to a tested door assembly (leaf, frame, hinges, closer and device) rather than to the device on its own. ## checking any supplier's claim in five minutes everything above can be verified without taking anyone's word for it, including ours, and a buyer who does the checks below before a quotation will save more money than any negotiation on price. a ul listing: search the manufacturer's name in ul product iq, ul's public certification directory. a genuine listing appears there under the company that holds it, with a file number and the product category it covers. if a supplier claims a listing and you cannot find it, ask for the file number; if they cannot give you one, you have your answer. note also whose name is on the listing: a device listed to a brand owner and made by a different factory is legitimate, but the listing belongs to the name in the directory, not to whoever is quoting you. an ansi/bhma grade: bhma publishes a directory of certified products. a grade claim that does not appear there is a claim about a test the supplier says they passed, not a certification, and those are different things for a specifier who has to defend a submittal. an en 1125 claim: ask for the report or certificate and read its scope: the issuing body, the reference, the date, the edition of the standard, and the exact model covered. for a ce-marked device, the marking should point to the body and the document behind it. our own en 1125 evidence is described above in exactly those terms (issuer, reference, date and the single model covered) because that is the standard of answer a buyer should expect from anyone. ## fire exit hardware: the listing within the listing in north american practice, a panic device on a fire-rated door is a further case again. it has to be panic hardware and it has to be suitable for the fire door, which in the ul system means hardware tested for fire door use as well as for panic operation, commonly described as fire exit hardware. a device listed only as panic hardware is not automatically acceptable on a rated opening, and a specification that says "ul listed fire exit hardware" is asking for both. this is also where fire claims on product pages deserve the most scepticism, ours included. a duration such as "1.5 hours" or "2.5 hours" means something only as the rating of a tested door assembly, identified in a report or a listing. standing alone next to a device, it describes an expectation, not evidence. ask what assembly was tested, by whom, and against which standard, and if the answer is a figure with no document, treat it as a figure with no document. ## if your specification says "ul listed" the first thing to establish is which doors the requirement actually covers. on many projects the listed requirement applies to particular openings (rated doors, escape routes, doors named in the fire strategy) and not to every door that carries a lever or a bar. a hardware schedule that marks the requirement opening by opening often turns out to need listed devices on a fraction of the doors rather than on all of them. for the openings that do require a listing, the requirement is not negotiable with us, and it would be wrong to pretend otherwise. our 307 and 311 have been submitted for testing, and until certificate numbers exist we will not imply a listing, a grade or a ul-recognised fire rating for them. for the openings that do not require one (back-of-house doors, stores, doors outside the regulated route) the conversation is an ordinary one about the leaf, the length and the trim, and we can have it today. what we will not do is suggest a substitution request to get round a written requirement. an architect who specified a listing did so for a reason, and a supplier who quietly supplies an unlisted device against that specification has transferred the risk to whoever signs the door off. better to know at inquiry, when the answer changes what you order, than at inspection, when it changes what you remove. ## why a listing costs more than a report buyers sometimes ask why a listed device is priced above an otherwise similar one with a test report. the answer is in the definition above: a report is a single test of a single model on a single date, while a listing is a continuing arrangement, with the certification body inspecting production periodically and the manufacturer maintaining the conditions of the listing between visits. that ongoing cost is real, it is carried by every device made under the listing, and it is what makes the listing mean something about the device in your particular carton rather than about one sample years ago. ## at goods-in: check the device, not the paperwork the directory search proves a listing exists. it does not prove the device in the carton is the listed one. a listed product carries the certification mark on the product or its label, and an inspector will look for it on the door, not in the submittal folder. so the last check happens when the delivery arrives: open one carton from each batch, find the mark or label on the device, photograph it, and compare it with the listing you looked up: company, product and category. a mark that does not match a directory entry, or a device with no mark at all where a listing was ordered, is a problem to raise with the supplier that day, while the goods are still in their packaging and still returnable. it takes ten minutes per delivery, and it is the only check in this article that looks at what was actually shipped. 305 307 311

title: What One Frameless Glass Door Actually Needs
subtitle: Insight
text: what one frameless glass door actually needs a frameless glass door is not a product, it is an assembly of six or seven parts ordered from three different categories. buyers quote the handle, forget the floor spring, and discover the over-panel patch on site. here is the whole list, in the order it gets forgotten. nobody sells a frameless glass door. what gets sold is a sheet of toughened glass with holes and notches cut into it before tempering, plus six or seven separate metal parts that clamp to it. the glass comes from a local processor. the metal comes from us. the part nobody remembers to order is almost always the same one, and it is not the handle. start at the bottom, because that is where the door's weight and its entire closing behavior live. a frameless door pivots on a floor spring, a hydraulic body set into the finished floor in a cement box, carrying the leaf's weight and controlling how fast it swings back. it is the most expensive single item on the list, it is the one with the longest lead time, and it has to be ordered before the floor screed is poured, because retrofitting one means cutting up a finished floor. our ju-series floor springs sit in the door-closers category rather than under glass, which is a catalog convention rather than a hint about what they are for, and it is a common reason a glass-door quote comes back missing its most important line. the floor spring does not touch the glass directly. a bottom patch fitting clamps to the lower corner of the leaf and engages the spring's spindle, transferring the load. at the top, a matching top patch fitting takes a pivot pin. those two are the minimum, and they are handed as a pair for a single door, which means a pair of doors needs two sets, mirrored, and ordering four identical patches gets you two doors that both open the wrong way. above the door, if the opening is taller than the leaf, there is a fixed glass over-panel, and the joint between door and over-panel takes an over-panel patch, a connector that clamps both sheets and carries the top pivot. this is the part that gets discovered on site. a buyer measures the door, orders top and bottom patches, and finds on installation day that the top patch has nothing to fix to, because the head of the opening is glass rather than structure. if there is glass above the door, there is a third patch in the order. then the lock, and here the sequence matters more than the part. a glass door lock is a patch-style body clamped to the leaf, engaging either a floor socket or a strike in the adjacent panel. both the lock body and its counterpart need cut-outs in the glass, and toughened glass cannot be cut, drilled or notched after tempering. every hole, every notch, every corner cut-out has to be on the processor's drawing before the sheet goes in the furnace. deciding to add a lock after the glass is made means buying the glass again. this is the single most expensive mistake on a frameless job and it is always a sequencing mistake, never a hardware one. ## the drawing is the order on a frameless job the real deliverable is not the glass and not the hardware. it is the cutting drawing the processor works from, and it is produced before either exists. every cut-out on that drawing comes from a specific hardware model: the notch depth for a patch fitting, the corner cut for a lock body, the hole centers for a pull handle, the position and size of the floor-socket recess. change the model and the drawing changes. approve the drawing and the model is fixed, because the sheet is about to be tempered and after that nothing can be altered. that makes the handover between three parties the actual risk on the project, and it is usually nobody's named job: the hardware supplier owns the cut-out dimensions: they come from the production drawing of the specific model, not from a generic glass-door template, and a template downloaded for a similar-looking fitting is the most common way a wrong notch reaches the furnace. the glass processor owns the limits: minimum distance from a hole to the edge, minimum distance between holes, the smallest radius they can cut, and the tolerance they hold. these vary by processor and by machine, and they are not something to assume from a previous job. ask, in writing, before the drawing is approved. somebody has to own the check: one person comparing the model numbers on the purchase order against the model numbers on the drawing, once, before it is released. that check takes ten minutes and it is the only thing standing between a specification change and a second sheet of toughened glass. the reason this sequence is unforgiving is physical rather than commercial. toughening puts the glass surface into compression and its core into tension, and the sheet only holds together because those two are balanced. cut it afterwards and the balance goes, which is why a tempered sheet does not chip when you drill it, it disintegrates. there is no careful way to add a hole later. there is only ordering the glass again. last, the pull handle, which is the part everyone starts with. ours run from 300mm (11-13/16") to 600mm (23-5/8") in the 100-series, in back-to-back and single-sided arrangements, and the number that matters is not the overall length but the fixing center, the distance between the two holes, because the holes are in the glass and the glass is already made. our published center distances come off the production drawings rather than off marketing copy, and they differ between models that look identical: 148mm (5-13/16") on the 100 and the 107, 147mm (5-13/16") on the 102, 125mm (4-15/16") on the 106. a millimeter is not a rounding error when the hole is already drilled. so the checklist for one door, in the order things go wrong: floor spring, bottom patch, top patch, over-panel patch if there is glass above, lock body, floor socket or strike, pull handle. then two numbers that govern all of them, the glass thickness, because patch fittings are made for a specific range and 10mm (3/8") and 12mm (1/2") are not interchangeable, and the fixing center on the handle. our patch range is built for 10 to 12mm (3/8" to 1/2") toughened glass; confirm the thickness with the processor before the fittings are ordered, not after. ## choosing the floor spring, and the decisions buried inside it it is the most expensive item, the longest lead time and the one that cannot be changed afterwards, so it is worth spending a paragraph on what actually selects it. leaf weight and leaf width, together: weight is what the unit carries; width is the leverage it has to control. a narrow heavy leaf and a wide light leaf are different problems, and a unit sized on weight alone will close a wide door either too slowly to latch or fast enough to be dangerous. send both numbers, and for glass send the thickness and the sheet size, a processor or the hardware supplier can turn that into a weight. hold-open, or not: a floor spring can be specified to hold the leaf open at a set angle. in a shop that is wanted daily. on any door that forms part of a fire or smoke compartment it is not permitted, because a held-open leaf is an open leaf. this is a decision about the building, taken once, and it is not a setting anybody should be changing on site. two speeds, not one: closing speed brings the leaf most of the way, and latching speed governs the last few degrees. a unit set to close gently enough to feel safe will not push a latch home; a unit set to latch reliably will slam if it carries that speed the whole way. both are adjustable and both should be set at commissioning, with the door in its final state, not before the floor covering goes down. the box, and water: the spring body sits in a cement box cast into the slab. in an entrance the box will meet water: rain carried in on feet, floor washing, and in some buildings the screed itself while it cures. the box has to be sealed and it has to drain somewhere, and this is the part that decides whether the unit is serviceable in five years or seized. what we do not publish is a leaf weight or width rating against each floor spring, for the same reason we do not publish one against the narrow-stile lock cases: the correct figure depends on the leaf, the glass and the installation far more than on our part, and a number invented for the part alone is worse than no number. send the leaf size and the glass thickness and ask for the unit by name. ## a pair of doors is not two single doors the list above is for one leaf. a double frameless entrance is the more common case in a shop or a lobby, and four things change, none of which follow from doubling the quantity. everything handed doubles as a mirrored pair, not as two of the same. patch fittings, lock body, floor spring if it is handed. ordering four identical top patches and four identical bottom patches produces two leaves that swing the same way, which on a pair means one of them fouls the other. say "one pair, left and right" rather than "quantity four". only one leaf usually locks: the standard arrangement is an active leaf carrying the lock and an inactive leaf held by a floor bolt or a shoot bolt into the head and the floor. that means the two leaves have different cut-outs, and therefore two different drawings from the same order. a processor sent one drawing and told to make two is a job that arrives with the lock notch in the wrong leaf. the meeting point has to be decided before the glass, not after. whether the leaves close edge to edge, whether there is a gap, and whether anything seals it. this governs the width of each leaf, and leaf width on a frameless pair is not simply the opening halved. the floor work doubles and has to be set out together: two floor spring boxes and, usually, a floor socket for the inactive leaf's bolt. all three are cast into the floor, all three have to be positioned from the same setting-out, and none of them can be moved afterwards. this is the item that turns a hardware error into a building error. the practical instruction is the same as for a single door, with one word added: send the opening width and how it is divided, and ask for the parts list as a pair. a pair quoted as two singles is missing at least the handing and usually the floor socket. one thing we do not currently publish, and should: which of our patch fittings, locks and floor springs are designed to work together as a set. we make all three and the combinations are known in the factory, but a buyer cannot see them here: the patch fittings and locks sit in different categories, the floor springs are not listed on this site at all, and nothing joins them up. until that is fixed on the site, send the export team the leaf size, the glass thickness, whether there is an over-panel and whether the door needs to lock, and ask for the parts list rather than for a price on a handle. it takes one email and it prevents the two failures above, both of which cost more than the hardware. f101 f110 f112 gl125 ss 100 107 ju-071

title: A Test Report Covers a Model, Not a Range
subtitle: Insight
text: a test report covers a model, not a range our en 1125 report covers one exit device: kd070/30-290. our durability report covers one lock: 607 ss et. neither covers the family it sits in, and a supplier who lets you believe otherwise has handed you a problem that surfaces at handover. there is a sentence that appears on hardware websites everywhere, and it is doing more work than it looks: "ce certified", "en 1125 approved", "tested to ansi grade 1". read as a claim about a company it sounds like a credential. read as a claim about a product it is unfinished, because certification does not attach to companies or to ranges. it attaches to the specific configuration that went into the test rig. our own documents are a good illustration, so here they are with their scope stated. an en 1125 report on panic exit devices operated by a horizontal bar, issued by intertek testing services shenzhen ltd., guangzhou branch, reference 130722068gzu-001, 7 november 2013, it covers model kd070/30-290. a tubular door lock durability test from the same laboratory, reference 140306043gzu-001, 28 april 2014, it covers 607 ss et. a ce certificate of conformity to en 1125:2008 from celab in italy, 2010, covering the panic exit device series. notice what that list does not say. it does not say every panic device we make is en 1125 tested. it does not say the 607 family is durability tested, it says one member of it is, in stainless steel, in the et function. change the finish, change the function suffix, change the backset, and you have changed the product the report describes, sometimes trivially and sometimes not. which of those changes matter is a question for the laboratory and the standard, not for a salesperson. this is also why the dates matter and why we print them. a 2013 report is a real report; it is also thirteen years old, and standards get revised. if a project needs current evidence against the current edition of a standard, the honest answer is that a re-test is required, and the useful answer tells you that before the order rather than after the inspector asks. the related distinction that catches people is between a test report and a certificate. a report is a laboratory's record of what happened to a sample: this device, these cycles, this result. a certificate of conformity is a body attesting that a product meets a standard, usually with an ongoing factory-production-control obligation behind it. they are different instruments with different weight, and "we have the paperwork" collapses the difference in a way that only helps the seller. separately from the product documents, our quality management system has been certified to iso 9001 since 2002. that is a real and useful thing, and it is worth being precise about what it means: iso 9001 says the factory has a documented, audited process for doing what it says it does. it is not a performance rating for any product. a factory can hold iso 9001 and ship a lock that was never tested to anything, entirely consistently. we publish the test documents' facts (title, issuer, reference number, issue date and the exact model covered) rather than the scans themselves, because the reports are the issuing laboratory's to distribute and republishing somebody else's document is not ours to do. if your specification needs the document in hand, ask and we will arrange it through the proper route. what is on our certifications page is everything you need to verify it exists and to see precisely how far it reaches. the practical upshot for anyone specifying: ask for the report that covers the model number you are actually buying, in the configuration you are actually buying it in, and read the scope line before the headline. if a supplier answers that question with a family name instead of a model number, that is the answer. third-party inspection before shipment is welcome here and does not need negotiating, name the inspector and we will book the date. ## reading a test report in five lines a test report can run to dozens of pages, but the lines that decide whether it answers your question fit on a card. read them in this order. who issued it, and are they accredited for this test? a laboratory is accredited for specific test methods, not for everything. a report from a well-known laboratory is strongest when the laboratory's accreditation covers the method used, and the report or the accreditation body's public register will say so. what exactly was tested? the sample description, model number, configuration, finish, function, and often a photograph or drawing of the sample. this is the scope line described above, and it is the line that decides whether the report is about the product you are buying. against which standard, and which edition? standards are revised, and a report states the edition it tested against. a specification that names a later edition is asking a question the older report may not answer. what were the results, under what conditions? a pass is a pass under the conditions of the test: the number of cycles, the load, the temperature, the door mass. read the conditions, not just the word "pass", and compare them with what your door will actually see. when, and who signed it? the date tells you how old the evidence is; the signatures and the report reference tell you it is a finished document rather than a draft. ## which changes usually matter the report covers a configuration, and a buyer will reasonably ask which variations of that configuration are still covered. the honest answer is that the laboratory and the standard decide, not the supplier, but the direction is usually predictable. changes to the mechanism, the materials of load-bearing parts, the bolt or latch, or the fixing arrangement tend to matter, because they change what the test was testing. changes of finish color tend not to matter for a mechanical durability test, but can matter a great deal for a corrosion test, where the finish is the thing being tested. a different backset or case size is a different product for most purposes. if a variation matters to your project, ask the question in writing and ask for the answer to cite the report or the laboratory. "it's the same product" from a salesperson is not the same as a statement from whoever ran the test. ## checking a document with its issuer any report or certificate can be checked with the body that issued it. laboratories and certification bodies can confirm whether a reference number is genuine, what it covered and whether it is still valid, and many run public registers for exactly this purpose. it is a routine request, and any supplier with genuine documents should welcome it. we give the issuer, reference number and date of each of our documents precisely so that this check can be made without asking us. ## inspection before shipment a test report says a sample passed; it says nothing about the carton in your shipment. that is the job of inspection before shipment, and it is the natural companion to reading a report carefully. an independent inspector visits before the goods leave, draws samples from the finished order (commonly according to a stated sampling plan, so both sides know in advance how many pieces are checked and how many faults are acceptable) and checks them against your specification: dimensions, finish, function, marking and packaging. as noted above, third-party inspection is welcome here and does not need negotiating. what makes it useful is agreeing the checklist before production rather than on the day: which dimensions, which functions, which finish reference, which carton markings. an inspection against a vague brief finds vague faults; an inspection against the approved sample and a written checklist finds real ones, while there is still time to correct them. ## when the report is old our en 1125 report dates from 2013, and our tubular lock durability report (140306043gzu-001) from april 2014; we say so on every page that mentions them. an old report is not automatically a worthless one, but whether it is acceptable is a decision for whoever approves the door, not for us. three questions settle most cases. has the standard been revised since the report, and does the revision change the tests that matter? has the product changed since the sample was tested, in any of the ways described above? and does the authority or the specification ask for evidence within a stated period? if all three answers are favorable, an older report may be accepted. if any is not, a re-test is the honest route, and it is better to know that when the order is being planned than when the inspector is on site. ## six questions to put to any supplier none of this is special to us, and a buyer can use the same questions on every supplier they compare. which report or certificate covers the exact model and configuration i am buying? who issued it, and are they accredited for that test? which standard and edition? what date? can i verify the reference with the issuer? and is it a test report on a sample or a certificate with ongoing production control behind it? a supplier who answers all six with specifics has evidence. a supplier who answers with a family name, a logo or "all our products are certified" has told you something too. the thread through all of it is the same: evidence is specific. a model, a configuration, a standard, an edition, a date, an issuer who will confirm it. ask for those, read the scope before the headline, and inspect the shipment against the sample you approved. doing so is not suspicion of any supplier, ours included; it is how a specification survives contact with an inspector. 607 sset

title: A Padlock Chained to a Knight in Germany
subtitle: Insight
text: a padlock chained to a knight in germany our principal found it on a german street, chained around the ankles of a cast-iron knight outside a hotel, and photographed it because the older a thing is the more it draws you in. we cannot tell you who made it or when, rust removes exactly the evidence that would answer that. we can tell you what is still legible in the metal, which is more than you would expect, and why we are not going to invent the rest. our principal was walking down a street in germany when he stopped at a hotel doorway. outside it stands a cast knight in armour, holding a shield whose inscription claims the year 998 and names richeza, queen of poland, granddaughter of the emperor otto ii. chained around the knight's ankles is a padlock, and it was the padlock he photographed. he sent the pictures to the company group with one line: put this on the website. the older something is, the more it pulls people in, and the more it shows we know what we are doing. he has been cutting moulds for door hardware since 1998, so when he says an object is worth looking at, the right response is to look at it. here is what we can see, and (because this matters more) here is where our seeing stops. start with how it is held together. eight domed rivets ring the body, two at the shoulders, two down each flank, two across the foot. that is a case assembled from plates, not cast in one piece and not welded: cut, stacked, drilled, riveted cold, and the domes are the heads spread by a hammer. it is the construction you use when the joint has to hold without heat, and it is the reason the thing has survived a century of weather with its shape intact while its surface went to rust. then the keyhole, which is the most talkative part of the whole object. there is a pin standing in the middle of it. a pin means the key is hollow (a barrel key that slides over it and is centered by it) and a hollow key with a wide slot beneath means a warded lock: fixed obstructions inside that the right key is cut to pass and the wrong one is not. this is not a pin-tumbler cylinder and it was never meant to be one. it is the mechanism that secured europe for several hundred years before cylinders replaced it, and you can identify it from two meters away once you know what the pin is for. ## what that mechanism actually resisted a ward is an obstruction, not a puzzle. the plates inside the case are cut so that a key of the right shape sweeps past them and a key of the wrong shape jams against them. nothing inside measures anything. there is no stack of pins to be raised to a shear line, no lever to be lifted to a gate, only a path that is either clear or blocked. that makes the mechanism very good at one thing and poor at another. it is almost impossible to jam with dirt, ice or paint, which is why locks of this kind hung on gates, sheds and outbuildings rather than on the front doors of banks, and it is a large part of why this one still turns after whatever it has been through. it is also defeated by a key with everything cut away except the part that throws the bolt. that key has a name everybody knows and almost nobody connects to its origin: a skeleton key is skeletal because the wards have been filed off it. three inventions ended the warded lock's career in serious work, and all three are on the public record with dates. robert barron's double-acting lever lock, patented in britain in 1778, made the lock measure the key rather than merely admit it, every lever had to be lifted to its own height, neither under nor over. jeremiah chubb's detector lock of 1818 added a mechanism that seized if any lever was lifted too far, so an attempt on the lock left evidence behind. and linus yale jr.'s pin-tumbler cylinder, patented in the united states in the 1860s, moved the measuring into a small separate cylinder that could be fitted into a case somebody else had made. that last one matters more than it sounds, and it is the direct ancestor of the euro profile discussed further down this page. once the measuring part is separable, the lock case stops being the security and becomes the housing, and the day the housing is standardized, any factory's cylinder can go into any factory's door. here is the honest part, and it cuts against the rest of this article. none of that dates the padlock in the photograph. warded padlocks did not stop being made when better mechanisms arrived; they got cheaper and kept selling, and they are manufactured today for lockers, gates and toolboxes where the job is to keep an honest person honest rather than to stop a determined one. the mechanism tells you what is inside. it does not tell you what century you are holding. then the thing that has no security function at all. across the upper body sits an oval plate in a brighter metal, engraved with a scalloped arc border, and two of the rivets pass straight through it. somebody decorated a lock that was going to hang outdoors and get filthy. nobody paid for that engraving because it made the lock harder to open, they paid for it because a lock is a thing people look at while they decide whether to trust what is behind it. we recognize the impulse. it is the same one that puts a consistent finish on a spec table. now the stop. we do not know who made this lock, in what year, or in what country. we do not know whether it is as old as the building it decorates or was bought in a market fifty years ago to dress a statue. rust removes exactly the evidence that would answer those questions: the stamp, the plating, the paint, the paper. a shape like this was made by hundreds of workshops across europe and asia for a very long time, and no honest look at it narrows that down. we could write the missing paragraph. a german workshop in the 1890s, a family name, a line about the smith who set those rivets, it would read beautifully, and it would be fiction. we are not going to, and the reason is not modesty. a buyer ordering a container of hardware from a factory they have never visited is buying one thing above all others: the belief that we do not make things up. that belief is indivisible. a supplier who will invent a provenance for a padlock on a blog will invent a backset for a lock case in a quotation, and the buyer who catches the first is right to assume the second. on this site, where a dimension is not published, you get a dash instead of a plausible number. this is the same rule applied to a story. the lock is also interesting for the opposite reason to the one people expect. it is anonymous, and for most of the history of this trade that was normal: a lock was identified by the man who made it, and if you did not know him you could not buy a replacement part. what ended that was not better locks. it was standards. the profile that every european lock case is machined for today is defined by din 18252 in germany and en 1303 across europe, to a tolerance that lets a cylinder from one factory drop into a body from another, in another country, forty years later. the country where our principal found this nameless lock is the same country that wrote the standard that made namelessness safe. that is what we make. our own euro-profile cylinders run 45, 54, 60, 65, 70, 80 and 90mm (3-9/16"), and not one of those figures is ours, they belong to the standard, and the entire value of the part is that we hit them exactly. a cylinder proudly two millimeters different is not a distinctive product; it is a part that does not fit. the anonymity of the old lock and the interchangeability of the new one are the same story told twice: first the maker's name was the guarantee, then the standard replaced it. which is where twenty-eight years actually goes. a mould for one exit device takes three to five months before it produces a part anyone would sell, and most of that is not cutting steel, it is running the tool in, measuring what comes out, and correcting the tool, because metal does not do what the drawing says it will. then come the tests the part has to survive: fire, impact, cycle life, pressure. none of that shows up in a photograph. it shows up in the hundred-thousandth part matching the first. ## if you ever want to read one yourself four things survive rust, roughly in that order, and one thing does not. how the case is joined: rivets, a folded seam, a weld bead or a single cast shell. this is readable under almost any amount of corrosion because it is structure rather than surface, you can feel a rivet through rust that has hidden everything else. rivets and folded seams mean the body was built up from plate. the shackle's geometry: look at whether the bolt catches the shackle at one end or at both. heel-and-toe locking (both legs held) is the stronger arrangement and the later one; a shackle held only at the heel can be swung clear if the free leg is cut or forced, which is why a cheap padlock and an expensive one can look identical from the front and behave nothing alike. the keyhole: covered above, and the single most informative square centimeter on any old lock. a pin means a hollow key. a plain slot means a flat key. a keyway with a shaped profile means a cylinder, and a cylinder means the lock is younger than everything discussed here. the decoration: engraving, a plate in a contrasting metal, a scalloped border. it tells you nothing at all about the mechanism and a great deal about who the thing was sold to. what does not survive is the maker's stamp. a stamp is a shallow displacement of the surface (a few tenths of a millimeter) and surface is precisely what rust consumes first. if you find an old lock with a legible name on it, you have found the rare one, and it is the only one of these five that can actually answer where and when. which leads to the one piece of advice in this article. do not take a wire brush to it. abrasive cleaning removes the last tenths of the only evidence that answers the question everybody asks first. we would rather look at a rusty lock that can still be identified than a bright one that cannot, and that preference is not sentimental, it is the same instinct that makes us publish a dash instead of a guess. for the record: we do not make padlocks. canton hyland makes door hardware (locks that go into a door rather than onto a chain) and there is no padlock anywhere in our catalog. this one is on the site because our principal photographed it in the street, not because it is a product. so the padlock goes on this page as something to look at, not something to claim. it is not ours, we did not make it, and we cannot tell you who did. what we can tell you is how it was put together, what kind of key it takes, and which part of it was pure pride, and that we can read it at all is because we spend our days at the other end of the same object's life. 45 snik 60 snkt 70 sndk

title: Cutsheets, CAD and BIM: What We Have and What We Do Not
subtitle: Insight
text: cutsheets, cad and bim: what we have and what we do not people arrive here searching for a cutsheet, a dwg, a bim object or a ficha técnica. some of that we publish today, some of it we can send on request, and one of it does not exist yet. saying which is which is more useful than a download page that promises everything. a recurring shape appears in the queries that reach this site: people are not looking for a product, they are looking for a file. a cutsheet for a lock. a draftsight or dwg model. a bim object with a ficha técnica. a sample pdf. in one case somebody pasted an entire bill-of-materials line (drawing number, position, material, application) straight into a search box, which is what a purchasing engineer does when they are trying to find the part that satisfies a drawing. those are all the same request underneath: give me something i can put into my own document. so here is the honest inventory, in the order of how much of it exists. dimensioned svg assets: 84 for hyde model slugs among 588 catalog records. of these, 72 appear on the 521 product listings with photographs that buyers can browse; the other 12 belong to records that are not listed. the drawings show dimensions supported by the published source data. they are product views, not door-cutting templates. a guessed hole position is worse than no drawing because it may be believed. specifications: on every product page, as a table rather than as prose. backset, center distance, material, finish codes, cycle life where it has been tested, door thickness range, handing. where a value is missing it is missing, not estimated. if you need those in a spreadsheet rather than a page, ask and we will send them. catalog: one pdf, current. it used to be two (a designed brochure and a generated export catalog) and on 2026-09-21 the brochure was withdrawn from the download list. the one that remains is a text pdf rather than a scan: the words in it are selectable and searchable,
