which means a search engine and an ai assistant can read it. it carries every published model with its specification table, bookmarks by family, an index at the back, and it opens as a two-page spread. the withdrawn brochure was a scan, and contained zero words as far as any machine was concerned. test documents: available on request, with their exact scope. we publish the facts of each one (laboratory, reference number, issue date and the specific model covered) and send the document through the proper route when a specification needs it. there is a separate article on why the scope line matters more than the headline. now the part we do not have. there is no bim library: no revit families or ifc objects. if a model has a dimensioned drawing, we can provide it with the specification as source material for a modeller, but the geometry and missing dimensions must be checked for that use. we publish svg product views, which can be imported into cad after checking units and scale; we do not maintain a native dwg library per model. two practical notes for anyone assembling a submittal. first, ask for documents by model number in the configuration you are buying (finish and function suffix included) because a drawing of the 60mm (2-3/8") backset version is not a drawing of the 45mm (1-3/4") one. second, tell us what the document is for. a cutsheet for a client approval, a drawing for a door manufacturer's machining setup and a specification for a tender each need a different thing emphasized, and we would rather send the right one than the largest one. ## door preparation is a separate request for hyde, the count of published door-preparation svgs is 0. a dimensioned product view does not specify a complete mortise pocket, spindle and cylinder holes, faceplate recess or fixing positions. if a door shop needs a cutting template, request a manufacturer-approved drawing for the exact model and configuration, or confirm the required dimensions in writing against a physical sample before machining. do not derive a missing cutting dimension by scaling a product svg. where a dimension is not published, treat it as an open question for the factory. what a door shop usually needs is a short list, and it is worth sending it with the request. for a mortise lock case: the case height, width and depth, the faceplate length, width and thickness with its corner shape, the backset, the center distance, the spindle size and the cylinder or keyhole position. for a tubular lock or deadbolt: the face bore diameter, the edge bore diameter, the backset and the door-thickness range. where our specification table already publishes a row, we will confirm it in writing against your configuration. where a row is blank, we will take it to the factory rather than estimate it. ## which document belongs in which submittal the same product can need four different documents depending on who will read them, and sending the right one saves a round of comments. client or architect approval needs the product photograph, specification table, finish and function. a door manufacturer needs confirmed installation geometry for the exact model; the product svg may help frame the question but cannot serve as a cutting template. a tender needs quotable specification rows. a compliance reviewer needs the test document's issuer, reference, date, model scope and, where required, the document itself through the proper route. most submittal delays come from sending the largest document instead of the right one: a whole catalog where one drawing was wanted, or a photograph where a scope line was. when one submittal has to serve several readers, send the documents as separate files, each named by model number and purpose, rather than as one merged pdf. a reviewer who needs only the test scope can then find it in seconds, and a later revision replaces one file instead of reissuing the whole package. it also lets each reader forward only the file that concerns their own part of the approval. ## turning our drawings into your own cad or bim object because there is no bim library, be specific about the object you need. an svg product view can be imported into a cad or modeling package after checking its units, scale and one stated dimension against the specification. only the dimensions actually published for that model are supported. do not infer hidden geometry, machining clearances or fixing holes from an outline. a modeller can use verified dimensions to create a simple envelope for coordination, then ask for any remaining data before treating it as a fabrication model. add parameters from the specification table only where they are published: model number with finish and function suffix, backset, center distance and door-thickness range where available. a schedule cannot rely on a value that the source record leaves blank. ## asking for data in bulk if you are building a product library for many models (a distributor setting up a catalog, or a consultant standardizing a specification) ask for the specification rows as a spreadsheet for the whole family rather than page by page. the rows are the same ones published on the site, missing values included, so the spreadsheet will show a gap exactly where the page does. treat a gap as a question to send back to us, not as a cell to fill from the neighboring model. and if your market expects a document we do not produce (a bim object in a particular format, a declaration in a particular template) tell us which, and for which models. we would rather know what is being asked for across projects than guess, and a request that names the format and the models is one that can actually be planned. ## getting the most out of the catalog pdf because the remaining catalog is a text pdf rather than a scan, it can be used as a working document and not only browsed. search it: typing a model number, a backset or a finish code finds every place it appears, which is the fastest way to see a whole family side by side. use the bookmarks to jump between product families, and the index at the back when you know the model but not where it sits. copy from it: the specification tables are real text, so they can be pasted into a quotation or a schedule without retyping, and without the transcription errors that retyping brings. it is also the document to give an ai assistant, if that is how your team works. a scanned brochure is a set of pictures to a machine; this one can be read, quoted and checked against the site. that was the reason the scanned brochure was withdrawn rather than kept alongside it. ## what a dash in any of our documents means the same rule runs through every document described here, and it is worth stating once. where a value is not published, our pages, drawings, spreadsheets and catalog show a dash or leave the row out; they do not show an estimate. a dash is not an error in the document. it is a question we have not yet been able to answer from the factory's data, and it is the right place to send an inquiry. ask about the dash, and the reply will be a measured number with its source, or a plain statement that we still do not have it. if you remember one line from this article, make it this: ask for the document by model number in the exact configuration you are buying, say who will read it, and treat every dash as a question. that combination gets the right file on the first reply far more often than a request for "everything you have", which usually turns out to be more than anyone needs and less than the one thing they did need. lc07 85×45mm 70sn

title: Five Months of Tooling: How the 311 Exit Device Was Made
subtitle: Insight
text: five months of tooling: how the 311 exit device was made a customer called at eleven at night asking for a price, came to the factory the next afternoon with a sample, and asked whether we could make it. three moulds, three toolmakers, one pause of over a year, and five months of trial-and-correction later, the 311 existed. this is what buying a custom exit device actually costs a factory, and why a lead time on a tooled product is not the same number as a lead time on a catalog one. the phone rang at eleven at night and somebody was still in the office to answer it. the caller wanted unit prices on exit devices we already make. we quoted, and then the conversation turned: he wanted to come and see the parts in his hands, the next day. he arrived the following afternoon with a colleague. they spent the visit going through the range, and they found several products that suited their own factory, not one. then they produced a sample of something we did not make, and asked whether we could produce it. we said yes. that sample became the 311. what follows is not a marketing story about responsiveness. it is an account of what the yes actually committed us to, written down because buyers asking for a custom exit device are quoted a price and a lead time, and almost never told what sits underneath them. three moulds, three different trades. an exit device is not one material, so it is not one mould. the 311 needed three: an abs mould for the push bar body, a steel stamping die for the pressed components, and a zinc-alloy die-casting mould for the cast parts. before any of them could be cut there was wire-cutting and drawing, the geometry has to be fixed on paper and in the electrode before it is fixed in steel. each of those three moulds belongs to a different craftsman. they are not interchangeable skills: the man who can hold a tolerance in a zinc die is not the man who knows how abs shrinks as it cools, and neither of them sets up a stamping die. so every correction is a three-way conversation, and a change to one part propagates into the other two. when a problem appeared in trial, all three had to agree on what the fix was before anyone cut metal. the pause. the development then stopped for more than a year for reasons outside the project (the international situation at the time) and was picked up again afterwards. that gap is worth stating plainly rather than editing out of the story. tooling programs are not immune to the world around them, and a buyer who is told a tooling schedule should know that the schedule assumes nothing interrupts it. three months to cut, five months to finish. once the work resumed, the complete set of three moulds was finished in three months. that is the number people expect to hear, and it is the smaller half of the truth. what followed was trial shots, and trials find things. where a trial showed something had to change, the mould itself was modified and shot again. then the zinc-alloy and stamped-steel components went through polishing, grinding, electroplating and assembly. from first trial to a tool that could be trusted to run took five months in total. not five months of waiting: five months of making a change, shooting again, and looking at what came out. ## why correction is the long half, and cutting is the short one three months to cut, five months to finish. that ratio surprises people, and there is a physical reason for it rather than a scheduling one. a mould can be opened, not closed: removing steel from a cavity is a morning's work. putting it back means welding and re-cutting, which changes the hardness of that area and risks the surface finish for every shot afterwards. so tools are cut deliberately steel safe (with material left in) and the trials are what tell the toolmaker where to take it away. that is why the number of trials cannot be predicted at the start: each one removes the uncertainty it was run to find. each material misbehaves in its own direction: abs shrinks as it cools, and not evenly, thick sections pull in more than thin ones, so a bar that came out of the cavity straight can be bowed an hour later. zinc die-castings come out with flash at the parting line and can carry porosity where the metal froze before it was fully fed. pressed steel springs back after the die opens, so a part formed to ninety degrees relaxes to something slightly over. none of these are faults. they are properties, and the tool has to be cut to anticipate them, which means cut, shoot, measure the error, and correct. and the three corrections interact: a change to the zinc casting to cure a porosity problem moves a face that the pressed component registers against. which is the point made above about three craftsmen: a correction is not a task, it is a negotiation between three tools that all have to agree afterwards. this is also why a trial part is not evidence on its own. a trial component is usually hand-finished (flash filed off, a face lapped flat) to see whether the geometry works. it says the design is right. it does not say the tool is ready to produce that part a hundred thousand times without a hand touching it, and those are two separate approvals. why one angle decides whether it works. the requirement is not only that the part looks right. every metal component has to fit every other one, and an exit device has to do a mechanical job while it does it. get one angle wrong and the product does not work, it is not a cosmetic defect, it is a device that will not release. that is the difference between tooling a piece of hardware and tooling a piece of trim, and it is why trial-and-correction takes longer than cutting did. ## four questions to settle before a single mould is cut tooling is the one purchase in this trade where the commercial terms are harder than the engineering, and where almost nobody writes them down until there is a dispute. four questions, settled in advance, remove nearly all of it. who pays, and how? tooling is either invoiced as a cost or amortised into the unit price over an agreed quantity. both are normal. they are not the same deal, and they behave very differently if the volume does not arrive: an amortised tool that never reaches its quantity leaves an unpaid balance somebody has to own. who owns the mould? paying for a tool and owning a tool are two different things, and the difference decides whether you can move production elsewhere. settle it in writing, in the same document as the price. is the geometry exclusive, and for how long? a distinct question from ownership. a buyer may fund a tool and still be happy for the factory to sell the product generally; another may need the shape restricted to their market. both happen. the one arrangement that causes trouble is the one where neither party said. what happens to the tool when it is idle, and when it is worn? a mould is a physical object that sits in a rack, rusts if it is not oiled, and has a finite life in shots before the cavity needs refurbishing. who stores it, who maintains it, who pays for the refurbishment, and what notice is required to move it, these are boring until the day a buyer wants the tool shipped and discovers no one agreed the answer. for the 311 specifically, we answered these by developing it ourselves: the moulds are ours, which is exactly why the geometry can be changed for the next customer who needs it changed. that is a statement about that product, not a set of standard terms, on a tool a customer funds, the answers are whatever the two parties agree, and our position is that they should be on the same page as the price rather than in somebody's memory. what this means if you are the buyer. three things follow from this account, and they are the reason it is published rather than kept as an anecdote. first, a tooled product and a catalog product are two different purchases with two different clocks. if a supplier quotes the same lead time for both, one of those numbers is wrong. second, the tooling is where a custom exit device is either right or wrong, and it is decided months before the first production order ships. that is an argument for visiting, for asking to see trial shots, and for approving a sample rather than a drawing. third (and this is the part we would rather say out loud) the 311 exists because a customer brought us a sample and we spent five months on it. the moulds are ours. that means the geometry can be changed for the next customer who needs it changed, including the center distance, which is why the 311 carries both 72mm (2-13/16") and 92mm (3-5/8") cylinder centers rather than one. a supplier who buys finished devices cannot offer that, because the mould is not theirs to alter. ## the stages to approve, and what each one actually proves a tooling program is not one approval at the end. it is a short series of them, and knowing what each stage can and cannot tell you is what stops a buyer signing off the wrong thing. the drawing: proves the intent, and nothing else. it is the cheapest place to change anything and the only place where a change costs nothing, which is the argument for spending longer here than feels comfortable. everything after this is steel. the first trial shots: proves the geometry: does it come out of the cavity, does it assemble, does the mechanism move. expect them to be imperfect, and expect them to be hand-finished. ask specifically which surfaces were touched by hand, because those are the surfaces the tool has not yet proved it can produce. the dimensional report: proves the tool against the drawing, feature by feature. this is the stage most often skipped on a hardware program and it is the one that finds the angle described above, a part can assemble on a bench and still be out of tolerance in a way that shows up on the hundredth unit. a pilot run: proves repeatability, which is a different property from correctness. parts taken from a continuous run, not selected from it, and preferably measured at the start and the end. a tool that drifts across a run is a tool that will produce a good first container and an argument on the second. the first production sample, approved and retained: both parties keep one. it is the physical reference that settles a later dispute in an afternoon instead of a fortnight, and it costs one part. none of this is exotic quality-management vocabulary. it is five checkpoints, and the reason to write them into the order at the start is that each one is cheap where it sits and expensive one stage later. that is the whole economics of tooling, and it is why five months of trial and correction is not a delay, it is the work. every product has a story behind it. this one took five months, three craftsmen and a phone call at eleven at night. 311 307 072

title: What OEM Actually Changes, and What It Does Not
subtitle: Insight
text: what oem actually changes, and what it does not putting your brand on a lock is four separate decisions, not one, and only one of them costs real money. three of them change nothing about the part. the fourth is the one that needs a mould. "do you do oem?" is the most common question our export desk receives and the least useful one, because yes is always the answer and it settles nothing. what the buyer actually needs to know is which of four different things they are asking for, since they sit at four very different points on the cost and lead-time scale. the first is packaging and marking. your logo on the box, your carton markings, your barcodes, your instruction sheet, your language. nothing about the hardware changes; what changes is what arrives on the pallet and what a customer sees on a shelf. this is the cheapest form of private label by a wide margin and for a distributor building a house brand it is often the whole of what is required. the second is branding on the part itself, your mark on the rose, the plate or the lever. this is a tooling question rather than a packaging one, because a logo on a stamped part comes from the die, but it is a small tooling question: it modifies an existing die rather than cutting a new one. decide it early: planning a mark into a first production run is much cheaper than adding one to a repeat. the third is finish. our catalog publishes polished brass, antique brass, satin nickel, satin chrome, black nickel, and satin and polished stainless, and a finish that is not on the standard list for a given model is usually a scheduling question rather than a development one, because the plating line already runs it for something else. a distinctive finish is the fastest way to a product that looks like yours and not like everyone else's, and it needs no new mould at all. the fourth is the part itself: a lever profile, a rosette shape, a plate, a backset, a case. this is where moulds and dies come in, and where the honest answer stops being a generality. if a mould exists for the form you want, we produce it. if it does not, we tool one, and tooling cost, sampling time and the minimum quantity that makes a custom run worthwhile depend entirely on the part. a rose is not a lock case. we quote those per project rather than publishing a range, because a range wide enough to be true would be too wide to be useful. what makes the fourth case workable here rather than a special project is that the tooling behind our catalog is our own. that is the difference between a factory and a trading office standing in front of one: when the die is in your building, a change of lever profile is a production decision made by people who can walk to the press. when it is not, the same request becomes an email to a third party whose schedule and quality you do not control, and the reason a buyer cannot get a straight answer on lead time is usually that the person answering does not have one either. start with what you have rather than with a specification. a physical sample is best; a drawing is nearly as good; a photograph with a dimension written on it is enough to begin. our engineering team will come back with what is required to make it, and will tell you plainly when what you have asked for is a new mould rather than a variation, because the difference between those two answers is weeks and it is better known at the start. ## what to send, for each of the four each kind of oem work starts from different material, and an inquiry that arrives with the right material gets a real answer in the first reply instead of the third. packaging and marking: your logo as a vector file rather than a screenshot; the carton marking text for each market, in the language it will be read in; your barcode numbers; the instruction sheet, or the text you want on it; and how many pieces you want in an inner box and an outer carton. on barcodes, one point that saves trouble later: the numbers belong to the brand owner, issued to you by your national numbering body. we print the numbers you give us; we cannot issue them to you, and a code borrowed from somebody else's range will eventually be rejected by a retailer's system. a mark on the part: which face it goes on, how large, and whether it is raised or recessed, because on a stamped or cast part the mark comes from the die, and the die is modified once. a drawing or a clear image of the mark at the size it will appear is enough to start. finish: a physical sample of the finish you want to match is better than any description, because two suppliers' "antique brass" can be visibly different colors. if you are specifying by code, remember that a bhma finish number needs the base metal as well as the appearance, as our article on finish codes explains. the part itself: a sample, a drawing or a dimensioned photograph, as above, and alongside it, the door preparation the part has to fit, the market it will be sold into, and a realistic quantity. the quantity is not a sales question. it is what decides whether a modified mould, a new mould or an existing catalog part is the sensible answer. ## your model number and ours private label changes the name on the product. it does not change the name on the test report, and that difference catches out buyers who sell into regulated markets. a test report or certificate names the product that was tested, by the manufacturer's model number. our own en 1125 test report, for example, covers one model, kd070/30-290, as set out on our certifications page. if that device were sold under your brand as, say, your model ex-200, an inspector holding your submittal and our report would see two different numbers and no link between them. the certificate would be genuine and would still fail to answer the question. the fix is administrative and cheap, and it should be done on the first order: keep a cross-reference sheet that maps each of your model numbers to ours, and put both on any submittal or technical file where a certificate is cited. it also protects you the other way, if a component changes on our side, the cross-reference tells you which of your products it affects. ## what does not change under private label it is worth being clear about the limits, because they are the part of oem most often assumed rather than asked about. rebranding a catalog product does not change how it performs or what it was tested to; its evidence stays tied to the model it was issued for. changing the part itself is different. a new lever profile on an existing mechanism is usually cosmetic in effect, but a changed case, bolt or mechanism is a new product for testing purposes, and anything a certificate covered has to be looked at again. our article on why the catalog is this wide describes that sequence, and our article on tooling a new exit device sets out its timeline. lead time follows the same line. a packaging or finish change runs on catalog lead time, which starts at 30 days from order confirmation. a modified die adds the modification. a new mould takes three to five months before production can begin. ## approving the sample that everything is judged against every private-label program should have one physical reference that both sides keep: a pre-production sample, approved in writing, with the finish, the mark and the packaging exactly as they will be produced. the first order is checked against it, and so is every repeat order after it. without that sample, the second order is judged against somebody's memory of the first, and small drifts in color or marking become arguments rather than measurements. ask for the sample to be sealed or labeled with the date and the order it approved, keep yours somewhere safe where it will still be found in two years, and send a new one for approval whenever anything on the specification changes. ## who owns what three things are worth settling in writing before production rather than assuming. your artwork and your barcode numbers are yours, and it is reasonable to have it written down that they are used only on your orders. moulds and dies cut for your part are the subject of their own agreement (who pays, who owns them, whether they are exclusive and what happens to them when orders stop) and our article on tooling a new exit device goes through those four questions. and exclusivity on a form or a finish is something agreed for a defined product and market, not something implied by having asked for it first. two things worth fixing before anything else, in any of the four cases. confirm the function and handing you need, because et, bk and ps are functions and not finishes and an entire order in the wrong one is unusable. and confirm the finish across every item in the set: if the lever is black, the hinges, the cylinder escutcheon and the visible screws should be black too, and mixed finishes within one door are the single most common thing we catch on a first private-label order. production lead time starts at 30 days from order confirmation; the exact date depends on the models, quantities and finishes on your order. 607 sset 70sn

title: Why the Catalog Is This Wide: 28 Years of Cutting Moulds for Other People's Doors
subtitle: Insight
text: why the catalog is this wide: 28 years of cutting moulds for other people's doors almost nothing in this range was designed by us in the abstract. a buyer somewhere could not find a part in their own market, brought us a drawing or a sample, and we cut the mould. do that since 1998 and the catalog ends up looking like a map of other people's doors. people ask why one factory carries this many different products, and the honest answer is that we did not plan most of them. a buyer in one country goes looking for a part their market takes for granted, cannot find anyone at home who still makes it, and eventually finds us and asks whether we can make it from their sample. say yes to that question for twenty-eight years and you end up with a catalog that looks less like a product strategy and more like a map of the doors other people have to fit. what makes the answer possible is that metal moulds are the thing this factory is actually good at, and they are the work our engineers like most. a buyer arrives with a drawing, or more often with the part itself in a bag. we take the dimensions from it and cut a mould, sometimes changing what is inside the case and leaving the outside alone so it drops into an existing door preparation, sometimes the reverse, because the mechanism is fine and only the visible form has to match what that market expects. a new metal mould takes three to five months. that figure surprises people who assume tooling is a manufacturing detail, and it is the reason a custom part is a commitment rather than an order: for three to five months there is nothing to show the buyer, and at the end of it the first parts come off the press and are usually not right yet. what follows is the part nobody photographs. the stamped steel components and the zinc-alloy die castings come out of their moulds and are run in together, and at the start they bind. a fit is a few degrees off; two parts that should slide against each other catch instead. so the mating angles are adjusted and the parts are run again, and again, until every component moves against the next one smoothly and the assembly does what a lock is supposed to do, which is work the same way on the ten-thousandth operation as on the first. only then does it go to batch production, and the testing does not stop there, because a thing that works on the bench is not yet a thing that works coming off a line. what the tests are depends on the product: fire tests for a fire-door device, impact tests, cycle-life tests, load and pressure tests. a panic bar and a door viewer are not asked the same questions. after our own testing, a product goes for whatever the buyer's market recognizes. for europe that is ce, and our exit devices are tested to en 1125. for north america the relevant listings are ul and ansi/bhma, and we should be precise here rather than vague: we do not hold those today. the 307 and the 311 have been submitted for testing, and until certificate numbers exist we will not imply otherwise, both ul's product iq and the bhma directory are public, a specifier can check in a minute, and a supplier caught rounding up on a certification has told that specifier everything they need to know about the rest of the datasheet. twenty-eight years of doing this, one buyer's requirement at a time, is how the range got here. the effect is that a buyer from somewhere we have never shipped to often finds the thing they need already sitting in our catalog, because someone from a neighboring market asked for it eleven years ago. we are glad when that happens. it means a problem that belonged to them is already solved, and it means the mould we cut for one buyer has gone on being useful long after that first order. what we get out of it is not only the tooling. every one of those requests taught us something about a door standard, a fixing convention or an installation habit we did not know before, and it came from the person who had to live with it. the catalog is the visible part; the education is the part that keeps the factory able to answer the next question. ## what "wide" means, counted it is easy to call a catalog wide and harder to say what that means, so here is the count for this site as it stood in september 2026: 588 entries in fifteen product families. the largest are knob locks (92 entries), lever handles (62), hardware accessories such as stops, flush bolts and viewers (63), lock cases (58), bathroom accessories (55) and panic exit devices (49). at the other end sit sliding hook locks (3), door closers (9) and deadbolts (11). that shape is not an accident, and it is worth reading the right way. the big families are the ones where every market has its own habit: a knob lock backset one country installs by default, a lock case center distance another insists on, a finish a third expects on every lever. each request added a variant rather than a new line of business. the small families are small because we are not a specialist in them. if your project turns on a door closer with a particular test rating, a closer specialist is likely to serve you better than nine entries in our catalog, and we would rather say that than stretch. ## the cost of a wide catalog, and who pays it breadth has a price, and on this site the buyer can see it. as of september 2026, 112 of those 588 entries carry no specification rows at all, and 67 have no photograph. the data is thinner than the range, because the range grew one buyer's request at a time and the paperwork for each part was written for that buyer, not for a public page. we will not close that gap by copying. a backset or a length borrowed from a similar-looking neighbor is the most plausible kind of wrong number there is, and a wrong dimension is paid for in a container, not on a page. so when an entry is missing a row, the row is missing on purpose, and the answer is a question to us: we measure the part against its drawing and reply with the number and where it came from. the other cost is codes. a wide range multiplies suffixes (finish times function times, sometimes, a door thickness) and two entries that look like the same part can differ in the one row that matters. the rule that follows is dull and saves money: order by the full code, never by a photograph or a family name, and check the one row your door depends on before the order is confirmed. ## three ways into the catalog nobody should read nearly six hundred entries. there are three faster ways in, depending on what you already have. from a model number you already buy: if you are replacing a supplier, start with their code and the dimensions that make it fit, the door preparation, the backset, the fixing centers. our article on cross-referencing a lock you already buy sets out which rows decide whether two parts are interchangeable and which are cosmetic. from the door: if you are specifying rather than replacing, start with the opening: the door type, the leaf thickness, the backset the frame allows, and whether the door is a fire door or on an escape route. those rows eliminate most of the catalog before finish or form is even discussed, which is the right order, because finish never changes what fits. from the part in your hand: if what you have is a sample, send it, or send photographs taken square-on next to a ruler, plus the door it came off. tell us the market it is sold into, because that is often what explains a dimension that looks odd to us and normal to your installers. ## when we already make something close most inquiries end in one of three places, and it helps to know which one you are heading for before you commit. the first is an exact match. we give you the model number, and the order is a catalog order: production lead time starts at 30 days from order confirmation, with the exact date set by the models, quantities and finishes involved. the second is a modification of a mould we already own. changing a lever profile, a rosette, a plate or a backset is a normal order here rather than a special project, precisely because the moulds and dies behind the catalog are ours. this is often the best answer for a buyer who needs a part to drop into an existing door preparation: keep the parts that fit, change the part that is seen. the third is a new mould, with the three to five months described above and the fitting and testing that follow it. our article on what it takes to tool a new exit device walks through that timeline and the questions to settle before the steel is cut, who pays for the mould, who owns it, and what happens to it afterwards. the judgement between the second and third is usually a judgement about what really has to match. the door preparation is a hard constraint: if the holes are already in a thousand doors, the part has to fit them. the form and finish are usually negotiable, and a buyer who can accept an existing form often saves the whole tooling timeline. so: send the drawing, or send the sample. if we already make it, we will tell you the model number and you will have it faster than anything custom. if we do not, we will tell you honestly what the mould costs in months before you commit to it, and that conversation, rather than a price list, is where most of these products started. 311 307 305 dc02
